options.label: B

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pre-tracheal fascia

Thyroid masses moves with swallowing because the thyroid gland is enclosed by the pre-tracheal fascia.

Pre-tracheal fascia encloses the thyroid gland to form its false capsule. Pretracheal fascia is attached to the larynx and this attachment is responsible for the movement of the enlarged thyroid gland on deglutition.

The ligament of Berry, also called the suspensory ligament extends from the cricoid cartilage to the thyroid. It is formed by the condensation of the pre-tracheal fascia. Its attachment prevents the thyroid gland from sinking down into the mediastinum.

Correct answer: A. Retraction of the scapula

The muscles marked in the above image are rhomboids minor and major. These muscles cause retraction of the scapula.

Rhomboids minor and major are innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve. They are supplied by the dorsal scapular artery or the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery.

Muscles involved in movements of the scapula are:

  • Protraction (forward movement): Serratus anterior and pectoralis minor are prime movers. Rhomboid muscles control the rate and range of movements. The upper part of the latissimus dorsi acts like a strap across the inferior scapular angle in protraction.
  • Retraction (backward movement): Middle trapezius and rhomboids.
  • Elevation: Trapezius, Levator scapulae.
  • Depression: Usually gravity alone is sufficient for the depression of the scapula. When required, a part of the serratus anterior, pectoralis minor, and trapezius are used.

questions.text: All of the following are t‍rue about the phrenic ner​ve except that :
questions.raw_text: All of the following are true about the phrenic nerve except that :

options.label: A
options.text: It is a purely motor nerve‍

options.label: B
options.text: It arises mainly from C4 s‍pinal nerve

options.label: C
options.text: It is formed at the latera‍l border of scalenus ante​rior

options.label: D
options.text: The right phrenic nerve pa‍sses through the vena cav​al opening

questions.correct_answer: A. It is a purely motor nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a purely motor nerve

All of the following are true about the phrenic nerve except option A as it is a mixed nerve (sensory and motor nerve).

Each phrenic nerve provides the sole motor supply to its hemidiaphragm. In its thoracic course, each phrenic nerve supplies sensory branches to the mediastinal pleura, fibrous pericardium, and parietal serous pericardium.

The phrenic nerve is a mixed nerve derived mostly from the C4 ramus and also receives contributions from the C3 and C5 ventral rami.

It is formed at the lateral border of the scalenus anterior. At the root of the neck, the right phrenic nerve runs anterior to the second part of the right subclavian artery from which it is separated by scalenus anterior muscle. The phrenic nerve lies posterior to the right subclavian vein.

The right phrenic nerve is shorter and more vertical than the left. The right phrenic nerve passes through the vena caval opening. The left phrenic nerve passes through the muscular part of the diaphragm just anterior to the central tendon.

The phrenic nerve is responsible for the referred pain which usually occurs when there is inflammation of the diaphragmatic pleura, e.g. in basal pneumonia, pleural effusions, or with irritation of the peritoneal pleura, as with a subphrenic abscess. It is frequently felt at the tip of the shoulder due to the common root of origin of the phrenic nerve and the nerves supplying the shoulder.

Correct answer: D. Colle's fascia

Colle's fascia prevents the extravasation of the urine from spreading into the thigh and anal triangle. 

Scarpa's fascia is continuous with the superficial fascia of the scrotum and becomes the Colles' fascia. In women, it continues into the labia majora and is continuous with the fascia of the perineum. Colle's fascia has the following attachments:

  • Posterior - perineal membrane. It prevents the extravasation of fluids such as blood, pus, or urine into the anal triangle. 
  • Lateral - ischiopubic rami and fascia lata along Holden's line. This line extends from the pubic tubercle laterally for 8 cm. It prevents the extravasation of fluids into the thigh. 

Option A: Camper's fascia is the superficial fatty layer of the superficial fascia of the abdomen.

Option B: Scarpa's fascia is the deep membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the abdomen.

Option C: Buck's fascia is the deep fascia of the penis 

Clinical significance:

When a urethral injury occurs, urine can extravasate into the superficial perineal pouch, penis, scrotum, labia majora and the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.text: What condition is depicted‍ by the subcutaneous veno​us circulation shown in t‌he image?
questions.raw_text: What condition is depicted by the subcutaneous venous circulation shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inferior vena caval obstruction

The given clinical scenario with the upward flow of subcutaneous venous circulation can be seen in inferior vena cava obstruction.

The level of the umbilicus is a watershed area for venous and lymphatic circulation. The systemic veins anastomose with tributaries of portal veins at the umbilicus. Normally, venous blood and lymphatics flow upwards above the plane of the umbilicus and downwards below this plane. 

  • In inferior vena cava obstruction, the blood flow in the veins of the anterior abdominal wall is completely upward.
  • In superior vena cava obstruction, the blood flow in the veins of the anterior abdominal veins is completely downward.
  • In portal hypertension with dilated abdominal veins, the blood flow is away from the umbilicus, radiating like a star from the umbilicus (caput-medusae).

Causes of superior and inferior vena caval obstruction:

Causes of SVC obstruction Causes of IVC obstruction 

 

1. Mediastinal malignancy

2. Mediastinal fibrosis

3. Retrosternal thyroid

4. Aortic aneurysm

5. Radiation fibrosis

6. Iatrogenic
  1.  Thrombosis extension
  2.  Tumor invasion
  3.  Extrinsic compression (Eg: Pregnancy, abdominal mass)
  4. Coagulopathy
  5. Sepsis, dehydration, immobility
  6. Iatrogenic

Splenic vein thrombosis is one of the prehepatic causes of portal hypertension, in which the portal venous system is affected before it enters the liver.

The muscle marked in the image is the piriformis and the clinical features are suggestive of piriformis syndrome. This occurs due to the entrapment of the sciatic nerve.

Piriformis syndrome is a clinical condition characterized by the compression of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis muscle. This can occur due to inflammation of the piriformis muscle. The patient will present with pain along the distribution of the sciatic nerve which is also known as sciatica. It is triggered by sitting for a long time or running, climbing stairs, or applying firm pressure directly over the piriformis muscle.

Early signs include pain, tingling, or numbness in the buttocks. Later it may lead to severe pain extending down the length of the sciatic nerve.

questions.text: A 12-year-old presented wi‍th fever and difficulty s​wallowing. He had swellin‌g in the marked region an​d was advised to undergo ​surgery. Post-surgery the‍ gauze continued to soak ‌with blood. Which of the ​following vessels must ha​ve been injured?
questions.raw_text: A 12-year-old presented with fever and difficulty swallowing. He had swelling in the marked region and was advised to undergo surgery. Post-surgery the gauze continued to soak with blood. Which of the following vessels must have been injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paratonsillar vein

The given image is a cadaveric specimen with the arrow pointing towards, the tonsillar fossa, and the given clinical vignette is suggestive of tonsillitis. Post tonsillectomy hemorrhage is commonly venous in origin, from the paratonsillar/ external palatine vein. 

Torrential hemorrhage can be due to injury to an aberrantly large or aberrantly placed tonsillar arterial branch of the facial artery.

Blood supply of the tonsils: 

Arterial supply:

  • The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the main supply.
  • Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery.
  • Ascending pharyngeal branch of the external carotid artery.
  • Dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery.
  • Descending palatine branches of the maxillary artery.

Venous supply:

  • Veins from the tonsils drain into paratonsillar vein which joins the common facial vein and pharyngeal venous plexus.

Types of Hemorrhage seen during/post tonsillectomy:

  • Primary hemorrhage:
    • Occurs during surgery due to injury to blood vessels.
    • Can be controlled by pressure, ligation, or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.
  • Reactionary hemorrhage:
    • It occurs within 24 hours of surgery.
    • It may be due to dislodgement of the clot, slippage of ligature, or return of blood pressure to normal.
    • It is managed by removal of clot and application of pressure or vasoconstrictor.
    • If not controlled the patient is anesthetized and hemorrhage is managed by re-exploration.
  • Secondary hemorrhage:
    • It occurs between 24 hours to 10 days (most common between 5th to 8th postoperative days).
    • It is due to sepsis and premature separation of the membrane.
    • The patient is started on IV antibiotics and if not controlled, general anesthesia is given and the bleeding vessel is electrocoagulated or ligated.

Correct answer: B. 4

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral medullary syndrome/Wallenberg syndrome. This may result from a stroke affecting the ipsilateral (right-sided, in this case) vertebral artery marked as '4' in the image above.

Lateral medullary syndrome: The clinical findings correspond to the neuroanatomical structures affected in the lateral portion of the medulla:

  • Descending tract and nucleus of CN V (trigeminal)- loss of pain and sensation over the ipsilateral half of face.
  • Inferior cerebellar peduncle – ipsilateral ataxia (gait and limb)
  • Lateral spinothalamic tract – loss of pain and temperature sensation over the contralateral half of the body. 
  • IX and X CN - ipsilateral paralysis of palate, vocal cord, diminished gag reflex giving rise to dysphagia, dysarthria.
  • Vestibular nucleus - Nystagmus, diplopia, vertigo, nausea
  • Descending sympathetic tract – ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis).

The lateral medullary syndrome may also occur as a consequence of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) stroke. PICA is a branch of the vertebral artery.

Correct answer: C. Left colic and middle colic arteries

The middle and left colic arteries contribute to the formation of the marginal artery of Drummond at the splenic flexure. The splenic flexure (Griffith's point) is a watershed area of the colon which is more prone to ischemia. 

The anastomotic vessel that runs in the mesentery along the inner margin of the colon is called the marginal artery of Drummond. From this artery, numerous small branches are given to the large bowel. It is formed by:

  • Branches of superior mesenteric artery - middle colic, right colic, and ileocolic arteries
  • Branches of inferior mesenteric artery - left colic, sigmoid, and superior rectal arteries

When ischemia occurs at Griffith's point, the blood supply in this region is augmented by another arterial loop called the inner arterial arc (of Riolan). This arc connects the main trunk of the middle colic artery with the ascending branch of the left colic artery.

Note: Sudeck's point is another watershed area present at the rectosigmoid junction. The sigmoid artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery at this site.

questions.text: Arrange the following even‍ts of embryonal developme​nt during the second to t‌he fourth week in the seq​uence in which they occur​: Formation of the neural‍ plate Formation of the n‌otochordal process Format​ion of the primitive stre​ak Notochordal plate sepa‍rates from endoderm to fo​rm true notochord Formati‍on of the notochordal pla‌te
questions.raw_text:
Arrange the following events of embryonal development during the second to the fourth week in the sequence in which they occur:

  1. Formation of the neural plate
  2. Formation of the notochordal process
  3. Formation of the primitive streak 
  4. Notochordal plate separates from endoderm to form true notochord
  5. Formation of the notochordal plate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3, 2, 1, 5, 4

The correct sequence in which the above events occur is 3, 2, 1, 5, 4: Formation of the primitive streak, notochordal process, neural plate, notochordal plate, and finally, the notochordal plate separates from the endoderm to form the true notochord.

The primitive streak is formed around day 15. This is followed by the formation of definitive endoderm and the formation of mesoderm.

This mesoderm extends cranially to form the notochordal process around day 17. Meanwhile, the mesoderm present lateral to midline gets divided into paraxial, intermediate, and lateral plate mesoderm. The lateral plate mesoderm splits into two layers- somatic mesoderm and splanchnic mesoderm, separated by the intraembryonic coelom.

Formation of the neural plate begins between days 19 and 20. The cranial and caudal parts of the neural plate represent the future brain and spinal cord, respectively.

The notochordal process fuses transiently with the endoderm to form a notochordal plate after day 20. Finally, around day 22, the notochordal plate separates from the endoderm to form a solid, definitive notochord.

Vesicoureteric junction is the narrowest part of the ureter.

The ureter is constricted at 5 places:

  4. Vesico-ureteric junction
  5. At its opening in the lateral angle of the trigone

These are regarded as surgical constrictions of the ureter. However, the anatomical constrictions are only three of them (1, 2, and 4).

1. Alveolar duct

2. Lobar bronchi

3. Terminal bronchiole

4. Alveolar sac

5. Segmental bronchi

6. Respiratory bronchiole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2→5→3→6→1→4

The following is a sequence of the intrapulmonary anatomy from proximal to distal: Trachea → Main Bronchi → Lobar Bronchi → Segmental Bronchi → Terminal Bronchiole → Respiratory Bronchiole → Alveolar Duct → Alveolar Sac → Alveoli

According to Weibel’s model, the respiratory tract is divided into 23 generations, consisting of conducting (upper 16 generations) and respiratory zones (lower 7 generations). It begins at the trachea (designated as zero) and ends with alveoli (last generation).

The epithelial layer transitions from a pseudostratified columnar layer in the upper airways (trachea, bronchi) with submucosal secretory glands to a cuboidal epithelium (bronchioles), and finally, to a flat squamous epithelium in the alveoli, facilitating efficient gas exchange in the respiratory zone. 

As we progress downward, the following changes occur in the structure of the airways: 

  • The number of mucus-secreting cells/secretory glands decreases.
  • The amount of cartilage in the airway wall decreases.  
  • The quantity of smooth muscles increases from trachea to terminal bronchioles but decreases from respiratory bronchioles to alveoli.
  • The amount of dead space decreases.
  • The number of cilia decreases such that they are absent in alveoli.
  • The surface area and volume progressively increase, facilitating easy gas exchange.
  • The number of flat squamous cells (Type 1 pneumocytes) increases.

The marked structure is the falciform ligament of the liver. It is an embryological derivative of ventral mesentery, which itself arises from septum transversum.

  2. Ligaments of the liver: all ligaments of the liver except ligamentum teres are derived from the ventral mesentery. This includes falciform ligament, right and left triangular ligaments, and coronary ligaments. 

Dorsal mesentery connects the abdominal organs to the posterior abdominal wall. It runs from the lower end of the esophagus to the cloacal region of the hindgut. Depending on the abdominal organ to which it is attached, it has multiple regions: dorsal mesogastrium, mesoduodenum, mesentery proper (to the small intestine), mesocolon, mesoappendix, mesosigmoid, and mesorectum. Couinaud classification is the commonly used classification of the liver. It divides the liver into eight segments. It is based on the distribution of portal venous branches in the liver parenchyma. Each segment has its own dual vascular inflow, biliary drainage, and lymphatic drainage.

The left lobe is composed of the left lateral segment (Couinaud’s segments II and III) and the left medial segment (segment IV). The right lobe is composed of segments V, VI, VII, and VIII, with segments V and VIII making up the right anterior lobe and segments VI and VII making up the right posterior lobe.

Segment I corresponds to the caudate lobe of the liver and segment IV corresponds to the quadrate lobe of the liver. Segment IV is divided into segments IVa and IVb.

All the Couinaud segments are supplied by the portal vein and hepatic artery for the arterial supply. Venous drainage of Couinaud segments II to VIII drained into right and left hepatic veins except for segment I (Caudate lobe) which drains directly into the Inferior vena cava. All segments drained lymph into respective right and left hepatic ducts.

Correct answer: B. Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

During the contraction of the skeletal muscle, the Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Option B is correct.

Excitation-contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fiber (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle.

The steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle are as follows:

  • Motor-neuron discharge causes the release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate, which binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
  • This causes increased Na+ and K+ conductance in the endplate membrane, leading to the generation of end-plate potential, which is a local potential.
  • When the local endplate potential reaches a threshold for the muscle fiber, an action potential is generated.
  • The generated action potential passes inward through the T tubules, leading to the spread of depolarisation.
  • The depolarization of the muscle fiber causes the release of Ca2+ from terminal cisterns of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion to thick and thin filaments.
  • The calcium released, binds to troponin C, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin.
  • The formation of cross-linkages between actin and myosin and sliding of thin on thick filaments causes contraction of the skeletal muscle.

Steps in relaxation:

  • The cytoplasmic calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, by the action of SERCA (sarcoplasmic endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase).
  • Once the calcium concentration is lowered, the interaction between actin and myosin ceases, and the muscle relaxes. 
Other options:
 
Option A: Incorrect - Ca2+ is not released from mitochondria. It is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Option C: Incorrect - Extracellular calcium levels play an important role in muscle contraction. When there is a decrease in extracellular calcium as in hypocalcemia, the voltage-gated sodium channels are activated, which causes sodium influx. The increased intracellular sodium concentration causes sustained depolarization, which may lead to tetany.
Option D: Incorrect - Voltage-gated calcium channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum are activated by a depolarizing stimulus, which causes the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increased calcium concentration will eventually lead to muscle contraction.

Reabsorption of sodium in different parts of the nephron are:

  • Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): 
    • Nearly 60% of the filtered sodium is reabsorbed in the PCT. Solutes mainly absorbed in the proximal tubule are sodium, chloride, bicarbonate, phosphate, lactate, glucose, amino acids etc. 
    • In early PCT, the main sodium channels used for reabsorption are Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT), Na+-H+ exchanger, Na+-amino acid cotransporter, Na+-phosphate cotransporter, etc. 
    • In distal PCT, due to high chloride concentration in the lumen, it favors NaCl reabsorption, driven by Cl− gradient. 
    • The total solute and water reabsorption are proportional to each other. Thus, the entire proximal tubule also reabsorbs nearly 60% of the filtered water (isosmotic reabsorption). 
  • Loop of Henle:
    • The thin descending limb has no active transport of Na+ outside the lumen but the loop is permeable to water, making the tubular fluid hypertonic.
    • A thick ascending limb reabsorbs nearly 30% of the Na+ by Na–2Cl–K cotransporter, an example of secondary active transport. This loop is impermeable to water. Since some of the solutes are reabsorbed and water is not reabsorbed, it dilutes the tubular fluid. Other ions like Ca 2+, and Mg2+ are also absorbed here. 
  • Distal convoluted tubule: Approximately 7% of the filtered load of sodium chloride is reabsorbed in the early distal tubule. This occurs due to the presence of sodium chloride co-transporter. Even this segment dilutes the tubular fluid as it is impermeable to water. 
  • Cortical collecting tubule: The remaining 3% of the filtered Na+ is absorbed via ENaCs (epithelial sodium channels) in this duct.  This portion is regulated by aldosterone to maintain homeostasis in Na+ balance.

Clinical aspect: 

i) Barrter syndrome is a congenital renal disorder due to mutation in Na–2Cl–K cotransporter, ROMK K+ channel, ClC–Kb Cl− channel, or barttin. It is characterized by chronic urinary Na+ loss, with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and alkalosis.

ii) Gitelman syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting the sodium chloride co-transporter in the distal tubules, leading to decreased sodium chloride reabsorption. 

iii) Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder where mutation results in increased activity of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the distal and collecting tubules. This leads to increased reabsorption of sodium and water causing hypertension and metabolic alkalosis.

questions.text: The following process wher‌e transportation is along​ the concentration gradie‍nt is an example of:
questions.raw_text: The following process where transportation is along the concentration gradient is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facilitated diffusion

The given image shows a glucose transporter that transports glucose from a higher concentration to a lower concentration. This is an example of facilitated diffusion. 

When carrier proteins help in the movement of substances in the direction of their chemical or electrical gradients (downhill movement), no energy input is required and the process is called facilitated diffusion.

Glucose transporters also referred to as GLUTs, are transport proteins in the cell membrane responsible for the transfer of glucose into the cells by facilitated diffusion. Facilitated diffusion involves the passage of molecules or ions inside the cell membrane by binding to a carrier/ transport protein. 

For example, insulin stimulates glucose entry into the cells via facilitated diffusion by increasing the number of glucose transporters (GLUTs) in the cell membrane. This type of insulin-dependent glucose transport via GLUT 4 is observed in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and adipose tissues. 

Other options - 

Option A. Simple diffusion - It is along the concentration gradient but is not carrier-mediated. In the cell, examples of molecules that can use simple diffusion to travel in and out of the cell membrane are water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen. They pass directly through the cell membrane without energy along the concentration gradient.

Option C. Primary active transport - It is a form of cellular transport requiring energy in the form of hydrolysis of ATP to ship and transfer molecules against a membrane with chemical or electrical gradient differences. The important examples of primary active transport include sodium-potassium ATPase, proton pump, and calcium ATPase.

Option D. In secondary active transport, the active transport of sodium is coupled to the transport of other substances. Examples include symport of sodium with glucose (luminal membranes of mucosal cells in the small intestine), sodium-potassium ATPase, and Ca2+ in the cardiac muscle cells.

questions.raw_text: In the following pressure-volume loop diagram of left ventricle, the mitral valve will close at the point:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Point 2

The closure of the mitral valve corresponds to point 2, which marks the beginning of the isovolumetric contraction phase.

 The pressure-volume curve represents the changes in volume and pressure in the left ventricle during a single cardiac cycle. The relationship between ventricular pressure (Y-axis) and volume (X-axis) throughout the cardiac cycle is represented by this loop.

  • Point 1 - Mitral valve opens
  • Point 2 - Mitral valve closes
  • Point 3 - Aortic valve opens
  • Point 4 - Aortic valve closes

Phase I: Period of filling:  

  • In the given diagram, the period of filling lasts from point 1 to point 2.
  • At point A, the volume of blood present in the left ventricle is the end-systolic volume which corresponds to about 50 ml. It is at this point that the mitral valve opens and the venous blood flows into the left ventricle from the left atrium.
  • At point B, the end of the period of filling—the amount of blood present in the left ventricle is called the end-diastolic volume which corresponds to about 120 ml. It is at this point that the mitral valve closes.

Phase II: Period of isovolumic contraction:

  • In the given diagram, the period of isovolumetric contraction lasts from point 2 to point 3.
  • At point B, the mitral valve closes and the volume of the ventricle does not change as all the valves are closed. However, the pressure inside the ventricle continues to rise.
  • At point C the ventricular pressure increases to become equal to the pressure in the aorta (80 mm Hg) and then the aortic valve opens.

Phase III: Period of ejection

  • In the given diagram, the period of ejection lasts from point 3 to point 4.
  • At point C, the aortic valve opens and the volume of the ventricle decreases as the blood flows out of the ventricle into the aorta.
  • The systolic pressure continues to rise as the ventricle contracts.
  • At point D the aortic valve closes.

Phase IV: Period of isovolumic relaxation

  • In the given diagram, the period of relaxation lasts from point 4 to point 1.
  • At point D, the aortic valve closes and the ventricular pressure falls back to the diastolic pressure level. 
  • This decrease in intraventricular pressure occurs without any change in volume.
  • At point A, the ventricle now has an end-systolic volume of 50 ml of blood similar to the beginning of the cycle.

questions.text: A normal healthy adult par‌ticipated in a respirator​y study that was conducte‍d to understand the respi​ratory functions. In the ‍upright position, an incr​ease in all of the follow‌ing parameters can be see​n with respect to the bas​e of the lungs except?
questions.raw_text: A normal healthy adult participated in a respiratory study that was conducted to understand the respiratory functions. In the upright position, an increase in all of the following parameters can be seen with respect to the base of the lungs except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ventilation-perfusion ratio

In the upright position, an increase in the ventilation-perfusion ratio (V/Q ratio) is not seen with respect to the base of the lungs. At the base of the lung, the V/Q ratio is decreased. 

V/Q ratio is the ratio of alveolar ventilation (V) to pulmonary blood flow (Q) for the lungs at rest. The average value of the V/Q ratio throughout the lungs is 0.8. When this ratio is mismatched, it can cause CO2 retention (when solely, ventilation is impaired) or lowered arterial O2 (when perfusion is impaired). 

Normally, in the upright position, the V/Q ratio in the normal lungs markedly undergoes changes from the apex to the base due to the effect of gravity as shown below - 

 

At the base of the lung:

Both ventilation and perfusion increase since the flow is towards gravity.

Increased ventilation is due to the increase in intrapleural pressure compared to the apex, thereby making the intrapulmonary intrapleural pressure difference less at the base. Thus, due to this low-pressure difference, the lung is less expanded compared to the apex. This makes the ventilation per unit volume rise as the lung expansion is relatively small. 

The alveolar pressure also decreases thus reducing the compression of the vessels and increasing the pulmonary blood flow at the base. An increase in perfusion is more than an increase in ventilation, i.e., denominator increases. Hence, the ratio decreases.

At the apex (against gravity):

Both ventilation and perfusion decrease since the flow is against gravity.

The reason for decreased ventilation is that at the start of inspiration, intrapleural pressure is more negative thus making the intrapulmonary intrapleural pressure difference increase at the apex. The apex is above the level of the heart and capillary pressure at the apex is close to atmospheric pressure thus decreasing the blood flow. But, a decrease in perfusion is higher than a decrease in ventilation. Hence, the ratio increases.

options.label: B
options.text: Root value of the reflex i‌s L5 - S2

options.label: C
options.text: It is a monosynaptic stret‌ch reflex

options.label: D
options.text: Efferent is acted upon γ-m‌otor neurons of the hamst​ring muscles

questions.correct_answer: C. It is a monosynaptic stretch reflex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is a monosynaptic stretch reflex

From the given scenario, the resident is performing a knee jerk reflex (patellar reflex) on this patient. 

Knee jerk or patellar reflex is elicited by tapping the patellar tendon resulting in contraction of the quadriceps muscle. It is an example of a deep tendon reflex or myotatic stretch reflex as stretching the muscle causes reflex contraction. 

The reflex arc in the knee jerk reflex consists of only one synapse between afferents and efferents. Hence, it is also an example of a monosynaptic reflex. 

Reflex arc of knee jerk reflex -  

Tapping the tendon causes a stretch of the muscle spindle which is present within the muscle. The muscle spindle is a sensory proprioceptor responsible for identifying the length of the muscle fibers. The Ia afferent sensory fibers in the muscle spindles are activated in response to the stretch. These Ia afferent fibers go to the spinal cord at the dorsal root ganglia and stimulate the alpha-motor neurons. This results in the contraction of the muscle that was initially stretched. The neurotransmitter at the central synapse is glutamate.

The femoral nerve L2-L4 mediates the patellar reflex.

 

Clinical aspect: 

  • Brisk, hyperactive deep tendon reflexes are seen in upper motor neuron lesions affecting the descending spinal tracts like the corticospinal tract. 
  • Hypoactive or absent reflexes are seen in lower motor neuron lesions or the lesions affecting the components of the reflex arc. Absent reflexes can be seen in diabetes, deep sleep, coma, nerve block, spinal anesthesia etc. 
  • The pendular knee jerk, in which tapping the patellar tendon results in to-and-fro movements of the limb is seen in cerebellar lesions. The increased swinging occurs due to hypotonia of both flexors and extensors leading to a lack of restraint on each other.

questions.text: Which of the following has‌ the lowest oxygen concen​tration in fetal circulat‍ion?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following has the lowest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior vena cava

Among the fetal blood vessels mentioned above, the superior vena cava (SVC) has the lowest oxygen concentration. It carries deoxygenated blood from the upper part of the body to the right atrium.

The pO2 of SVC is about 12-14 mmHg whereas the pO2 of the umbilical artery is about 20-25 mm Hg. This is because the SVC carries only deoxygenated blood, whereas the umbilical artery carries a mix of oxygenated blood from the ascending aorta and deoxygenated blood from systemic circulation.

Fetal circulation:

The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein. From the umbilical vein, 50% of the blood enters the hepatic circulation and 50% bypasses the liver to enter the inferior vena cava. Thus, the inferior vena cava, which also carries blood from hepatic veins, kidneys, and from lower extremities, carries a mixture of deoxygenated and oxygenated blood. So, the highest percentage of oxygen in fetal circulation is in the umbilical vein, followed by the inferior vena cava. 

The blood then enters the heart via the right atrium. The right atrium also receives purely deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava. This blood then enters the pulmonary artery. Since fetal lungs are collapsed, most of the blood enters the descending aorta via ductus arteriosus and is then distributed to the body. 

Finally, some of this blood from the aorta and the lower parts of the body is pumped back to the placenta via umbilical arteries. Hence, they contain a mix of both oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

The lung function of a patient is tested using a spirometer, and the following recording is noted. The technician looks at the graph and enters the following values in the report.

Tidal volume (TV) is the amount of air that moves into the lungs with each inspiration or the amount of air that moves out with each expiration during quiet breathing. In this patient it is 0.5L. The normal values are 500-750 mL.

Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) is the air inspired with a maximal inspiratory effort in excess of the tidal volume. In this patient, it is 6-3L = 3L. The normal values are around 2L.

Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is the volume expelled by an active expiratory effort after passive expiration. In this patient it is 2.5-1.5 = 1L. The normal value is around 1L.

Inspiratory capacity (IC) is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level. It can be calculated as TV+IRV which is 0.5L + 3L= 3.5L. The normal value is around 2.5L.

Expiratory capacity (EC) is the maximum amount of air expired after a normal inspiration. It is calculated as TV+ERV, which is 0.5L + 1L = 1.5 L. Normal value is around 1.5L

Vital capacity (VC) refers to the maximum amount of air expired after full inspiration. It is calculated as TV+IRV+ERV. In this patient it is 0.5+ 3+1 =4.5L. The normal value is around 3.5L.

Other important lung values:

The forced vital capacity (FVC), is the largest amount of air that can be expired after a maximal inspiratory effort.

Forced expiratory volume in the first second, FEV1, is the fraction of the vital capacity expired during the first second. 

Respiratory minute volume (RVV) is a measurement of the amount of air that enters the lungs per minute. It is calculated as respiratory rate X tidal volume.

Maximal voluntary respiration (MVV), is the largest volume of gas that can be moved into and out of the lungs in 1 min by voluntary effort.

Total lung capacity is the total volume of the lung. It can be calculated by adding tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, and residual volume. Normal total lung capacity is around 5L.

Correct answer: D. Iodide trapping

Iodide trapping (iodide uptake) is not catalyzed by thyroid peroxidase. Oxidation, organification, and coupling are catalyzed by it.  

Steps in synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormone: 

  • Iodide uptake: The basolateral sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) actively takes up I- (iodide) from the circulation into the follicular cells. The process of concentrating iodide in the cell is known as iodide trapping. Iodide is then transported into the colloid through a pendrin (chloride-iodide) transporter.
  • Thyroglobulin synthesis: Thyroglobulin (Tg), is a large glycoprotein rich in tyrosine residues. It is synthesized by the thyrocytes and secreted into colloid.
  • Iodination of thyroglobulin: This is regulated by the thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzyme. TPO has three functions:

Glucose enters beta cells of the pancreas via GLUT-2 receptors. This ATP causes the closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels and hence depolarization. This leads to opening voltage-gated calcium channels and Ca2+ influx. This stimulates the fusion of the insulin-containing vesicles with the cell membrane and the secretion of insulin into the extracellular fluid by exocytosis.

Whenever hypertonic saline is added to the extracellular fluid (ECF), the extracellular osmolarity increases. It causes osmosis of water out of the cells into the extracellular compartment. Whenever hypotonic saline is added to ECF, the osmolarity of ECF decreases. Osmolarity decreases in both the compartments.

  • x descent corresponds to the atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.
  • v wave represents atrial filling during ventricular systole and peaks at the second heart sound.
  • y descent represents passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after tricuspid valve opening.

questions.raw_text: A normal healthy adult participated in a respiratory study that was conducted to understand the respiratory functions. In the upright position, an increase in all of the following parameters can be seen with respect to the base of the lungs except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ventilation-perfusion ratio

In the upright position, an increase in the ventilation-perfusion ratio (V/Q ratio) is not seen with respect to the base of the lungs. At the base of the lung, the V/Q ratio is decreased. 

V/Q ratio is the ratio of alveolar ventilation (V) to pulmonary blood flow (Q) for the lungs at rest. The average value of the V/Q ratio throughout the lungs is 0.8. When this ratio is mismatched, it can cause CO2 retention (when solely, ventilation is impaired) or lowered arterial O2 (when perfusion is impaired). 

Normally, in the upright position, the V/Q ratio in the normal lungs markedly undergoes changes from the apex to the base due to the effect of gravity as shown below - 

At the base of the lung:

Both ventilation and perfusion increase since the flow is towards gravity.

Increased ventilation is due to the increase in intrapleural pressure compared to the apex, thereby making the intrapulmonary intrapleural pressure difference less at the base. Thus, due to this low-pressure difference, the lung is less expanded compared to the apex. This makes the ventilation per unit volume rise as the lung expansion is relatively small. 

The alveolar pressure also decreases thus reducing the compression of the vessels and increasing the pulmonary blood flow at the base. An increase in perfusion is more than an increase in ventilation, i.e., denominator increases. Hence, the ratio decreases.

At the apex (against gravity):

Both ventilation and perfusion decrease since the flow is against gravity.

The reason for decreased ventilation is that at the start of inspiration, intrapleural pressure is more negative thus making the intrapulmonary intrapleural pressure difference increase at the apex. The apex is above the level of the heart and capillary pressure at the apex is close to atmospheric pressure thus decreasing the blood flow. questions.text: An elderly patient was dia‌gnosed with ischemic hear‍t disease and was started‍ on beta-blockers. Howeve‌r, the patient continued ‌to have symptoms despite ‌it's use. questions.raw_text: An elderly patient was diagnosed with ischemic heart disease and was started on beta-blockers. However, the patient continued to have symptoms despite it's use. He was then started on ivabradine. This drug improves the symptoms of angina by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreasing the oxygen demand

Ivabradine decreases the automaticity in the sinoatrial node and thus reduces the heart rate. This reduction in the heart rate decreases the myocardial oxygen demand.

The oxygen requirement of the heart mainly depends on the work done by the heart. This work mainly depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance. An increase in these parameters will increase the oxygen requirement of the heart.

Important determinants of cardiac output are:

Stroke volume- It is the amount of blood pumped out of the heart during each heartbeat. This stroke volume increases whenever, there is increased venous return to the heart, increased end-diastolic volume (preload), and increased contractility. Contractility further depends on the initial length of the cardiac muscle fiber and the autonomic innervation.

Heart rate- Increased heart rate increases the cardiac output which in turn increases the oxygen requirement. Heart rate is controlled primarily by the autonomic nerves, with sympathetic stimulation increasing the rate and parasympathetic stimulation decreasing the rate.

Afterload- The tension at which the load is lifted is called afterload. As the afterload increases, the heart has to work more in order to pump blood to the organs. This in turn results in increased oxygen requirement. It is dependent on the peripheral resistance. 

Drugs used in the management of angina either decrease the work done by the heart or increases the blood flow to the heart.

  • Nitrates- They increase the cGMP and cause venodilation. It mainly results in an increase in venous capacitance and a decrease in the ventricular preload. They might also increase coronary flow in some areas and in variant anginas.
  • Calcium channel blockers- Blocking the calcium channels leads to the relaxation of vascular smooth muscles and decreased impulses in the conduction system. This leads to decreased peripheral resistance, decreased blood pressure, decreased contractility, decreased heart rate, and decreased oxygen requirement of the heart.
  • Beta-blockers- They decrease the oxygen requirement by decreasing the heart rate, blood pressure, and contractility. Some drugs like carvedilol and nebivolol also cause vasodilation.

Newer antianginal drugs

  • Ranolazine- It inhibits the late sodium current and reduces the intracellular calcium concentration. It reduces diastolic tension, cardiac contractility, and work.
  • Trimetazidine- inhibits the fatty acid oxidation in the myocardium. It decreases the oxygen requirement of the heart.
  • Ivabradine- decreases the heart rate and decreases oxygen requirement.
  • Fasudil- It is a Rho kinase inhibitor. It is useful in coronary vasospasm.

Resting membrane potential (RMP) is the difference in the electrical potentials between the cytoplasm of the cell and the extracellular space.

The agglutination test in image 2 corresponds to the AB-positive blood group. The AB-positive blood group is the universal recipient type. 

Blood typing or blood matching is done before transfusions to avoid incompatibility. Red blood cells (RBC) are first separated from plasma and diluted with saline solution for an agglutination test. Anti-A and anti-B agglutinins are added to different portions. If RBCs are clumped/agglutinated, then an antigen-antibody reaction has occurred.

Antigens A and B are seen on the surfaces of the red blood cells. Depending on inheritance, people have one or both on the surface of their cells. When neither of them is present, the blood type is O. Based on the antigens present, blood is classified into four main types: O (OO), A (OA/AA), B (OB/BB), and AB. 

When the A or B agglutinins are absent in the body, corresponding anti-agglutinins (anti-A or anti-B) are found in the plasma. Those with AB blood group have no circulating anti-agglutinins and do not develop transfusion reactions due to ABO incompatibility. Therefore, people with type AB blood are called universal recipients. They are also considered universal plasma donors.

Rh type system is also essential for blood transfusion. The difference with the A-B-O system is that the antibodies to Rh antigen in people without Rh antigen occur after exposure and not spontaneously.

questions.text: What is the next step in e‌xcitation-contraction cou‍pling after the power str‍oke in skeletal muscle co‌ntraction?
questions.raw_text: What is the next step in excitation-contraction coupling after the power stroke in skeletal muscle contraction?

options.label: B
options.text: Cessation of calcium relea‌se from sarcoplasm

options.label: D
options.text: Attachment of ATP to myosi‌n head

questions.correct_answer: D. Attachment of ATP to myosin head
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Attachment of ATP to myosin head

In excitation-contraction coupling, the next step after the power stroke is the attachment of ATP to the myosin head. 

Muscle contraction occurs by sliding the thin filament over the thick filament. The sequence of events is as follows: 

  • Troponin I is bound to actin and tropomyosin. In a resting muscle, it covers the sites where actin interacts with myosin heads. The myosin head contains a tightly bound adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and an inorganic phosphate (Pi).
  • Following an action potential, Calcium ions (Ca2+) are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and cytosolic Ca2+ is increased. Simultaneously Ca2+ influx also happens through the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
  • The free Ca2+ binds with troponin C. This binding will weaken the troponin I interaction with actin and exposes the actin-binding site for myosin.
  • This results in the formation of myosin-actin cross-bridges.
  • The cross-bridge between the head of myosin and the active site of actin causes a conformational change in the head. This leads to the power stroke, which moves the thin filament relative to the thick filament. 
  • A new ATP molecule binds to the free site on myosin. The ATP is further hydrolyzed to ADP and phosphate ions. The binding of the new ATP molecule to the free site on myosin causes detachment of the head of myosin from actin. 
  • This causes a re-cocking of myosin head which completes the cycle.

Correct answer: B. Alpha-ketoglutarate deydrogenase

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of arsenic toxicity. Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (AKG) of Kreb's cycle is inhibited by this toxin, arsenite (inorganic arsenic salt).

α-Ketoglutarate is a rate-determining intermediate in Kreb's cycle. It has a crucial role in cellular energy metabolism as it acts as a precursor of glutamate and glutamine and promotes protein synthesis.

Alpha-ketoglutarate undergoes oxidative decarboxylation to form succinyl-CoA and CO2 with the help of the multienzyme complex, AKG dehydrogenase. This enzyme complex requires the cofactors, thiamin diphosphate, lipoate, NAD+, flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), and coenzyme A.

Arsenite inhibits this decarboxylation reaction and causes the substrate, α-ketoglutarate, to accumulate. 

Arsenic toxicity is either due to inhalation of toxic arsenic gas or chronic consumption of foods cooked in contaminated well water. It presents with malaise, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, hemoglobinuria, and renal failure. There may be hemorrhagic gastroenteritis, hypovolemic shock, and cardiovascular manifestations such as QT prolongation, polymorphous ventricular tachycardia, and congestive cardiomyopathy. Mees lines is a common dermatologic manifestation characterized by transverse white striae on the nail.

Arsenic toxicity is detected by measuring the 24-hour urine excretion of arsenic.

questions.raw_text: An undernourished child is brought for consultation. You prescribe a mineral supplement that is absorbed by the mechanism shown in the image below. Identify the supplement.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iron

The given image shows iron absorption and transport from a duodenal enterocyte into the blood, hence the mineral supplement prescribed can be identified as an iron supplement.

The following image shows in detail, the absorption of iron from a duodenal enterocyte.

Dietary iron is available in two forms - heme and non-heme iron. Initially, the ferric non-heme iron is reduced to ferrous iron by duodenal cytochrome B (ferric reductase) or by vitamin C. The reduced ferrous iron is then transferred into the enterocyte by DMT 1 (divalent metal transporter). 

Heme iron moves into the cytoplasm with the help of transporters. Here, it is metabolized to release ferrous iron, which then follows the same pathway as non-heme iron.

Once inside the enterocyte, it can either get stored as ferritin or transferred across the basolateral membrane by ferroportin. In the plasma, iron is transported in the Fe3+ form bound to transferrin, which is a transport protein. Hephaestin is a ferroxidase that oxidizes Fe2+ to Fe3+ before it is transported.

Hepcidin, a protein secreted from the liver plays a major role in the regulation of iron absorption. When the body’s iron stores are adequate it downregulates the expression of ferroportin and thereby iron absorption too. Thus, iron is trapped in the intestinal cells which is eventually sloughed off. Hepcidin also inhibits the release of iron from macrophages by binding to ferroportin. High hepcidin levels are seen in systemic inflammation and low hepcidin levels are seen in hemochromatosis.

Iron is an important component of

  • Hemoglobin
  • Myoglobin
  • Cytochrome P450 groups of enzymes
  • Components of the electron transport chain
  • Ribonucleotide reductase

Obesity, starvation or anorexia, hypogonadism, Addison's syndrome, and immobilization are associated with low BMR.

BMR is the energy required by an awake individual during rest. It is the minimum energy required to carry out vital functions of the body such as respiration, circulation, etc. 

It is calculated using oxygen consumption, calorific value (energy produced by 1 liter of oxygen), and surface area.

BMR is dependent on various factors:

  • Men have more BMR than women of the same body weight and age because women’s bodies contain proportionally more adipose tissue and fewer muscles. 
  • Elderly people have less BMR as the muscle tissue gets infiltrated with fat as age advances.
  • Low environmental temperature is associated with high BMI.
  • Exercise increases BMR.
  • The thyroid hormone has a direct role in increasing BMR.

The correctly matched option is 1-D, 2-C, 3-B, 4-A.

Rothera’s test by nitroprusside reagent is a specific test used to detect whether acetone or acetoacetate is present in the given sample of urine. A purple ring at the junction of two liquids indicates a positive test. Rothera's test does not detect β-hydroxybutyrate.  

The other test used for the purpose of detecting acetoacetate only is the ferric chloride test. It shows a burgundy red color that is graded from +1 to +4. False-positive results occur with drugs like salicylates and phenols. 

The image below shows the purple ring formed by a positive Rothera test.

 

Benedict's test is a test commonly used in the follow-up of diabetics for the detection of glucose in urine (glucosuria). It uses Benedict's reagent containing sodium carbonate, copper sulfate, and sodium citrate. Reducing sugars (containing a free aldehyde/ keto group) will reduce Benedict's reagent. Examples include glucose, fructose, and lactose.

The test is a semi-quantitative test. The blue color indicates no reducing sugar.

Hay's test is used for the detection of bile salts in urine. Normally, bile salts (sodium salts of taurocholic acid and glycocholic acid) are not present in urine. Thus, positive Hay's test indicates an obstructive pathology in the biliary system, leading to the backflow of bile into the circulation. This obstruction may be associated with either obstructive jaundice or hepatic jaundice.

Ehrlich's test is used to determine urinary and fecal urobilinogen. 

Porphobilinogens form a red aldehyde compound with Ehrlich reagent, which is insoluble in chloroform. A red color remaining after chloroform extraction is indicative of porphobilinogens. This test is positive in acute intermittent porphyria and hemolytic jaundice. It is negative in hepatic jaundice (later stages) and obstructive jaundice. The earliest sign of recovery in obstructive jaundice is the re-appearance of urobilinogen in urine.

Ketone bodies are not utilized in the liver because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase.

The above clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis characterized by excess production of ketone bodies. The liver cannot utilize the ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone) because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase (also called succinyl CoA acetoacetyl CoA transferase).

Ketone bodies are synthesized in the liver mitochondria (by ketogenesis) and transported in the blood to the peripheral tissues. Here they are utilized by the following steps:

  1. β-hydroxybutyrate (the most predominant ketone body) is oxidized to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase producing NADH.
  2. Acetoacetate is then activated to acetoacetyl CoA by transferring a CoA molecule from succinyl CoA by succinyl CoA-acetoacetyl CoA transferase (thiophorase).
  3. Acetoacetyl CoA is cleaved into two acetyl CoA molecules by thiolase and oxidized into CO2 by the TCA cycle.

When higher than normal ketone bodies are present in the blood or urine, it is called ketonemia or ketonuria, respectively. The overall condition is called ketosis. The metabolism of free fatty acids to produce ketone bodies is exaggerated in pathologic states such as starvation and diabetes mellitus, thus causing ketosis. The continued buffering and excretion of ketone bodies deplete the alkali reserve, causing ketoacidosis.

questions.raw_text: You are studying the visual pigment cycle in the physiology lab. Identify the substance that converts cis-retinal to trans-retinal.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rhodopsin

The substance that converts cis-retinal to trans-retinal is rhodopsin.

Rhodopsin is the visual pigment in the outer segment of rods responsible for scotopic vision (night/ dark vision). It is a light-sensitive pigment and consists of opsin and 11-cis retinal.

When light is absorbed by rhodopsin, it decomposes very quickly. This leads to an instantaneous change of the cis form of retinal into an all-trans form. This all-trans-retinal separates from scotopsin to produce bathorhodopsin. Bathorhodopsin is very unstable and decays to form lumirhodopsin, which then decays and forms metarhodopsin I, metarhodopsin II, and finally, into the completely split products scotopsin and all-trans-retinal. 

Metarhodopsin II is also called activated rhodopsin, and it produces excitatory changes in the rods, which transmits optic nerve action potentials. to the central nervous system.

Re-formation of rhodopsin involves the conversion of the all-trans-retinal back into 11-cis retinal. This requires metabolic energy and is catalyzed by retinal isomerase. 11-cis retinal then recombines with scotopsin to form rhodopsin. Rhodopsin now remains stable until it is triggered by light energy to start decomposing again.

Role of vitamin A: The second route of re-formation of rhodopsin involves the conversion of the all-trans-retinal into all-trans-retinol, which is a form of vitamin A. All-trans-retinol is converted into 11- cis retinol by isomerase. 11-cis retinol is then converted into 11-cis retinal, combines with scotopsin, and forms new rhodopsin.

Which of the following modifications occur posttranscriptionally to produce a mature eukaryotic mRNA?

Capping, polyadenylation, and splicing are the modifications that occur posttranscriptionally to produce a mature eukaryotic mRNA. Phosphorylation, hydroxylation, and trimming are modifications that occur posttranslationally.

A mature eukaryotic mRNA is formed after the pre-mRNA components of the heterogenous nuclear RNA (hnRNA) undergo the following posttranscriptional modifications in the nucleus:

  1. Addition of a 5′ cap: A 7-methylguanosine is attached to the 5′ terminal end of the mRNA via a 5′-to-5′ triphosphate linkage. This stabilizes the mRNA and allows initiation of translation.
  2. Addition of a 3′-poly-A tail: The poly-A tail is added by the nuclear enzyme, polyadenylate polymerase, after clevage of the polyadenylation signal sequence (AAUAAA) found near the 3′ end of the mRNA. This terminates eukaryotic transcription. Furthermore, it stabilizes the mRNA, allows it to exit from the nucleus, and helps in translation.
  3. Splicing: This is the process of removing introns (intervening sequences that do not code for proteins) and joining exons (the coding or expressed sequences), carried out by the spliceosome. Alternative splicing occurs in different tissues to produce varied number of proteins from a limited set of genes.

questions.text: Which of the following is ‌not a substrate for gluco‍se formation?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not a substrate for glucose formation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acetyl coenzyme A

Acetyl coenzyme A (CoA) is not a substrate for glucose formation.

Acetyl CoA and compounds that give rise to acetyl CoA alone like acetoacetate, lysine, and leucine cannot give rise to a net synthesis of glucose. This is because of the irreversible nature of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which converts pyruvate to acetyl CoA. These compounds give rise to ketone bodies instead.

The synthesis of glucose in the body, in the absence of dietary carbohydrates, occurs in two ways:

  • From liver glycogen, by a process known as glycogenolysis in the absence of dietary carbohydrates, for up to 24 hours.
  • De novo, from non-carbohydrate sources, by a process known as gluconeogenesis, when glycogen stores have depleted. This occurs primarily in the liver and to a lesser extent in the kidneys.

In gluconeogenesis, the substrates can be:

  • Oxaloacetate (from its conjugate acid, oxaloacetic acid) is a direct precursor of phosphoenolpyruvate
  • Pyruvate is an α-keto acid that can be converted to glucose.
  • Alanine is a glucogenic amino acid that is transaminated to form pyruvate by the enzyme alanine amino-transferase in the liver.
  • Lactate obtained from anaerobic glycolysis is released from skeletal muscles and RBCs into the blood. This is taken up by the liver in the Cori cycle to be oxidised to pyruvate, to eventually synthesize glucose 
  • Glycerol from adipose tissue is converted to dihydroxyacetone phosphate in the liver, which itself is an intermediate of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cytoplasm and mitochondria

Ornithine cycle/Krebs–Henseleit cycle/Urea cycle occurs in both the cytoplasm and mitochondria.

The reactions that take place both in the cytoplasm and mitochondria are:

  • H: Heme synthesis
  • U: Urea cycle
  • G: Gluconeogenesis
  • Pathway: Pyrimidine synthesis

Urea cycle disorders are all characterized by hyperammonemia, encephalopathy, and respiratory alkalosis. This is due to an accumulation of the precursors of urea, namely ammonia and glutamine.

The enzymes involved in the urea cycle with their related disorders are given below:

  • Carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase (CPS) 1 deficiency (hyperammonemia type 1) - rare and characterized by severe hyperammonemia.
  • Ornithine transporter deficiency (HHH syndrome) - is characterized by hyperornithinemia, hyperammonemia, and homocitrullinuria.
  • Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency (hyperammonemia type 2) - is inherited as an X-linked trait. Characterized by hyperammonemia and elevated glutamine levels in blood and CSF.
  • Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency - is characterized by increased citrulline, citrullinuria, and hyperammonemia.
  • Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency- leads to argininosuccinic acidemia and metabolic acidosis. Hyperammonemia is less severe, and argininosuccinate is found in urine and CSF.
  • Arginase deficiency- mild variety. Characterized by hyperargininemia and argininuria.

Clinical features of urea cycle disorders are common to all and include vomiting, avoidance of high-protein foods, intermittent ataxia, irritability, lethargy, and severe mental retardation. 

Long terms treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet.

questions.raw_text: Which of the following amino acid is likely to be most abundant in collagen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glycine

The most abundant amino acid in collagen is glycine.

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world. It consists of three alpha chains held together by hydrogen bonds forming a triple helical structure.

A striking characteristic of collagen is the occurrence of glycine residues at every third position, (Gly-X-Y) repeats.

Proline and hydroxyproline confer rigidity on the collagen molecule. Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine are formed by the post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues. This hydroxylation is catalyzed by the enzyme prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, and cofactors are ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and α-ketoglutarate.

Intracellular steps in the synthesis of collagen:

  • Signal peptide cleavage
  • Hydroxylation of prolyl residues and some lysyl residues, glycosylation of some hydroxylysyl residues
  • Intrachain and interchain S–S bonds formation in extension peptides
  • Triple helix formation

Extracellular steps in the synthesis of collagen:

  • Amino- and carboxyl-terminal propeptides cleavage
  • Collagen fibers assembly in quarter-staggered alignment
  • Oxidative deamination of h -amino groups of lysyl and hydroxylysyl residues to aldehydes
  • Intra- and interchain cross-links formation via Schiff bases and aldol condensation products

The percentage of cytosine in the DNA is 22%.

In the question, the concentration of thymine is given as 28%, therefore the concentration of adenine is also 28%, both of which add up to 56%. The remaining 44% (100-56) of the DNA consists of G-C base pairs. Of which the guanine constitutes 22% and the cytosine constitutes another 22%.

questions.raw_text: A young chemist notices a reaction system in which the rate of conversion of substrates to product is equal to the rate at which products are converted back to substrates. Which of the following properties regarding this reaction system is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The equilibrium constant i‌s a ratio of the reaction‍ rates

options.label: B
options.text: The rate constants of the ‌forward and backward reac‍tions are equal

options.label: D
options.text: The value of equilibrium c‌onstant increases with in‍crease in catalyst or enz‍yme concentration

questions.correct_answer: C. Equilibrium is a dynamic state
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Equilibrium is a dynamic state

Among the given options, Equilibrium is a dynamic state is the correct option.

In an equilibrium state, Although there is no net change in the concentration of substrates or products, individual substrate, and product molecules are continually being interconverted and hence it is said to be dynamic.

Some important properties of a system at equilibrium are:

  • The equilibrium constant (Keq) is a ratio of the reaction rate constants (not the reaction rates). 
  • At equilibrium, the reaction rates (not the rate constants) of the forward and back reactions are equal. 
  • The numerical value of the constant can be calculated by finding the concentrations of substrates and products.
  • If Keq is more than 1, the forward reaction is favoured. In such instances, the reaction is spontaneous and exothermic.
  • The concentration of the enzyme does not affect the Keq. The concentration of enzyme certainly increases the rate of reaction; but not the Keq or the ultimate state. Catalysts increase the rate of reaction but do not alter the equilibrium.

questions.text: Which of the following are‍ pro-apoptotic factors? B​AK BAX BCL2 BCL-XL MCL1
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following are pro-apoptotic factors?

  1. BAK
  2. BAX
  3. BCL2
  4. BCL-XL
  5. MCL1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 2

BAK and BAX are pro-apoptotic factors, whereas BCL2, BCL-XL, and MCL1 are anti-apoptotic proteins.

Apoptosis, also known as programmed cell death, occurs due to the activation and release of certain proteases known as caspases. These enzymes are regulated by a balance between the actions of pro- apoptotic and anti-apoptotic proteins on the permeability of the mitochondrial membrane:

  • Pro-apoptotic proteins increase membrane permeability, thereby causing leakage of proteins that initiate apoptosis, like cytochrome c.
  • Anti-apoptotic proteins keep the membrane impermeable, preventing the release of cytochrome c.

There are two apoptotic pathways-

  • The intrinsic or mitochondrial pathway
  • Extrinsic or death-receptor initiated pathway

The intrinsic pathway is triggered by DNA damage, accumulation of misfolded proteins, and loss of survival signals. This leads to leakage of pro-apoptotic proteins like cytochrome c into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome c binds to APAF-1 (apoptosis-activating factor-1), forming an apoptosome. This complex activates caspase 9. 

The extrinsic pathway is triggered by the engagement of death receptors on the plasma membrane. It activates caspases 8 and 10. 

The active forms of these caspases activate executioner caspases (3 and 6), which act on various cell components to cause nuclear fragmentation, DNA degradation, etc. Cytoplasmic blebs and apoptotic bodies are then formed, which are ultimately phagocytosed.

questions.text: Arrange the following cell‍ular events of inflammati​on in the correct sequenc‍e: Rolling Cytokine media​ted integrin activation A​dhesion Migration
questions.raw_text:
Arrange the following cellular events of inflammation in the correct sequence:

  1. Rolling
  2. Cytokine mediated integrin activation
  3. Adhesion
  4. Migration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

The correct sequence of cellular events that occur during inflammation is:

  • Rolling
  • Cytokine mediated integrin activation
  • Adhesion
  • Migration

The recruitment of leukocytes to the site of inflammation is a multi-step process, that is mediated by adhesion molecules and cytokines called chemokines. This process can be divided into sequential phases:

  1. In the lumen: margination, rolling and adhesion to the endothelium occurs.
  2. Migration of the leukocytes across the endothelium and vessel wall
  3. Migration in the tissues towards a chemotactic stimulus.

The process of leukocyte recruitment is as follows:

  • Margination: Because of dilation of the inflamed postcapillary venues, there is stasis of blood flow and hence more leukocytes assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface; this process of leukocyte redistribution is called margination.
  • Rolling: the slowed leukocytes then sense the signals from the endothelium and start rolling on the vessel wall.
  • Cytokine-mediated integrin activation: the attachment of leukocytes to the endothelial cells requires adhesion molecules that are activated by cytokines. The major families of proteins involved in adhesion and migration are selectins and integrins and their ligands.
  • Adhesions: the weak rolling interactions slow down the leukocytes and allow them to bind more firmly to the endothelium. Chemokines that were produced at the site of injury bind to the endothelial cell proteoglycans. These chemokines then bind to the rolling leukocytes and activate them. This is turn converts the ligands for β1 and β2 integrins, VLA-4 and LFA-1 present on the leukocytes to a high-affinity state.
  • This combination of cytokine-induced expression of integrin ligands on the endothelium and increased integrin affinity on the leukocytes leads to firm adhesion of leukocytes to the endothelium at the site of inflammation.
  • Leukocyte migration: this is the movement of leukocytes through intact endothelium, called transmigration or diapedesis. This occurs in postcapillary venules. This migration occurs through the inter endothelial gap towards the chemical concentration gradient created by the chemokines at the site of injury. This occurs with the help of adhesion molecules present in the intercellular junctions such as Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule (PECAM-1) or CD31.

Correct answer: B. Oligodendroglioma

The clinical scenario of frontal lobe tumor with seizures and the histopathology image showing the ‘fried egg appearance’ of tumor cells, points to the diagnosis of oligodendroglioma.

Oligodendroglioma is a subtype of infiltrating glioma. It is comprised of cells that resemble oligodendrocytes. The tumors are composed of sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm. This gives it the ‘fried egg appearance’. The tumor cells that infiltrate the cortex usually collect around the neuron and this is known as perineural satellitosis. Also, there is a delicate network of anastomosing thin-walled capillaries between the tumor cells, resembling 'chicken wire'.

Oligodendrogliomas account for 5 to 15% of all gliomas and most commonly are detected in the fourth and fifth decades of life. Patients may have had several years of antecedent neurologic complaints, often including seizures.

The lesions are found mostly in the cerebral hemispheres, mainly in the frontal or temporal lobes.

It is treated with a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. 

Other options:

Option A: Glioblastoma is a synonym for grade IV astrocytoma. Infiltrating astrocytomas and glioblastomas are usually seen in the cerebellum, brainstem, or spinal cord. Histologically, glioblastoma appears like an anaplastic astrocytoma with serpiginous foci of palisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation. 

Option C: Ependymomas in adults are in the spinal cord and near the ventricles, particularly the fourth ventricle. The microscopic appearance shows both true rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes. 

Option D: Schwannomas are benign tumors that often arise directly from peripheral nerves. On microscopy, they are comprised of dense areas called Antoni A  areas and loose areas referred to as Antoni B areas. Antoni A areas are eosinophilic and contain spindle cells arranged in intersecting fascicles with nuclear palisading. The central nuclear-free zones are called Verocay bodies. Schwannomas are a component of NF-2.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease characterized by the gradual destruction of the thyroid gland leading to thyroid failure. It is more commonly seen in females between 45 to 65 years of age. In the majority of cases, it is caused by the presence of circulating autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase.

Morphologically, there is a diffuse and symmetrical enlargement of the thyroid gland, with an intact capsule. Microscopic features include:

  • Extensive lymphocytic infiltrate containing small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and well-developed germinal centers
  • Hürthle cells, are epithelial cells that line atrophied thyroid follicles and contain eosinophilic granular cytoplasm

In most cases, there is a gradual development of hypothyroidism. However, in some patients, transient thyrotoxicosis may occur due to the release of thyroid hormones from disrupted thyroid follicles known as hashitoxicosis. Free T4 and T3 levels are elevated and TSH and radioactive iodine uptake are decreased in this phase. As hypothyroidism occurs, T4 and T3 levels fall, and TSH increases. Patients are also more susceptible to developing other autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes and systemic lupus erythematosus.

This type of cancer has an excellent prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate in 95% of cases.

In some cases, there may be transient thyrotoxicosis lasting for 2-6 weeks. Normal function returns after recovery.

WHO divides neuroendocrine neoplasms into four categories:

  • Atypical carcinoid 
  • Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma 
  • Small-cell carcinoma 

Carcinoid tumors are low-grade malignant epithelial neoplasms that represent 1% to 5% of all lung tumors. It is not related to smoking. Carcinoids may occur in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.

On gross examination, these tumors grow as fingerlike or spherical polypoid masses that project into the lumen of the bronchus or as collar button lesions, penetrating the bronchial wall to fan out in the peribronchial tissue.

Histologically, the tumor is composed of organoid, trabecular, palisading, ribbon, or rosette-like arrangements of cells separated by a delicate fibrovascular stroma. On electron microscopy, the cells exhibit the dense-core neurosecretory granules. 

Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for serotonin, neuron-specific enolase, bombesin, calcitonin, or other peptides.

questions.text: A 21-year-old previously h‍ealthy athlete suffers a ​sudden cardiac arrest whi‍le playing a sport. On au​topsy, it was found that ​there was hypertrophic ca‍rdiomyopathy. The gene en​coding for which of the f​ollowing proteins is most​ commonly mutated in this‌ condition?
questions.raw_text: A 21-year-old previously healthy athlete suffers a sudden cardiac arrest while playing a sport. On autopsy, it was found that there was hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The gene encoding for which of the following proteins is most commonly mutated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. β-myosin heavy chain

The gene encoding for β-myosin heavy chain (β-MHC) proteins is most commonly mutated in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

HCM is a common autosomal dominant disorder characterized by myocardial hypertrophy, abnormal diastolic filling (with preserved systolic function), and intermittent left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. It is the leading cause of unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy.

It is caused by mutations in genes that encode sarcomeric proteins, including myosin-binding protein C (MYBP-C) and β-MHC (MYH7). It can also rarely occur due to mutations in genes coding for cardiac TnI, TnT, and α-tropomyosin.

In HCM, myocardial hypertrophy occurs without ventricular dilation. Furthermore, there is asymmetric septal hypertrophy, where the ventricular septum is disproportionately thickened compared to the left ventricular free wall. The enlarged septum bulges into the ventricular cavity, giving it a banana-like shape. Hypertrophy is most marked in the subaortic region of the septum.

The most important histologic features in HCM are:

  • Massive myocyte hypertrophy
  • Myofiber disarray including that of myocyte bundles, individual myocytes, and contractile elements
  • Fibrotic narrowing of small intramural arteries
  • Interstitial and replacement fibrosis

The images below show normal cardiac myocytes and myofibril disarray in HCM, respectively:

 

Exertional dyspnea due to reduced cardiac output is seen, and a harsh systolic ejection murmur caused due to LVOT obstruction can be heard. Further, atrial fibrillation, stroke due to mural thrombus formation, and ventricular arrhythmias are common complications of HCM. 

β-adrenergic blockers can be used to decrease heart rate and contractility, and implantable cardioverter defibrillators are used for patients with ventricular arrhythmias.

Other options:

Option A: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) occurs due to truncating mutations in the titin gene. The heart in DCM is flabby and hypo-contracting, in contrast with the thick-walled, heavy, and hyper-contracting heart in HCM. Histology reveals hypertrophied myocytes with hyperchromatic distorted nuclei with a ninja star-like appearance, as shown in the image below. Variable degrees of interstitial and endocardial fibrosis is also present.

Option C: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is an autosomal dominant disorder that occurs due to mutations of genes encoding desmosomal junctional proteins. It typically manifests as right-sided heart failure and can cause sudden cardiac death. Histology shows loss of myocytes, fatty infiltration, and focal fibrosis.

Option D: HCM occurs due to mutations in the gene encoding α-tropomyosin. However, this is rare, and HCM occurs most commonly due to mutations in genes encoding myosin-binding protein C (MYBP-C) and β-MHC (MYH7).

questions.raw_text: A 52-year-old male patient presented with abdominal pain and melena. On endoscopy, a bleeding gastric mass with irregular borders was identified along the greater curvature of the stomach. Microscopy is as shown in the image below. Which of the following is a specific marker for the tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CD 117

The given clinical scenario and the histological picture showing spindle-shaped tumor cells are suggestive of gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), for which CD 117 is the specific marker. 

GIST is the most common mesenchymal tumor of the abdomen, with the most common site being the stomach. The tumor arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal or pacemaker cells of the gastrointestinal muscularis propria.

Most GISTs occur due to gain-of-function mutations in receptor tyrosine kinase KIT (~75%) or PDGRF-ɑ (~8%). 

The tumor peaks at 60 years of age. It is often associated with the Carney triad, a nonhereditary condition characterized by GIST, paraganglioma, and pulmonary chondroma. GIST also has a higher incidence in individuals with neurofibromatosis I.

Patients typically present with anemia (due to blood loss caused by mucosal ulceration) and symptoms of mass effect. However, GISTs may also be discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery.

Microscopically, GIST can be of two patterns:

  1. Spindle cell type: The tumor is composed of thin elongated cells.
  2. Epitheloid type: The tumor is composed of plump epithelial-like cells.

Mixed patterns may also be seen.

The most useful immunohistochemical marker is KIT (CD117) detectable in Cajal cells.

The prognosis depends on tumor size, mitotic index, and location (GISTs arising in the stomach are less aggressive than those arising in the small intestine). Complete surgical resection is the mainstay treatment. For unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic GISTs, imatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, can be used.
