questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old female patient presents with episodic headaches, sweating, and palpitations. Her blood pressure was recorded as 167/110 mmHg and lab investigations revealed elevated plasma metanephrines. An adrenal mass was seen on an abdominal CT scan and a biopsy confirms the diagnosis. Which clinical feature would you not expect to see in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oliguria

The clinical vignette with a patient having the given symptoms with elevated plasma metanephrines, and an adrenal mass is suggestive of a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. Polyuria (not oliguria) is an expected clinical finding.

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. 

Clinical features of pheochromocytoma are due to the autonomic effects of excess epinephrine and norepinephrine. 

  • Weight loss (option A) is due to the increase in catecholamines which increase basal metabolism.
  • Pallor (option B) is due to alpha 1-mediated vasoconstriction. 
  • Abdominal pain (option C) with nausea and vomiting is commonly seen.

Diagnosis of pheochromocytoma requires biochemical testing followed by imaging.

  • Urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines 
  • MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor 
  • MIBG Scintigraphy and PET Scans like Ga- DOTATE, DOPA- or FDG- PET can be used for extra-adrenal tumors and metastases

Treatment of pheochromocytoma:

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment. Preoperatively, an alpha-receptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) is given to control the effects produced by excess catecholamines. Beta-blockers are used to control tachycardia after adequate alpha blockade is achieved. This is to prevent unrestricted alpha-mediated vasoconstriction. Following surgery, lifelong yearly follow-ups should be done.

His wife says that he has been on treatment for Addison's disease two years back but had forgotten to pack his medication for the trip. What is the drug of choice for this man?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrocortisone

This clinical scenario is suggestive of an adrenal crisis triggered by missed medication. In this patient who is a known case of adrenal insufficiency, IV hydrocortisone is the drug of choice.

However, in patients with newly diagnosed adrenal insufficiency, dexamethasone is used for the treatment of adrenal crisis. This is because dexamethasone is not measured in cortisol assays and would not interfere with the diagnostic tests, whereas hydrocortisone interferes with cortisol assays.

Acute adrenal insufficiency requires the immediate initiation of the following therapeutic strategies:

  • Rehydration - saline infusion at an initial rate of 1 L/h with continuous cardiac monitoring.
  • Glucocorticoid replacement - bolus injection of 100 mg hydrocortisone, followed by the maintenance dose of 100–200 mg over 24h.
  • Mineralocorticoid replacement - initiated once the daily hydrocortisone dose has been reduced to <50 mg as higher doses of hydrocortisone have sufficient mineralocorticoid action.

A 66-year-old male patient presented with complaints of fatigue and chronic back pain. On evaluation, he was found to have anemia and hypercalcemia. The X-ray of his skull is given below. Which of the following is not seen in this patient?

  1. Plasma cells in 24-hr urine analysis

  3. Normocytic normochromic anemia 
  4. Osteolytic bone lesions
  5. Elevated ESR

Correct answer: B. 1 and 2 only

Statements 1 and 2 are incorrect/ not seen in this patient.

The given X-ray of the skull demonstrating the typical “punched out” lesions in an elderly male with chronic back pain, fatigue, anemia, and hypercalcemia are highly suggestive of multiple myeloma. It is characterized by normal serum alkaline phosphatase (due to the absence of osteoblastic activity), and plasma cells in bone marrow (not in urine).

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with an increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia.

Signs and symptoms:

  • Bone pain is the most common symptom
  • Pathologic fractures
  • Recurrent bacterial infections
  • Renal failure
  • Normocytic normochromic anemia, elevated ESR, hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma)
  • Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray
  • Electrophoresis: M spikes
  • Urinalysis: Bence Jones proteinuria
  • Bone marrow biopsy: Plasma cells

A patient with asthma is being evaluated. His FEV1 values were measured before and after the administration of a short-acting beta-agonist. Which of the following values represents the minimum change required to demonstrate the reversibility of obstruction after administration of bronchodilators in this condition?

FEV1 - Forced expiratory volume in the first minute

FVC - Forced vital capacity

options.label: A
options.text: > 12% increase in FEV1/FVC‌ ratio and 200 mL increas‍e in FEV1

options.label: B
options.text: > 50% increase in FEV1/FVC‌ ratio and 500 mL increas‍e in FEV1

options.label: C
options.text: > 20% increase in FEV1/FVC‌ ratio and 410 mL increas‍e in FEV1

options.label: D
options.text: > 6% increase in FEV1/FVC ‌ratio and 100 mL increase‍ in FEV1

questions.correct_answer: A. > 12% increase in FEV1/FVC ratio and 200 mL increase in FEV1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. > 12% increase in FEV1/FVC ratio and 200 mL increase in FEV1

Reversibility of obstruction in asthma has to be demonstrated by a minimum of 12% increase in FEV1/FVC ratio and 200 mL increase in FEV1 in response to inhalation of short-acting beta-agonist (SABA).

In asthma, there is reversible bronchoconstriction leading to wheezing, breathlessness, and cough. Thus, on administering an SABA, there is bronchial relaxation and relief of symptoms. 

Asthma is generally diagnosed clinically based on symptoms alone. However, some other conditions can be misdiagnosed as asthma such as causes of wheezing (bronchogenic carcinoma, foreign body aspiration), cough (gastroesophageal reflux, chronic bronchitis, rhinitis), and dyspnea (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary edema, or obesity). Misdiagnosis would lead to a delay in management. Thus, it is ideal that the clinical diagnosis of asthma is confirmed by pulmonary function tests. 

  • Spirometry: It is a non-invasive investigation that can be used to approximate lung volumes. This shows an obstructive pattern
    • Decreased FEV1.
    • Decreased or normal FVC.
    • Decreased FEV1/FVC.
  • Bronchodilator reversibility: Spirometry is performed both before and after inhalation of a short-acting bronchodilator (400 mcg of β2 agonist or 160 mcg of anticholinergic). A 12% and 200 mL increase in FEV1 compared to pre-bronchodilator value is diagnostic of asthma in adults. 
  • Bronchial provocation test: Provocative stimulus (histamine, methacholine, inhaled mannitol, exercise, eucapnic hyperventilation with dry or cold air) is used to test the presence of airway hyperresponsiveness.  A fall of ≥20% in FEV1 from baseline, with a standard dose of methacholine (methacholine challenge test), is diagnostic of asthma.
  • Peak expiratory flow (PEF): PEF readings are taken twice daily for over 2 weeks. The average daily diurnal PEF variability of >10% is diagnostic of asthma in adults.

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a form of functional renal failure without any renal pathology that occurs in some patients with advanced cirrhosis or acute liver failure. The pathophysiological hallmark is severe renal vasoconstriction.
 
There are two types of HRS:
  • Type 1 HRS: There is progressive impairment in renal function and a marked decline in creatinine clearance within 1–2 weeks of presentation.
  • Type 2 HRS: There is a drop in glomerular filtration rate with elevated creatinine levels. It has a better prognosis than type 1 HRS.

Ultrasound of the kidney shows normal study and hyaline casts may be observed, indicating prerenal failure.

Management:

  • Stop diuretics
  • Albumin infusion at 1g/kg/day
  • Medical management:
    • Vasopressin analogs- terlipressin
    • Somatostatin analogs- octreotide
    • Alpha-adrenergic agonists- midodrine, noradrenaline
  • Definitive treatment: Liver transplantation

She has‌ a history of recurrent m‌iscarriages. ECG shows a ​sinus rhythm. Echocardiog‌raphy revealed small vege​tation on both sides of t‌he mitral valve. What is ‍the most probable diagnos​is?
questions.raw_text: A 40-year-old woman presented with an episode of sudden left-sided weakness and speech difficulty which resolved spontaneously within 24 hours. She has a history of recurrent miscarriages. ECG shows a sinus rhythm. Echocardiography revealed small vegetation on both sides of the mitral valve. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Libman-Sacks endocarditis

The given presentation of neurological deficit resolving within 24 hours indicates a transient ischemic attack (TIA). The history of recurrent miscarriage points toward antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). These factors, along with the pattern of vegetations on the mitral valve, are strongly suggestive of Libman sack’s endocarditis.

Libman sack’s endocarditis is a type of non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE). It is associated with autoimmune conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. The deposition of immune complexes leads to the formation of small (1 to 4 mm), sterile vegetations on heart valves. 

Vegetations can occur anywhere on the valve surface, on the chordae, or even on the atrial or ventricular endocardium. Histologically, there is intense valvulitis and fibrinoid necrosis of the valve substance.

Patients may present with symptoms of stroke or TIA's due to emboli from the vegetation.

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoantibody-mediated acquired thrombophilia characterized by recurrent arterial or venous thrombosis and/or pregnancy morbidity. It primarily affects females. APS may either be primary or secondary to other autoimmune diseases, mainly SLE (secondary). The diagnosis of APS should be seriously considered in cases of thrombosis, cerebral vascular accidents in individuals <55 years of age, or pregnancy morbidity in the presence of livedo reticularis or thrombocytopenia. Laboratory criteria for APS include lupus anticoagulant (LA), anticardiolipin (aCL) antibody assay, and Aanti-β2GPI (glycoprotein 1) antibodies assay.

Other options:

Option A: Infective endocarditis is a microbial infection of the heart valves or the mural endocardium. The classic hallmarks of infective endocarditis are vegetations on heart valves. They are large, irregular masses on the valve cusps that can extend onto the chordae. Vegetations in infective endocarditis are friable, bulky, destructive lesions composed of fibrin, inflammatory cells, and microbes. 

Option C: Marantic endocarditis or Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis is characterized by the deposition of small (1 to 5 mm), sterile, non-destructive thrombi along the line of closure of the leaflets of the cardiac valves. A hypercoagulable state is a predisposing factor for marantic endocarditis.

Option D: Rheumatic heart disease is the inflammation of the endocardium and the left-sided valves that typically results in fibrinoid necrosis within the cusps or tendinous cords. Vegetations in RHD are small (1-2 mm) along the lines of closures of the valve leaflets. Irregular subendocardial thickenings are termed MacCallum plaques.

questions.text: A 70-year-old woman admitt‌ed to the surgical ward h‍ad been diagnosed with he​parin-induced thrombocyto‌penia. Which of the follo‍wing is not a suitable ne‌xt step for this patient?‌
questions.raw_text: A 70-year-old woman admitted to the surgical ward had been diagnosed with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Which of the following is not a suitable next step for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Switch to warfarin

Switching to warfarin is not a suitable next step for patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). 

Warfarin should not be administered in HIT until platelets return to their baseline level. If warfarin was administered, give vitamin K to restore the INR to normal. 

Patients with HIT, particularly those with associated thrombosis, have increased thrombin generation that can lead to consumption of protein C. If these patients are given warfarin without a concomitant parenteral anticoagulant to inhibit thrombin or thrombin generation, the further decrease in protein C levels induced by the vitamin K antagonist can trigger skin necrosis.

HIT is a life-threatening complication of exposure to heparin. It occurs more with unfractionated heparin than with low molecular weight (LMW) heparin. It is more common in surgical patients and more common in women than in men.

HIT results from an autoantibody directed against endogenous platelet factor 4 (PF4) in complex with heparin. These antibodies bind simultaneously to the heparin-PF4 complex and to platelet Fc receptors, activating the platelets and generating platelet microparticles. This can cause catastrophic arterial and venous thrombosis.

Features:

  • Thrombocytopenia: Platelet count of ≤100,000/μL or a decrease in platelet count of ≥50%
  • Platelet count falls 5–10 days after starting heparin.
  • Venous thrombosis more common than arterial thrombosis

Investigations:

  1. ELISA to detect antibodies against heparin-PF4 complexes (most sensitive)
  2. Platelet activation assays
  3. Serotonin release assay (most specific)

Treatment:

  1. Stop all heparin.
  2. Give an alternative anticoagulant, such as lepirudin, argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or rivaroxaban.
  3. Do not give platelet transfusions.

Other options: 

Option A - Heparin should be discontinued if the patient has HIT. 

Option B - Lepirudin can be administered as it is an alternative anticoagulant. 

Option D - Rivaroxaban can be given as it is an alternative anticoagulant.

The above image depicts a classical fish mouth (microstomia) appearance seen in systemic sclerosis/scleroderma.

Scleroderma or Systemic Sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune rheumatic disease in which there is a 4:1 female predominance.

A wide spectrum of clinical features are seen in Scleroderma:

  • Severe pruritus
  • Initially, puffiness and non-pitting edema of fingers
  • The skin later becomes indurated, thickened, and fixed to underlying structures resulting in sclerodactyly
  • Vasospasm and digital ulceration
  • Most patients have dysphagia and GERD
  • Mask-like facies is seen due to the waxy nature of skin and lack of wrinkles, expressionless facies, mat‐like telangiectases, microstomia, perioral furrowing, and beak‐like nose.

The antibodies tested in systemic sclerosis include:

  • Antinuclear antibody (ANA) - positive in most cases of systemic sclerosis. The absence of this antibody suggests considering an alternate diagnosis.
  • Anticentromere antibody (ACA) - usually positive in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
  • Antitopoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis 
  • Anti-RNA polymerase III antibody - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Other options:

Option B: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that most commonly presents with arthralgia with early morning stiffness. Other important features of SLE include malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, pleuritis, pericarditis, and lupus nephritis. ANA, Anti-dsDNA antibodies, and anti-Smith antibodies are positive in SLE. 

Option C: Angular stomatitis is the soreness at the angles of the mouth extending outwards in the folds of the facial skin.

Option D: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is caused by coxsackievirus. It is an exanthematous fever affecting mainly young children, characterized by oral and pharyngeal ulcerations and a vesicular rash of the palms and soles that may spread to the arms and legs.

questions.text: Match the following: First‌-degree heart block Mobit‍z type 1 heart block Mobi​tz type 2 heart block Com‌plete heart block
questions.raw_text:
Match the following:

  1. First-degree heart block
  2. Mobitz type 1 heart block
  3. Mobitz type 2 heart block
  4. Complete heart block
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1- c, 2- a, 3- d, 4- b

The correctly matched pairs are 1- c, 2- a, 3- d, and 4- b.

The different types of heart blocks are:

First Degree Heart Block: It occurs due to slowing of conduction through the AV junction. It is characterized by prolonged PR > 0.2s and equal RR intervals.

 

Second Degree Heart Block: It occurs due to the intermittent failure of electrical impulse conduction from the atrium to the ventricle. It is characterized by a missed QRS. It is of two types:

  • Mobitz type 1/ Wenckebach occurs due to the decremental conduction of electrical impulses in the AV node. It is characterized by a progressive PR elongation leading to an eventual drop in the QRS complex. This may be seen in young athletes.

 

  • Mobitz type 2 occurs in the distal or infra-His conduction system and is often associated with intraventricular conduction delays.  It is characterized by an intermittent failure of conduction of the p wave without any change in the preceding impulses. On ECG there is a fixed PR interval and missed QRS.

 

Third Degree Heart Block/Complete Heart Block

It occurs when none of the impulses from the atria are conducted to the ventricles. It is characterized by

  • Escape rhythm
  • RR equal, PP equal
  • P waves > QRS waves
  • No relationship between P & QRS

This patient with gastrointestinal symptoms and positive IgM- HAV is likely to have acute hepatitis A infection and requires supportive treatment. 

Since most patients recover spontaneously, only supportive treatment is required. 

Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is an icosahedral, non enveloped virus that causes hepatitis A infection. HAV is transmitted by the fecal-oral route. Usually, it is due to contamination of food or water. It may transmit from person to person due to poor hygiene. It mostly is of mild nature, with only 0.1% of patients developing fulminant hepatitis.

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette given is intrinsic acute kidney injury (AKI). The history of crush injury is suggestive of rhabdomyolysis leading to AKI.

AKI is defined as a decline in kidney function within 7 days, resulting in the accumulation of nitrogenous waste and other toxic metabolites usually excreted in the urine. It includes a variety of conditions that share some common features such as elevated creatinine levels and reduced urine output. It is broadly divided into three categories:

  • Prerenal azotemia 
  • Intrinsic parenchymal disease
  • Postrenal obstruction

Intrinsic causes can further be divided into acute tubular necrosis, acute glomerulonephritis, and acute interstitial nephritis. Ischemia and nephrotoxins are the main causes of acute tubular necrosis. Nephrotoxins can be exogeneous such as vancomycin, cisplatin, and iodinated contrast agents used for CT imaging. Endogenous toxins include myoglobin, uric acid, and hemoglobin. Crush injuries, heat stroke, and myopathies can result in rhabdomyolysis releasing large amounts of myoglobin. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is usually ≤ 40.

In acute tubular necrosis, urinary sodium is >20 mEq/L. 

Prerenal azotemia arises due to a reduced renal plasma flow. Common causes include hypovolemia, liver failure, and congestive heart failure. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is ≥ 40 and urinary sodium is usually <20mEq/L.

Bladder outlet obstruction, urethral obstruction, and benign prostatic hyperplasia lead to postrenal azotemia. Urinary sodium can be variable.

The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis on biopsy. This finding is commonly seen in the tissues obtained from the lungs, upper airways, skin, and rarely in the kidneys.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation, multiple demyelinating plaques, and relapsing and remitting symptoms. It occurs due to infiltration of the white matter by T cells and macrophages leading to axonal damage and neurodegeneration. It presents abruptly or insidiously with variable intensity of symptoms depending on the location. 

The most common symptoms experienced are as follows:

  1. Sensory symptoms:
    1. Paresthesia, pins and needles sensations, hypoesthesia
    2. Horizontal cut-off on limbs for sensory involvement suggests lesions at the level of the spinal cord 
    3. Pain
  2. Optic neuritis:
    1. Reduced visual acuity, color perception, dimness in the central visual field, unilaterally or bilaterally.
    2. Periorbital pain
    3. Funduscopy: optic disc swelling, pallor
  3. Weakness of limbs
    1. Loss of strength, speed, dexterity
    2. Gait disturbance
    3. Upper motor neuron weakness
    4. Pyramidal signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia
    5. Babinski sign positive
  4. Facial weakness 
  5. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia - bilaterally
  6. Ataxia, vertigo

  • Uthoff symptom -neurological symptoms produced by elevated core body temperature
  • Tonic seizures and dysarthria
  • Trigeminal neuralgia, and facial myokymia 
  • Bladder dysfunction as detrusor hyperreflexia or detrusor sphincter dyssynergia
  • Fatigue

MS can have three different clinical courses: 

  1. Relapsing or bout onset (90%) of cases. Here, there is complete recovery between episodes. As the disease progresses, the recovery may not be complete. 
  2. Secondary progressive MS starts as relapsing MS but then experiences decreased function as a result of the attacks.
  3. Primary progressive MS (10% of the cases) has a consistent decline in function from disease onset. They do not have discrete episodes. 

Diagnosis of MS requires at least two or more episodes of symptoms and two or more signs that show the involvement of noncontiguous white matter tracks. The symptoms must last for at least one day and must be separated chronologically by one month.

questions.raw_text: A 57-year-old unresponsive male patient is brought to the hospital. He is pulseless and is not breathing. His lead II ECG rhythm strip is shown in the image below. What is the treatment for the given ECG abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Defibrillation

The ECG with no identifiable P wave, QRS complexes, and irregular rhythm is ventricular fibrillation (VF) and the treatment is defibrillation. 

Ventricular fibrillation is a disorganized ventricular rhythm. In a heart with ventricular fibrillation, there is little to no cardiac output as there is irregular cardiac contraction. In patients outside the hospital, sustained ventricular tachycardias are a common cause leading to ventricular fibrillation.

VF is a shockable rhythm. Thus, defibrillation must be performed in order to restore normal sinus rhythm according to advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) guidelines. In defibrillation, an electrical current is passed into the myocardium which 'resets' it by converting the dysrhythmia into a normal sinus rhythm. 

When the timing of electric current is adjusted according to the R waves or the QRS complex of the cardiac cycle, it is known as synchronized shock, which is administered in cardioversion. In ventricular fibrillation, because of irregular cardiac electrical activity, there are no R waves or QRS complexes to which the cardioversion can be synchronized. In the given clinical vignette, this patient's symptoms along with the image findings showing heliotrope rash are highly suggestive of dermatomyositis. Dermatomyositis involves CD 4+ cells, perimyseal infiltrates, and is associated with underlying malignancy. 

Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal skeletal muscle weakness, muscle inflammation, and a variety of characteristic skin manifestations. The pattern of muscle involvement helps distinguish a myopathy from a cerebral, spinal cord, neuronal or neuromuscular junction cause. It is commonly associated with an underlying malignancy.

Classic signs-

  • Heliotrope rash/ eyelid erythema- Violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids
  • V sign- Confluent macular erythema over the lower anterior neck and upper anterior chest
  • Shawl sign- Confluent macular erythema over the upper back and lateral aspect of arms
  • Gottron’s papules- Erythematous papules and plaques over extensor surface of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints
  • Gottron's sign- Erythematous rash over the extensor surfaces of joints such as the knuckles, elbows, knees, and ankles. 
  • Mechanic’s hands- Rough, hyperkeratotic lines on the lateral and palmer areas of the fingers
  • Scalp erythema and hair loss
  • Facial rash- Confluent erythema in the malar distribution involving the cheeks, nasal bridge, and nasolabial folds
  • Nail fold changes
  • Flagellate erythema- Linear erythema on the upper back with pruritus
  • Poikiloderma- Mottled pattern of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules with telangiectasias
  • Cutaneous calcinosis- Accumulation of calcium deposits in the skin.

Laboratory evaluation of patients with dermatomyositis will reveal elevated serum creatinine kinase and antinuclear antibodies. Electromyography will reveal features of myopathy. Histology will show perifascicular atrophy and immunohistochemical staining will reveal myxovirus resistance protein A, a sensitive and specific marker. 

Treatment of dermatomyositis is immunotherapy with high-dose glucocorticoids being the first line. Methotrexate can be started as the second line if the patient presents with severe weakness, other organ system involvement, or those with risk of steroid complications like patients with diabetes, osteoporosis, or postmenopausal women. Otherwise, second-line agents are only started in patients who do not show improvement after 2-4 months of treatment with prednisone or those who cannot be maintained on a low dose. Triple therapy with intravenous immunoglobulin or rituximab may be required.

questions.raw_text:
A woman is brought to the casualty in an unconscious state with no signs of injury to the body. Her arterial blood gas analysis report reveals the following values. Among the given conditions, which of the following can lead to this clinical scenario?

  • pH- 7.32
  • pCO2- 36 mm Hg
  • HCO3- - 18 mEq/L
  • Sodium levels- 136 mEq/L
  • Chloride levels- 109 mEq/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diarrhea

In the given scenario, the underlying disorder in this patient is metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. Among the given options, diarrhea will lead to this scenario as diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonates.

The diagnosis can be arrived at by the following steps:

Step 1: A pH of 7.32 indicates acidosis.

Step 2: Plasma HCO3- is 18 mmol/L

Step 3: Arterial pCO2 is within the normal range.

Therefore the patient has metabolic acidosis.

Step 4: Calculate the anion gap. 

Anion gap = Na+-(Cl-+HCO3-)

= 136-(109+18)

= 9, which is a normal anion gap.

Causes of normal anion gap acidosis (NAGMA) are:

  • Diarrhea
  • External pancreatic or small-bowel drainage
  • Ureterosigmoidostomy, jejunal loop, ileal loop
  • Drugs- Calcium chloride, magnesium sulfate, cholestyramine
  • Proximal and distal renal tubular acidosis
  • Potassium-sparing diuretics
  • Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers

Causes of high anionic gap acidosis (HAGMA) are:

  • Methanol poisoning
  • Uremia- renal failure
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis
  • Propylene glycol
  • Lactic acidosis
  • Ethanol poisoning
  • Salicylate poisoning

Other options:

Options A, C, and D: This will give rise to metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap.

Although all airflow is diminished, expiratory prolongation predominates, and mean expiratory flow < mean inspiratory flow. Vocal cord paralysis causes a variable extrathoracic upper airway obstruction in which only the inspiratory curve would be flattened.

Asbestos fibers induce oxidative injury due to the generation of reactive oxygen species by the transition metals on the surface of the fibers as well as from cells engaged in phagocytosis. These mechanisms result in lung fibrosis.

Irregular or linear opacities initially in the lower lung fields are the hallmark of asbestosis in chest radiographs. A gound glass appearance in the lung fields may be seen.

The test shown above is Schirmer's test and the likely diagnosis is Sjögren's syndrome. 

Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune disorder that involves lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands. This manifests as xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes). It is associated with autoantibodies anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B.

Keratoconjunctivitis sicca can be diagnosed by Schirmer's test. This test measures the quantity of tears produced. Two marked strips of paper are placed between the globe and the lower eyelid and the patient is instructed to close their eyes for 5 minutes. The tears produced spread along the paper by capillary action. The distance is measured. A score of more than 10 mm is considered to be normal while that of less than 5 mm is considered deficient. 

A number of other systems can be involved as well. For example, atrophic gastritis, esophageal mucosal atrophy, and vaginal dryness. Extraglandular or systemic manifestations can also be present. These manifest as fatigue, arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon, and myalgia. 

Diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome requires the following: 

  • Eye and/or mouth dryness
  • Eye tests disclose keratoconjunctivitis sicca
  • Mouth evaluation reveals dry oral mucosa and/or
  • Presence of anti-Ro or anti-La autoantibodies

A labial biopsy is a must to confirm the diagnosis and determine the prognosis. 

Treatment of Sjögren's syndrome is directed at treating the symptoms and complications. Artificial tears can be used for dry eyes and propionic acid gel for vaginal dryness. Pilocarpine can help increase oral secretions and hydroxychloroquine can be used to treat arthritis.

On examination, she was grossly unstable and the bilateral pulses were unequal. ECG showed nonspecific ST-T changes. What is the next best investigation?

Correct answer: B. Transesophageal echocardiography

The given clinical presentation with acute onset chest pain, loss of consciousness and diaphoresis with bilaterally unequal pulses and ECG showing nonspecific ST-T changes is suggestive of aortic dissection, and as the patient is hemodynamically unstable, the next best investigation is transesophageal ECHO.

Aortic dissection occurs when a defect or flap occurs in the intima of the aorta. Predisposing factors include mainly age, hypertension, Marfan syndrome, and pregnancy. The most typical presentation of aortic dissection is a tearing interscapular pain. Wilson's disease is an autosomal-recessive condition caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, which encodes for the ATPase that removes copper, preventing its accumulation in the liver and brain. Liver disease is the most common manifestation in children which can present as hepatomegaly (cirrhosis in advanced stages) with or without splenomegaly, subacute or chronic hepatitis, and acute liver failure. Neurologic features consist of dysarthria, dystonia, rigidity, tremors, and choreiform movements due to copper deposition in the basal ganglia. Psychiatric symptoms encompass personality changes, such as irritability and anger, as well as depression and anxiety. 

Kayser–Fleischer (KF) rings (deposition of copper in Descement's membrane) are present in 95% of patients with neurological symptoms and absent in half of the young patients with liver-related Wilson disease. After treatment KF ring resolves. Coomb's negative hemolytic anemia may also be seen. Hemolytic anemia can result from the release of copper into the circulation from the liver. Additional manifestations of Wilson's disease comprise renal tubular acidosis, delayed puberty, and osteoarthritis.

Diagnosis is made by the presence of a KF ring and decreased levels of serum copper and ceruloplasmin. Increased 24-hour urine copper excretion is seen. Hepatic copper content greater than 250 μg/g dry weight measured by liver biopsy is the gold standard. 

Copper intake should be restricted to <1 mg/day. Initial treatment involves copper-chelating agents D-penicillamine and trientine with concurrent use of pyridoxine. Penicillamine may worsen neurologic symptoms, so trientine is an alternative. Ammonium tetrathiomolybdate is another chelating agent being investigated for patients with neurologic disease. 

Zinc is used in presymptomatic patients due to its ability to impair the absorption of copper. Liver transplantation is considered in advanced stages.

The likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario with serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1g/dL and ascitic fluid protein <2.5 g/dL is late Budd Chiari syndrome.

Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) can be used to differentiate between ascites due to portal hypertension and non-portal hypertensive ascites. It represents the pressure within the hepatic sinusoids and correlates with the hepatic venous pressure gradient.

It is given by the formula: SAAG = Serum albumin level - Ascitic fluid albumin level.

Interpretation of SAAG:

  • SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is due to increased pressure in the hepatic sinusoids. It reflects the presence of portal hypertension.
  • SAAG <1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is not related to portal hypertension. It may be due to infection or malignancy.

In cases with high-SAAG (≥1.1), ascitic protein level analysis further helps in identifying the etiology:

  • ≥2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids are normal and are allowing the passage of protein into the ascites as in early Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • <2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids have been damaged and scarred and no longer allow passage of protein as in late Budd-Chiari syndrome

questions.raw_text: Which of the following is associated with steatorrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Short bowel syndrome (SBS)

Short bowel syndrome is associated with steatorrhoea which is defined as excess fat in stools (>7g/day) due to poor absorption of lipids.

Short bowel syndrome refers to intractable diarrhea with malabsorption of nutrients after intestinal resection or intestinal bypass surgery leading to malnutrition. The features of short bowel syndrome usually appear when the length is less than 200 cm of the small bowel, but the length and nature of the remaining bowel are also important. The common causes of short bowel syndrome include acute mesenteric ischemia, Crohn’s disease, trauma and radiation enteritis in adults, and bowel atresia and midgut volvulus in children

The clinical features include:

  • Intractable diarrhea (due to hypergastrinemia and gastric hypersecretion, or unabsorbed bile salts in the colon).
  • Steatorrhea (due to the depletion of the bile salt pool), gallstones (due to interruption of the enterohepatic cycle of bile salts).
  • Renal stones (due to increased absorption of oxalate in the colon).
  • Peptic ulcer (due to hypergastrinemia and gastric hypersecretion).
  • Fat-soluble (vitamin A, D, E, and K) and B12 vitamin deficiencies.

Initial treatment priorities include repletion of fluid and electrolytes lost in severe diarrhea by initiating total parenteral nutrition (TPN). Home parenteral nutrition is the mainstay of the treatment. Long-term management involves:

  • Administration of oral cholestyramine to bind with bile salts
  • Dietary fat restriction
  • Parenteral vitamin and mineral supplements
  • Proton pump inhibitors to lower gastric pH
  • Octreotide to reduce the volume of GI secretions
  • Antimotility agents such as loperamide hydrochloride to delay small-intestinal transit
  • Hormonal therapy such as growth hormone, glutamine, and GLP-2 (glucagon-like peptide-2) analog (teduglutide) are used to promote intestinal adaptation.  

 Other options:

Option B: Primary lactase deficiency leads to defective absorption of lactose. It does not affect lipid absorption.

Option C: Pernicious anemia is due to an absence of gastric parietal cell-intrinsic factor which is necessary for the absorption of vitamin B12

Option D: Wilsons disease is associated with increased absorption of copper and is not a part of malabsorption syndrome.

It leads to obstruction to the flow of bile thereby causing leaking of conjugated bilirubin into the circulation. It may also be termed as noncystic obliterative cholangiopathy. Correct answer: C. Orchidopexy

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of cryptorchidism and the next best step is to perform an orchidopexy.

Orchidopexy is the treatment of choice for incompletely palpable unilateral undescended testis. Orchidopexy is usually performed before the boy reaches 12 months of age to avoid the following complications remembered by the mnemonic TESTIS:

T- Torsion
E- Epididymorchitis
S- Sterility
T- Trauma (Increased risk)
I- Increased risk of inguinal hernia (Most commonly occurring complication)
S- Seminoma (Increased risk)

About 4% of boys are born with one or both testes incompletely descended. About two-thirds of these reach the scrotum during the first 3 months of life, but full descent after that is uncommon.

Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac.  It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The testes can arrest anywhere during descent, and the most common site is the inguinal region.

Phases of testicular descent:

  • Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis, and this descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances.
  • Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac, and this phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve.

The exact pathogenesis remains unknown; however, deficiency in gonadotropins and Mullerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) and increased expression of estradiol in the placenta are thought to play a role. 

Cryptorchidism is histopathologically characterized by the following: 

  1. Testicular atrophy: thickening of the basement membrane, arrested germ cell development, marked hyalinization
  2. Tubules showing Sertoli cells but no spermatogenesis
  3. Increase in the interstitial Leydig cells 
Other options:

Option A: Cryptorchidism is associated with testicular atrophy and dysfunction, which result in sterility. Cryptorchid testes carry a 3–5-fold higher risk for testicular cancer (usually seminoma). Thus, observation is never the policy.
 
Option B: When the testis is not palpable, ultrasound may be helpful in identifying the intracanalicular testis, while laparoscopy may be needed to differentiate between the abdominal testis and a truly absent testis. Since here testis is made out in the inguinal region, laparoscopy is not the next best line of management.
 
Option D: Orchidectomy should be considered if the incompletely descended testis is atrophic, particularly in the postpubertal boy if the other testis is normal.

Surgery in hypospadias is done to correct problems with the urinary stream and for cosmetic reasons. Surgery depends on the site of the hypospadias.

In a patient with abdominal pain with sterile pyuria, the given image finding points towards a diagnosis of a putty kidney.

The putty kidney is a characteristic finding of genitourinary tuberculosis (TB), specifically renal TB. The given image shows a homogenous and ground glass-like calcification of the kidney appearing like putty.

It is caused by the dissemination of the organism through the bloodstream and is thus is always a secondary TB. There is either reinfection or reactivation of old TB.

Genitourinary TB is a cause of sterile pyuria. Diagnosis is confirmed with a tuberculin test, or at least 3 consecutive early-morning specimens of urine are examined for acid-fast bacilli. They are stained with a Ziehl–Neelsen stain and subsequently cultured.

CT is the most sensitive modality and is the preferred means of visualizing renal calcifications. CT urography is done to assess the various stages of renal TB and its manifestations which are as follows:

  • Early: Papillary necrosis
  • Progressive:
    • Multifocal strictures
    • Generalized or focal hydronephrosis
    • Mural thickening and enhancement
    • Poorly enhancing renal parenchyma
  • End-stage:
    • Progressive hydronephrosis
    • Amorphous dystrophic calcification that involves the entire kidney - putty kidney

Treatment involves short-course therapy with antitubercular drugs like pyrazinamide, isoniazid, and rifampicin. Partial nephrectomy, nephrectomy, or reconstructive surgery is often done.

Staghorn calculus is found in urinary infection with Proteus, Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus usually, and is not a cause for sterile pyuria. (Option C)

Psoas calcification is a muscle calcification and might be seen developing after acute renal failure and rhabdomyolysis. (Option D)

The given x-ray shows silicone breast implants in a patient. MRI showing the linguine sign in post-silicone breast implant patients indicates intra-capsular silicone rupture.

After implantation of a silicone or saline breast implant, a fibrous capsule (scar) forms around the implant shell. In an intracapsular rupture, the contents of the implant are contained by the fibrous scar, while the shell appears as a group of wavy lines. This has been termed the linguine sign. It is seen in intra-capsular rupture of a breast implant.

Multiple hyperintense foci on T2-weighted images are sometimes found within the implant lumen. These findings are referred to as the “salad oil sign” or “droplet sign”.

Intracapsular rupture on MRI.

Breast implants are technically simple and it facilitates achieving symmetry. The implant in submuscular plane is better whenever a muscle is not removed during surgery. If the muscle is removed as in radical mastectomy, then a subcutaneous implant is placed. Silicone gel implants are used.

Complications may include pain, exposure of implant and rupture, infection, calcifications, displacements, intracapsular or extracapsular rupture and silicone granulomas.

MRI  of the breast can be used in the following cases:

  • To detect scar recurrence in women with a history of conservative breast surgery  
  • To assess the extent of high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)
  • To assess multifocality and multicentricity in lobular cancer 
  • It is the best imaging modality for women with breasts implants
  • As a screening tool in high-risk women with a positive family history.

Generally, ultrasound(USG) is the preferred modality of imaging in suspected cases of extracapsular rupture. The Snowstorm sign on USG is seen in extracapsular rupture. (Option-B)

The procedure shown in the image is Whipple's procedure. 

The following structures are removed during Whipple’s procedure:

  • Distal stomach
  • Duodenum
  • Proximal jejunum
  • Head of the pancreas
  • Gallbladder
  • Common bile duct (CBD)

The Whipple procedure is a complex surgery done for carcinomas involving the head of the pancreas. It is done only in cases when:

  • The entire duodenum has to be removed e.g. in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
  • Tumour encroaches in the first part of the duodenum, or stomach
  • A clear resection margin is not achieved by pylorus-preserving pancreatoduodenectomy

Option B: In Billroth II loop gastrojejunostomy, two-thirds of the stomach is removed, the duodenal stump is closed and the stomach is anastomosed to the jejunum. It helps to re-establish gastrointestinal continuity following antrectomy for complicated peptic ulcer disease.

Option C: Kasai procedure or Roux-en-Y hepato-porto-enterostomy is done for all types of extrahepatic biliary atresia. It involves the excision of all extrahepatic bile duct remnants up to the liver capsule and the gallbladder. Following this, a Roux-en-Y loop of jejunum is mobilized and anastomosed to the exposed area of the liver capsule above the bifurcation of the portal vein creating a portoenterostomy.

The Kasai procedure or Roux-en-Y hepato-porto-enterostomy is shown in the image below.

Correct answer: D. Laying open fistulotomy shows improvement but does not eradicate the disease

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of fistula-in-ano. Laying open fistulotomy is the surest management method to eradicate the disease. 

Fistula-in -ano:

A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal hollow tract or cavity that is lined with granulation tissue and that connects a primary opening inside the anal canal to a secondary opening in the perianal skin.

The most common cause is perianal abscess. Other causes include tuberculosis or Crohn's disease.

Symptoms:

  • Perianal pain
  • Discharge - intermittent purulent discharge (which may be bloody) 

Goodsall's rule:

Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula.

  • Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract.
  • Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

Exceptions to Goodsall’s Rule

However, exceptions to this rule often occur: Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

Investigations:

The investigations available for fistula-in-ano are as follows:

  • Fistulogram
  • Endoanal ultrasound
  • MRI
  • Computed tomography (CT) scan
  • Endocoil MRI
  • Hydrogen peroxide–enhanced 3-D endoanal ultrasonography

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard investigation for fistula imaging. It helps us to identify the secondary extensions of the track, which when missed may cause persistence of the fistula. (Option-A)

Treatment:

  • Control of constipation
  • Sitz bath
  • Fistulotomy
  • Fistulectomy
  • Ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT)
  • Setons
  • Advancement flaps

Important points to remember:

Laying open is the surest method of eradication, but sphincter division may result in incontinence due to sphincter dysfunction(Option-C)

Seton's technique:

Seton’s technique is used in the management of fistula-in-ano. The seton should be non-absorbable, non-degenerative, and comfortable. A seton is a drain placed through a fistula to maintain drainage and/or induce fibrosis. It is left in place for 3 months. Seton's technique induces fibrosis and has very good evidence of healing. If there is evidence of good healing it is removed. (Option-B)

For fistulas that involve more than 30% of the sphincter or those which are distal to the dentate line, loosely placement of seton through the track helps to facilitate drainage of any sepsis and to preserve the sphincter.

This may be converted to a cutting seton by gradually tightening at regular intervals to promote fibrosis and to slowly cut through the involved sphincter muscle, thus helps in eliminating the fistula while maintaining the continuity of the sphincter.

The given image shows the procedure of obtaining a split-thickness skin graft using a handheld Humby knife. The best cosmetic appearance is generally seen with full-thickness skin grafts. 

The most preferable donor site is buttock in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh.

  • The graft is taken from the donor site with a handheld Humby knife or dermatome knife.
  • Grafts are perforated to allow exudates to escape and improve ‘take’. It can further be meshed to allow expansion.
  • Grafts will take up only on the beds which are vascularized, hence preparation of wound bed is an essential step.
  • Skin grafts are completely dependent on nutrition on the tissue over which they are placed and can heal well over muscle, perichondrium, and periosteum. They do not take well over bone or cartilage or on tissue that has been irradiated or infected or is hypovascular.
  • A clean healthy wound bed with a meshed graft tied in place to stop movement will encourage take.
  • The presence of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci is a contraindication in grafting as it can destroy split grafts completely and also convert donors to full-thickness defects.
  • The donor area is dressed appropriately and the dressing is opened after 10 days and not earlier. 

The given image shows Humby's knife. The average thickness of the graft obtained from a Humbys knife is 0.3 mm.

 

Split thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts.

Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. 

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

  • Large grafts can be harvested.
  • In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns.
  • Uptake is good. Meshing can be done i.e. small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this and this improves graft take up. 
  • Meshing also allows the graft to expand.

Advantages of full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft:

  • It has a lesser degree of post graft contraction
  • Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.

The non-expanding subcapsular hematoma over 30% of the surface area is suggestive of grade II splenic injury. These patients are managed by angiography and embolization, and if it fails, the next step in management is a spleen-saving technique or splenorrhaphy.

Splenorrhaphy is a procedure done to preserve the spleen parenchyma. These involve all the surgical procedures done to save the spleen parenchyma while splenectomy is the entire surgical removal of the viscera. Splenorrhaphy should not be performed if the patient is unstable if there are multiple injuries or extensive splenic injury. 

Grades of splenic injury:

Grade Injury
I Non-expanding subcapsular hematoma (<10% of surface area) or laceration, <1 cm of parenchymal depth
II Non-expanding subcapsular hematoma (10-50% of surface area) or laceration, 1-3 cm of parenchymal depth which does not involve the trabecular vessels
III

Hematoma > 50% of surface area or expanding

  • Ruptured subcapsular or parenchymal hematoma,
  • Intraparenchymal hematoma >5 cm or expanding Or
    Laceration, >3 cm parenchymal depth or involving
    trabecular vessels
IV Laceration involving segmental or hilar vessels leading to major devascularization (>25% of the spleen)
V Shattered spleen
or
A hilar vascular injury that devascularizes the spleen.

Management of splenic trauma:

Grade I and II injuries:

They are usually hemodynamically stable and are managed non-operatively. Initially, these patients are managed conservatively with regular monitoring of vitals, hematocrit, and serial CECT.

If the grade of injury is found to increase, then angiography and embolization of the bleeding vessel are done to achieve hemostasis. If angiography and embolization fail to achieve hemostasis, or if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable, then a splenorrhaphy is done.

Grade III injuries that are hemodynamically stable are managed like that of grades I and II, while those that are hemodynamically unstable are managed like that of grades IV and V.

Grade IV and V injuries patients are usually hemodynamically unstable and splenectomy is done.

Other options: 

Option A: Repeat angiography and embolization are unlikely to help as it has already failed once in this patient. 

Option B: Conservative management will not stop the ongoing hemorrhage that is present in this patient. It is useful in patients who are no longer bleeding. 

Option C: Splenectomy is not required in this patient as they have a grade II injury and are still hemodynamically stable.

Buerger's disease is a progressive nonatherosclerotic segmental inflammatory disease that most often affects small- and medium-sized arteries, veins, and nerves of the lower extremities. It is characterized by occlusive disease of small- and medium-sized arteries, thrombophlebitis of the superficial or deep veins, and Raynaud’s syndrome.

The normal aortomesenteric angle is between 38-65 degrees.   • Profound weight loss
  • Abdominal surgery
  • Inflammatory diseases of the abdomen
  • Immobilization in a cast that increases lordosis and accentuates the angle of the SMA with the aorta (cast syndrome)

  • Laparoscopic lysis of the ligament of Treitz is beneficial in a few cases.
  • The following surgical procedures can be done- duodenojejunostomy, gastrojejunostomy, and duodenal derotation (Strong procedure).

  • Secondary metastasis: Fine-needle aspiration and biopsy is performed. Tests for pheochromocytoma should always be done before this procedure to avoid precipitating a hypertensive crisis.

Correct answer: C. Mechanical ventilation

The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing contiguous rib fractures on the right side suggest flail's chest.

It is characterized by contiguous rib fractures and paradoxical respiration following blunt trauma to the chest wall. Mechanical ventilation (like Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is the management of flail chest with respiratory failure.

Flail Chest :

  • A flail chest occurs when a segment of the chest wall does not have bony continuity with the rest of the thoracic cage.
  • This condition results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, i.e. 2 adjacent ribs or 3 or more ribs fractured in two or more places.
  • The blunt force required to disrupt the integrity of the thoracic cage typically produces an underlying pulmonary contusion as well.

Clinical Features:

On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and less air, therefore, moves into the lungs. On expiration, the segment moves outwards(paradoxical respiration).

Diagnosis - Made clinically, not by radiography. To confirm the diagnosis the chest wall can be observed for the paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment for several respiratory cycles and during coughing. Voluntary splinting as a result of pain, mechanically impaired chest wall movement, and the associated lung contusion are all causes of hypoxia and respiratory failure.

The patient is also at high risk of developing a pneumothorax or hemothorax.

Treatment

  • Chest strapping or splinting should be avoided
  • Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates) or epidural analgesia and physiotherapy.
  • IPPV (Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is reserved for cases developing respiratory failure despite adequate analgesia and oxygen.

Other options:

Option A: Chest tube drainage can be done in traumatic pulmonary contusion associated with pneumothorax or hemothorax

Option B: Intrapleural local analgesia can be given if the patient has a chest tube inserted. Since the chest tube drainage is only done after stabilising the patient, intrapleural analgesia is not the best line of treatment at this stage.

Option D: Surgical fixation of the fracture is done only in patients with severe chest injury and pulmonary contusion. Also, surgery should be proceeded only after the patient's condition is stabilised.

Gastroschisis represents a congenital anomaly characterized by a defect in the anterior abdominal wall. The abdominal contents protrude through this defect. questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Addisonian crisis

The given clinical scenario of hypotension with no presence of bleeding and bilateral adrenalectomy is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis. It is a life-threatening condition caused due to sudden insufficiency of adrenal hormones.

Acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal or addisonian's crisis) is a medical emergency caused due to a precipitating illness unmasking insufficiency or trauma or severe sepsis causing adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome) or surgical removal of the glands. It presents with non-specific symptoms such as shock with fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypocalcemia and electrolyte imbalances. It may be often misdiagnosed as an acute abdominal emergency.

Adrenal insufficiency can be primary (due to adrenal pathology), secondary (due to pituitary pathology- lack of ACTH) or tertiary (due to hypothalamus pathology- lack of CRH). Adrenal crisis requires immediate intervention owing to its high mortality rate. Immediate rehydration is initiated with a saline infusion at 1 litre/hr with continuous cardiac monitoring. 

Other options :

Option b : SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion) involves excessive secretion of ADH despite normal or low plasma osmolality. This causes water retention, diluting serum sodium, and increasing urine osmolality. The resultant fluid overload can cause nausea, vomiting, and low BUN.

Option c : Central diabetes insipidus (DI) is a disorder of the posterior pituitary. It is characterized by decreased ADH leading to large volumes of urine production. Patients present with excessive thirst, nocturia, and urinary frequency. 

Option d : Cerebral salt wasting syndrome results from hypersecretion of atrial natriuretic peptide. It is seen primarily with central nervous system disorders including brain tumors, head trauma, hydrocephalus, neurosurgery, cerebrovascular accidents, and brain death. It is associated with hyponatremia, polyuria and elevated urinary sodium excretion. Treatment is by restoring intravascular volume with sodium chloride and water.

According to the AAST Spleen Injury Scale, how would you grade this injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Grade III

Any injury in the presence of laceration of the spleen greater than 3 cm, accompanied by a subcapsular hematoma covering more than 50% of the surface area is considered as Grade III as per the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) spleen injury scale.

The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt trauma to the abdomen. The severity of splenic injury is graded by the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) spleen injury scale.

Management of Splenic trauma:

Grade I and II injuries:

  • They are usually hemodynamically stable and are managed non-operatively.
  • Initially, these patients are managed conservatively with regular monitoring of vitals and serial CECT.
  • If the grade of injury is found to increase, then angiography and embolization of the bleeding vessel are done to achieve hemostasis.
  • If angiography and embolization fail to achieve hemostasis, or if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable or if there is a contrast blush, then a splenorrhaphy is done.

Grade III injuries that are hemodynamically stable are managed like that of Grades I and II, while those that are hemodynamically unstable are managed like that of Grades IV and V.

Grade IV and V injuries: These patients are usually hemodynamically unstable and splenectomy is done.

questions.raw_text:
A 28-year-old patient presents with difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids for the past nine months. A barium swallow test was performed, and the results are shown in the accompanying image. Based on the Chicago classification, what are the accurate statements?

1.Type I is classical type associated with nonrelaxing LOS and absent peristalsis in the body of the oesophagus. 

2.Type II is associated with absent peristalsis and Pan esophageal pressurisation.

3.Type III is associated with premature spastic contractions with DCI >450 mmHg·s·cm with ≥20% of swallows.

4.Type III is associated with premature spastic contractions with DCI >540 mmHg·s·cm with ≥20% of swallows.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1,2,3

The above clinical scenario along with the barium swallow showing a bird beak appearance are suggestive of achalasia cardia and according to Chicago classification option d is correct, which includes statement 1,2,3 as follows.

  1. Type I is classical type associated with nonrelaxing LOS and absent peristalsis in the body of the oesophagus.
  2. Type II is associated with absent peristalsis and Pan esophageal pressurisation.
  3. Type III is associated with premature spastic contractions with DCI >450 mmHg·s·cm with ≥20% of swallows.

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder. It is characterized by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation in response to swallowing. These abnormalities cause a functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction. 

Esophageal manometry shows:

  • Incomplete LES relaxation in response to swallowing.
  • High resting LES pressure.
  • Absent esophageal peristalsis.

On performing a timed barium study, barium will be retained for more than five minutes. The fluoroscopic examination will reveal a dilated esophagus that tapers to form a bird's beak at the gastroesophageal junction as seen in the image above. Endoscopy and biopsy are usually carried out to rule out cancer. 24 hr pH monitoring is used in the diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

Medical management with sublingual nitroglycerin, nitrates, and calcium-channel blockers for symptomatic relief. Pneumatic dilatation and Botox injection

Surgical management is treatment of choice :

  • Laparoscopic Heller's myotomy is the definitive management - The major complication associated with this procedure is gastro-oesophageal reflux. So it is best to combine it with partial anterior fundoplication (Heller–Dor operation).
  • Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is a recently introduced, advanced natural-orifice approach for myotomy.
  • Open Esophageal Myotomy - rarely done.

questions.raw_text: A 4-year-old-boy was brought to emergency department with complaints of acute radiating pain in right iliac region and during surgery the following structure was found. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meckel’s Diverticulum

The clinical history and the image are both suggestive of Meckel's Diverticulum.

Meckel’s diverticulum is a true diverticulum, which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel. The diverticula which contain all the layers of the intestine are called true diverticula. It is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct that develops during weeks 5-7 of gestation.

The rule of 2's (Mnemonic for Meckel’s diverticulum) :

  • 2 types of heterotopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic)(Option d).
  • 2% incidence
  • located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve
  • approximately 2 inches in length
  • Usually symptomatic by 2 years of age

The most common presentation is painless, massive, lower GI bleed in children younger than 5 years. Meckel's diverticulum can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.

A bleeding Meckel's diverticulum may be confirmed by a 99 mTc-pertechnetate isotope scan to detect ectopic gastric mucosa. 

Surgical treatment is the definitive therapy for Meckel’s diverticulum. A simple V-shaped diverticulectomy with transverse closure of the ileum is the ideal surgical approach.

The following diagram shows the various anomalies that arise as a result of the failure of normal regression of vitellointestinal duct:

Other Options:

Option A: The most common tumor of the appendix is the well-differentiated neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor. This neoplasm, which is almost always benign, most frequently forms a solid bulbous swelling at the distal tip of the appendix.

Option B: Adenocarinoma of  the appendix is very rare, accounting for 0.5% of all gastrointestinal cancers. They are detected in 0.08 to 0.1% of appendectomy specimens. Mucinous is a subtype of the adenocarinoma of  the appendix.

Option D: In bowel loop obstruction, the obstructed bowel loops are centrally located and lie transversely. In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. Additionally, a distended cecum may exhibit a gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.

Correct answer: D. The catheter tip lies in the proximal superior vena cava

In the scenario provided, the statement that "the catheter tip lies in the proximal superior vena cava" is false. The correct positioning is in the distal superior vena cava.

Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) is the provision of all nutritional requirements via the intravenous route, without utilizing the gastrointestinal tract.

Indications: TPN is indicated when a patient’s energy and protein needs cannot be met through enteral feeding. Common clinical scenarios include:

  • Massive resection of the small intestine
  • Presence of intestinal fistulae
  • Prolonged intestinal failure for other reasons

TPN can be administered through:

Central Venous Catheter:

  • Inserted via the subclavian vein (Option c) or internal/external jugular vein.
  • Preferred for long-term parenteral nutrition.
  • Hickman lines are commonly used for long term parenteral nutrition (Option a) and are inserted with fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance.
  • These lines include a small cuff to minimize line dislodgement and reduce the risk of line sepsis.

Peripheral Line:

  • Appropriate for short-term feeding (up to 2 weeks).
  • Can be administered via a dedicated catheter (PICC line) or a conventional short cannula in a peripheral vein.
  • PICC lines have a mean duration of survival of about 7 days (Option b ).
  • Disadvantage is thrombophlebitis.

Catheter Tip Positioning:

  • A post-insertion chest X-ray is essential to confirm the absence of pneumothorax.
  • Correct positioning of the catheter tip in the distal superior vena cava to minimize the risk of central venous or cardiac thrombosis.

On examina​tion, the swelling moves ​with protrusion of tongue‌ and deglutition. What is​ the acquired complicatio​n associated with the giv​en condition?
questions.raw_text: A 25 year old male complaints of a painful midline swelling persistent since many years associated with clear watery discharge since 1 week. On examination, the swelling moves with protrusion of tongue and deglutition. What is the acquired complication associated with the given condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Papillary cell carcinoma o‌f thyroid gland

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroglossal fistula

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a thyroglossal cyst and thyroglossal fistula is the acquired complication of Thyroglossal cyst. 

A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital midline neck swelling that typically presents during childhood. It represents the persistence of the thyroglossal tract. It can occur anywhere along the migratory course of the duct: 

Beneath foramen cecum → Floor of mouth → Suprahyoid → Region of thyroid cartilage → Subhyoid (most common site)

Clinical features of thyroglossal cyst:

  • Classically the cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion. This indicates attachment to the hyoid bone. 
  • Swelling is smooth, soft, fluctuant (cystic), nontender, mobile, often transilluminant.
  • Thyroid fossa is empty, if there is no thyroid in normal location.

Complications of thyroglossal cyst:

  • The most common complication is infection.
  • Thyroglossal fistula is an acquired condition that either follows infection of the cyst which bursts open or due to inadequate removal of the cyst.
  • 1% of thyroglossal duct cysts are found to be malignant of which the most common type of cancer is papillary (85%).

Sistrunk’s operation is performed to excise the cyst and prevent a recurrence. It involves excision of the whole thyroglossal tract, involving removal of the body of the hyoid bone, and suprahyoid tract through the tongue base to the vallecula at the site of the primitive foramen cecum along with the core of tissue on either side.

Other options :

Option a : Papillary cell carcinoma of thyroid gland is the most common thyroid carcinoma. It is most common in iodine-sufficient areas, children, and those exposed to ionizing radiation. The mean age of presentation is a 3rd-4th decade and is more common in women than men (2:1). Dysphagia, dysphonia, and dyspnea are associated with local invasion. It usually presents as a cold nodule on the scan.

Option b : Infection is the most common complication of thyroglossal cyst.

Option d : Cystic hygroma is usually seen in neonates and early childhood. They are cystic swellings filled with lymph fluid and are characteristically brilliantly translucent. They occur in the neck and can involve the parotid, submandibular, tongue, etc. The swelling is soft and partially compressible. Definitive treatment is the excision of the swelling.

questions.text: During rounds, a surgery r‌esident instructed the in​tern to closely monitor t‍he burns patient for prop​er fluid resuscitation. W‍hat is the best parameter​ to assess the adequacy o​f fluid resuscitation in ‌a patient?
questions.raw_text: During rounds, a surgery resident instructed the intern to closely monitor the burns patient for proper fluid resuscitation. What is the best parameter to assess the adequacy of fluid resuscitation in a patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urine Output

Urine output is the best parameter to monitor adequacy of fluid resuscitation and is the best measure of end organ perfusion.

Adequate end-organ perfusion is best indicated by urine output of  >0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h. However, it does not give a minute-to-minute value.

Urine output should be between 0.5 and 1.0 mL/kg body weight per hour. If the urine output is below this, the infusion rate should be increased by 50%. If the urine output is inadequate and the patient is showing signs of hypoperfusion, then a bolus of 10 mL/kg body weight should be given.

Signs of hypoperfusion include, restlessness with tachycardia, cool peripheries and high hematocrit.

The average normal urine output is approximately 1500 mL/day. A minimum urine output of 400 mL/day is essential to excrete the end products of protein metabolism.

Fluid loss occurs mainly by four routes:

  • Lungs: Approximately 400 mL of water is lost in expired air every 24 hours.
  • Skin: In a temperate climate the loss is between 600 and 1000 mL/day.
  • Urine: The normal urine output is approximately 1500 mL/day.
  • Faeces: About 60 and 150 mL of water are lost daily in patients with normal bowel function.

The level of consciousness is an important marker for cerebral perfusion.

The only clinical indicators of perfusion of the gastrointestinal tract and muscular beds are measures of lactic acidosis (lactate and base deficit) and mixed venous oxygen saturation.

Other options:

Option A: Central venous pressure (CVP) is the mean pressure in the superior vena cava, used for estimation of preload and right atrial pressure.

Normal CVP ranges from 2 to 7 mm Hg (3 to 9 cm H2O). A sick or injured patient with a CVP <3 mm Hg is presumed to be volume depleted and may be given fluids with relative safety. However, CVP is unreliable in assessing volume status or left ventricular function with respect to resusitation.

Options C and D: Blood pressure and oxygen saturation do not reflect body fluid levels.

Correct answer: A. Hadfield’s operation

The given clinical scenario with mammography showing broken needle calcification is suggestive of duct ectasia, Hadfield’s operation is the next best step in management of duct ectasia as the condition is not resolving with antibiotics.

Duct ectasia is the focal dilatation of the lactiferous ducts. It is the most common cause of nipple discharge in non-lactating women. This condition is strongly associated with smoking.The initial stage of this disease consists of dilatation of one or more lactiferous ducts. These ducts get filled with stagnant brown or green-colored secretions which is shown in the image below: 

 

In the later stages, the accumulation of fluid in the lactiferous ducts leads to infection and inflammation, due to irritation, causing periductal mastitis. If the condition does not resolve, it can lead to the formation of a subareolar mass or abscess, and even mammary duct fistulas. The persistence of this condition eventually leads to fibrosis, which can cause slit-like retraction of the nipple.

Mammography showing the characteristic broken needle calcification which is shown in the image below:

Initial episodes can be managed with antibiotics. Recurrent episodes of the disease are best managed by Hadfield operation (cone Excision of the major ducts). This operation consists of the excision of all the major lactiferous ducts.  

Other options:

Option b : Webster operation is a circum-areolar operation done for the excision of fibroadenoma.

Option c : Microdochectomy is performed If a single duct is involved which is Duct papilloma.

questions.raw_text: Considering the distinctive radiological finding presented below, what is the most probable diagnosis, and what is the suggested management?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute pancreatitis, intrav‌enous fluids and pain man​agement

options.text: Chronic pancreatitis, panc‌reatic enzyme replacement​ and pain management

options.text: Pancreatic cancer, surgica‌l resection or chemothera​py

questions.correct_answer: B. Chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic enzyme replacement and pain management
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic enzyme replacement and pain management

The given image shows the chain of lakes appearance in the biliary tree. This is seen in chronic pancreatitis. Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy is indicated to manage digestive insufficiency, while pain management strategies are crucial for symptom control.

The chain of lakes appearance is due to a dilated main duct with clubbing and dilatation of the side branches - due to scarring and strictures in the pancreatic duct caused by repeated inflammation. 

Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disease in which there is an irreversible destruction of pancreatic tissue. Patients can present with steatorrhoea i.e., the passage of offensive-smelling large stools due to fat malabsorption. It is more common in males, with a male: female ratio of 4:1. ERCP is the most sensitive radiologic test for the diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis. 

Other options:

Option A: Acute pancreatitis caused by gallstones or alcohol can present with pancreatic edema and inflammation. Acute pancreatitis is not associated with strictures and obstruction. CT shows acute interstitial pancreatitis with diffuse swelling of the pancreas and peripancreatic inflammatory changes (arrows). The pancreas was well-perfused without evidence of necrosis.


Option C: Pancreatic cancer typically presents with irregular ductal narrowing or masses, not the beaded and dilated appearance of the chain of lakes sign. Surgical resection or chemotherapy are treatment options for pancreatic cancer, depending on the stage and spread of the disease.


Option D: Pancreatic pseudocysts appear as fluid-filled collections separate from the ductal system, unlike the chain of lakes pattern within the duct itself. Percutaneous drainage is a minimally invasive procedure for managing symptomatic pseudocysts.

H​e is febrile and tachycar‌dic. The given findings w​ere seen on bedside radio​logical imaging. Which am​ong the following is a li‍kely cause of this?
questions.raw_text: A 42-year old alcoholic and a chronic smoker presented with bouts of vomiting and stabbing pain in the epigastrium. He was binge drinking shortly before the symptoms started. He is febrile and tachycardic. The given findings were seen on bedside radiological imaging. Which among the following is a likely cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peptic ulcer perforation

In the given clinical scenario, the diagnosis is suggestive of Pneumoperitoneum and the likely cause for this would be peptic ulcer perforation.

Gastric ulcers are more prone to perforate than bleed. Thus, these perforations lead to pneumoperitoneum which is an emergency and warrants immediate surgical intervention. 

The classical description of a patient with a perforated peptic ulcer is described in three stages:

Stage of peritonism: Initial 6 hours - patient presents with an acute burning epigastric pain with or without vomiting. Leakage of gastric acid into the peritoneal cavity causes diaphragmatic irritation which may lead to pain referred to the shoulder tip (Option D) and tracking of fluid in the right para-colic gutter may lead to right iliac fossa pain. Abdominal guarding with diminished abdominal movements on respiration is noted and the patient avoids movement to prevent pain. Tachycardia (Option B) is noted but pyrexia does not set in.
Stage of reaction: the symptoms temporarily subside due to the dilution of the exudate in the peritoneal cavity but abdominal rigidity remains (Option A).
Stage of diffuse peritonitis: sunken face, hollow cheeks, dry mucous membranes (facies hippocratica) with fever, tachycardia, low volume pulse and increasing abdominal distension.
Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Perforation is an indication for surgical exploration. Perforations less than 1 cm can be closed primarily with an omental patch repair, while larger perforations may require a distal gastrectomy with a roux-en-y reconstruction. Patients require prolonged PPI therapy postoperatively.

 Other options: 

A. Tension pneumothorax - presents with a rapid hemodynamic compromise with absent breath sounds. Pneumoperitoneum rarely is caused by pneumothorax, and downward displacement of air is more likely seen in retroperitoneal spaces.

C. Boerhaave syndrome or spontaneous esophageal rupture - occurs in alcoholics after binge drinking, due to forced vomiting from the closed glottis.  Pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema are seen here. 

D. Mallory Weis tear - longitudinal mucosal tear resulting in upper GI bleeding. It is commonly seen in alcoholics.

Split thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ) is a partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis. Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles.

  • The most preferable donor site is buttock in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children.

She is diagnosed with squamous cell cancer involving  >2/3rd of lip. Management is done using the flap reconstruction surgery, as shown in image below. Identify the flap used?
