Correct answer: D. Abbe Estlander flap

The patient has squamous cell carcinoma affecting more than two-thirds of the lip, and the treatment involves reconstruction using an Abbe-Estlander flap. It is  based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves only the commissure, the Estlander flap is used, and the Abbé flap is used for midline defects. Abbe-Estlander Flap is used for mixed defects.

Lip cancer most commonly occurs in men from 50 to 70 years old but can be seen in younger patients. Risk factors include sunlight exposure, smoking, and tobacco use. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of lip cancer. But commonly occurring cancer in the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

Most lip cancers occur in the lower lip followed by the upper lip and commissure. Fournier's gangrene is a polymicrobial infection and a type of necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, external genitalia, and perianal region. Risk factors include immunocompromised states such as HIV, alcoholism, diabetes, etc.  SGLT-2 inhibitors like canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin can also cause Fournier's gangrene. questions.raw_text: A patient came with complaints of  pain in right upper abdomen with yellowish discolouration of eyes. The ultrasound finding is given below. According to WHO classification the cyst belongs to which of the following type?

Correct answer: C. CE 2

The given USG showing the hydatid cyst with multiple septations and a rosette or honeycomb appearance, it is classified as CE 2 according to the WHO classification and Type III according to the Gharbi classification.

Classification of hepatic hydatid cysts is given in the image below.

Hydatid Cyst is a zoonotic infection caused by the Echinococcus species(dog tapeworm ). Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus. Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human-to-human transmission.

The clinical presentation of a hydatid cyst is largely asymptomatic until complications occur. The most common presenting symp­toms are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. The most frequent sign is hepatomegaly.

Approximately 75% of hydatid cysts are located in the right lobe of the liver and are solitary.

CT scan is the best imaging modality for hydatid cysts. It shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline with septa. Diagnosis is suggested by the finding of a multiloculated cyst on ultrasound and is further supported by the finding of a floating membrane within the cysts on a CT scan. Active cysts contain a large number of smaller daughter cysts (multi-vesicular rosette-like cystic lesions with daughter cysts) which is characteristic of hydatid cysts of the liver.

If there is a disruption of the inner layers of the cyst, the following signs may be noted:

  • Water lily sign/ camalote sign - air-fluid level with a floating membrane (as shown below)
  • Rising sun sign/ serpent sign - a double-wall, dry cyst with crumpled membranes lying at its bottom
  • Empty cyst sign - when all the contents are removed 

The ultrasound of an active hydatid cyst shows multiple septations and a rosette or honeycomb appearance (as shown below), it is classified as WHO CE 2 or Gharbi type III.

Other options :

Option a : WHO CE 3a or Gharbi Type II - water-lily sign is seen in hydatid infections when there is detachment of the endocyst membrane which results in floating membranes within the pericyst that mimic the appearance of a water lily, on USG.

Option b : WHO CE 3B or Gharbi type III - Cyst with daughter cyst in solid matrix.

Option d : WHO CE 4 or Gharbi Type IV - Cyst with heterogenous hypoechoic or hyperechoic contents. No daughter cyst.

questions.raw_text: Symptoms of thoracic outlet syndrome can be reproduced when the patient has both arms in the 90° abduction-external rotation position and asked to open and close the hands slowly over a 3-minute period. This provocative test is called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Roos test

The test described in the question is a provocative test for thoracic outlet syndrome called Roos test (Extended arm stress test).

Roos test or EAST Test (Extended Arm Stress Test):

Method:

  • The patient has both arms in the 90° abduction-external rotation postion.
  • The patient is to open and close the hands slowly over a 3-minute period.

Inference:

  • Reproduction of symptoms suggests compression.

The following image below demonstrates the Roos test.

Provocative tests for Thoracic Outlet Syndrome:

Adson test (Scalene Manoeuvre):

Method:

The examiner locates the radial pulse and the patient is asked to:

  • Turn the head towards the affected side
  • Extend the neck
  • Take deep breath and hold

Inference:

A positive test is indicated by a disappearance of the pulse.

Halsted Test (Costoclavicular Manoeuvre):

Method:

  • The examiner locates the radial pulse and draws the patient's shoulder down and back as the patient lifts their chest in an exaggerated "attention" posture.

Inference:

  • A positive test is indicated by an absence of a pulse.

Wright Test (Hyperabduction Manoeuvre)

Method:

  • Patients arm is hyperabducted to 180o and externally rotated

Inference:

  • Loss of radial pulse suggests compression

Allen Test:

Method:

  • The patient is asked to clench both fists tightly for 1 minute at the same time.
  • Pressure is applied over both radial arteries simultaneously so as to occlude them.
  • The patient then opens the fingers of both hands rapidly, and the examiner compares the colour of both. The initial pallor should be replaced quickly by rubor.
  • The test may be repeated, this time occluding the ulnar arteries.

Inference:

  • If the artery is occluded, the colour does not return and pallor remains longer on the affected side.

Membranous urethral rupture usually occurs following a road traffic accident, crush injury, or a fall. It is associated with pelvic fracture and extraperitoneal bladder rupture.

There is typically marked bruising of the pubic area, scrotum and penis. If the diagnosis is suspected, a Retrograde urethrogram(RGU) performed with water-soluble contrast media is confirmatory.

A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as practicable using the Seldinger technique. When suprapubic urinary diversion has been achieved then no further urological management is required until the patient has stabilised. Correct answer: A. Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis

The given clinical scenario with an asymptomatic patient having air under the diaphragm without evidence of peritonitis (sterile pneumoperitoneum) is suggestive of pneumatosis intestinalis.

Pneumatosis Intestinalis presents as multiple gas filled cysts of the gastrointestinal tract. Most common site is jejunum>ileocecal region >colon. It has Equal incidence among males and females and it most commonly occurs in the 4th-7th decades of life. Pneumatosis in neonates is usually associated with necrotizing enterocolitis. The histiopathological finding shows a honeycomb appearance with thin walled cyst ehich break easily and spontaneous rupture of cyst give rise to pneumoperitoneum.

Clinical features are mostly nonspecific,most commonly diarrhea, abdominal pain, abdominal distention, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, and mucus in stools. Diagnosis on plain films is radiolucent areas within the bowel wall (appear as grape-like clusters or tiny bubbles) and alternatively, barium contrast or CT studies can be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Treatment include, management of the uncomplicated primary disease and when symptoms demand treatment, the first line is intermittent high flow oxygen therapy, providing a concentration of 70% continuously for 5 days by nasal specula. The cysts may also resolve with antibiotics, particularly metronidazole and in resistant cases, maintenance treatment with sulfasalazine may be helpful.

  2. Confirmation of fetal presentation
  3. Determine the fetal orientation
  4. Determine which fetal pole occupies the fundus.

The correct sequence is 4, 3, 2, 1:

Leopold First maneuvre - Determine which fetal pole occupies the fundus

Leopold second maneuver - Determine the fetal orientation

Leopold third maneuver - Confirmation of fetal presentation

Leopold fourth maneuver - Determine the degree of descent

Leopold’s first maneuver (fundal grip) is used to determine which fetal pole occupies the fundus.

Leopold’s second maneuver (lateral grip) can be used to determine the fetal orientation based on whether the back is facing anteriorly, transversely, or posteriorly. The palms are placed on either side of the maternal abdomen and gentle deep pressure is exerted. The fetal back is felt as a hard-resistant structure and the fetal limbs are felt as multiple small irregular parts.

Leopold’s third maneuver (Pawlik’s grip) helps to confirm fetal presentation. It is done by grasping the lower part of the maternal abdomen with the thumb and fingers of one hand. The palpation of a hard and round mass indicates that the presenting part is the fetal head. A movable mass suggests that the presenting part is not engaged. If the presenting part is breech, it is felt as a large nodular mass.

Leopold’s fourth maneuver (pelvic grip) helps to determine the degree of descent. The examiner faces the mother's feet, and the fingertips of both hands are positioned on either side of the presenting part. They exert inward pressure and then slide along the axis of the pelvic inlet.

She has had an abortion at 12 weeks of gestation five years back and healthy twins were delivered at term three years ago. Which of the following is the correct representation of her obstetric score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. G3P1A1L2

This woman has had three pregnancies in total (previous abortion, previous twin pregnancy, and current twin pregnancy) with the first pregnancy aborted in the first trimester (12 weeks) and the second pregnancy resulting in the delivery of twins at term. Therefore, her obstetric score would be G3P1A1L2 (Gravida - 3, Para - 1, Abortion - 1, Live birth - 2).

Gravida indicates the number of times a female has been pregnant. It includes present as well as past pregnancy, irrespective of the period of gestation.

Para indicates the number of previous pregnancies that had progressed beyond the period of viability (28 weeks of gestation or more).

Terminologies used in pregnancy:

  1. A nullipara is one who has never completed a pregnancy to the stage of viability. She may or may not have aborted previously.
  2. A nulligravida is one who is not now and never has been pregnant.
  3. A primipara is one who has delivered one viable child. Parity is not increased even if the fetuses are many (twins, triplets).
  4. A primigravida is one who is pregnant for the first time.
  5. A multigravida is one who has previously been pregnant. She may have aborted or have delivered a viable baby.
  6. A multipara is one who has completed two or more pregnancies to the stage of viability or more. A pregnant woman with a previous history of four births or more is called a grand multipara.

It is customary in clinical practice to summarise the past obstetric history by 2 digits

First digit: Number of viable births
Second digit: Number of abortions
Both digits connected with a “+” sign affixing the letter P.
Thus, P1+2 denotes patient had 1 viable birth and 2 abortions.

In this woman, it is denoted as P2+1 as the patient had twin delivery at term and 1 abortion.


In some centres, it is expressed by 4 digits connected by dashes, P(A-B-C-D)
A: Number of term pregnancies (37-42 weeks)
B: Number of preterm pregnancies (28 to less than 37 weeks)
C: Number of miscarriages (less than 28 weeks)
D: Number of children alive at present.

Note: The period of viability is when the fetus is capable of independent existence. The WHO defines it to be 24 weeks while the Indian definition is 28 weeks.

Which of the following parameters are included in the modified Biophysical profile score?

  1. Oxytocin challenge test
  2. Contraction stress test
  3. Amniotic fluid index
  4. Vibroacoustic nonstress test
  5. Amniotic fluid volume

Correct answer: B. 3 and 4

Vibroacoustic nonstress test/Nonstress test (NST) and Amniotic fluid index (AFI) (options 3 and 4) are included in the modified biophysical score.

Biophysical profile (BPP)/Manning score provides a means of accessing fetal health. Involves the measurement of the following: (Mnemonic: BATMaN)

  • B-Breathing 
  • A-Amniotic fluid volume (AFV)
  • T-Tone of fetus
  • M-Movements of fetus
  • N-Non Stress Test (NST)

Normal score: >=8 (with normal AFV). The maximum score is 10.

Abnormal scores:

  • 8/10 with decreased AFV: suspicion of chronic fetal asphyxia
  • 6/10: Possible fetal asphyxia
  • 4/10: Probable fetal asphyxia
  • 0-2/10: Almost certain fetal asphyxia

Maternal sedatives and narcotics can significantly lower the score.

The biophysical profile was modified to includes two parameters- the biweekly vibroacoustic nonstress test or Nonstress test and the AFI. 

The nonstress test describes fetal heart rate acceleration in response to fetal movements, using a Doppler to detect fetal heart rate acceleration. Fetal movements are recorded as perceived by the mother. Acoustic stimula­tion nonstress test is one in which a loud external sound is used to startle the fetus and provoke heart rate accelerations.

  • Normal modified BPP: Reactive nonstress test with AFI>5cm
  • Abnormal modified BPP: nonreactive nonstress test or AFI <5 cm 

Oxytocin challenge test (Contraction stress test): The fetal heart rate and uterine contrac­tions are recorded simultaneously with an external monitor. If at least three spontaneous contractions of 40 seconds or longer are present in 10 minutes, uterine stimulation is not required. If required, it can be done with iv oxytocin or nipple stimulation.

A positive test(abnormal) is uniform repetitive late fetal heart rate decelerations, which could indicate uteroplacental insufficiency. A negative test would show no late or significant variable decelerations.

The nonstress test is a test of fetal condition, while the contraction stress test is a test of uteroplacental function.

Contraindications of contraction stress testing:

  • Compromised fetus
  • Previous history of cesarean section
  • Complications likely to produce preterm labor
  • Antepartum hemorrhage
  • Multiple pregnancies

  • Simple with atypia: simple hyperplasia with features of nuclear atypia (variation in nuclear shape, size, and prominent nucleoli)
  • Complex without atypia: glands are markedly crowded and irregular
  • Complex with atypia: complex hyperplasia with atypical nuclear features. 

However, there is generally no clear histological distinction between the above mentioned classification, so endometrial hyperplasia is classified into hyperplasia without atypia and atypical hyperplasia/endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia.

Simple with atypia 8%
Complex with atypia 29%

Sling operations are recommended in cases of nulliparous prolapse for those who wish to retain menstrual and child-bearing function. Mackenrodt’s and uterosacral ligaments of the uterus are strengthened, by using nylon or Dacron tapes as slings. A ring pessary is used for patients who cannot be surgically managed, such as pregnant patients, patients in puerperium, and very elderly women unfit for surgery. It is used in adjunct with pelvic floor physiotherapy. Pessaries provide mechanical support to the pelvic organs. The first step after fitting the pessary to check if the pessary is adequately retained is to ask the patient to perform Valsalva's manoeuvre or cough and see if the pessary is in place. After being placed, they need to be changed every 3 months. 

Fothergill's repair also known as Manchester's operation is suitable for women under 40 years who are desirous of retaining their menstrual and reproductive functions. questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presen‌ts with dysmenorrhoea, me​norrhagia, and infertilit​y. After ruling out other​ possible causes, the gyn‌ecologist suspects endome‍triosis. Which of the fol​lowing investigations wil​l be most helpful in the ​diagnosis?

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laparoscopy

In the given clinical scenario, the investigation that will be most helpful in the diagnosis is laparoscopy.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterus. The patient usually presents with symptoms of abdominal pain, dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and infertility. The presence of puckered spots in the posterior fornix is pathognomonic of endometriosis. It is an estrogen-dependent disease of the childbearing age group. The most common site of occurrence is the ovary, followed by the pouch of Douglas.

The gold standard for the diagnosis of endometriosis is visual inspection by laparoscopy, preferably with histological confirmation. Typically, there are small black dots, the so-called powder burns/tattooing seen on the uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas. 

Role of laparoscopy in endometriosis:

  • To detect and diagnose pelvic endometriosis.
  • Locate the site of endometriosis and staging.
  • To take biopsy
  • To surgically treat endometriosis by ablation, removal.

Other investigations:

  • CA-125 levels are raised in endometriosis.
  • Monocyte chemotactic protein (MCP-1) levels are raised in the peritoneal fluid of women with endometriosis.
  • Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an echo-free cyst, low level echoes or clumps of high-density level echoes representing clots.

The image below shows powder burns/tattooing appearance of endometriosis on diagnostic laparoscopy.

Other options:

Option A: Hysteroscopy and Endometrial Biopsy: These evaluate conditions within the uterine cavity, such as polyps or hyperplasia, but endometriosis involves ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus, making this investigation unhelpful for its diagnosis.  

Option B: Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS): While TVUS can detect ovarian endometriomas, it cannot reliably identify peritoneal or deep infiltrating endometriosis, limiting its utility in providing a comprehensive diagnosis.  

Option C: Hysterosalpingography (HSG): This test is primarily used to assess tubal patency and uterine contour in infertility workups but does not provide direct visualization of endometrial implants, making it unsuitable for diagnosing endometriosis.

questions.text: An incidental ovarian mass‌ is found when evaluating​ a 19-year-old girl for k​idney stones. The mass is​ removed and its contents‌ are shown below. What is‍ the likely diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: An incidental ovarian mass is found when evaluating a 19-year-old girl for kidney stones. The mass is removed and its contents are shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mature teratoma

The likely diagnosis in this patient with an asymptomatic ovarian mass consisting hair, bone, and sebaceous material is a mature teratoma. 

Teratomas are germ cell tumors. They contain embryonic tissues leading to the differentiation of cells along these pathways. There are three classes of teratomas:

  • Mature (benign) teratomas (eg: Dermoid cyst)
  • Immature (essentially malignant) teratomas (eg: solid teratoma)
  • Monodermal (highly specialized) tumors (eg: Struma ovarii)

Mature cystic teratoma, also known as dermoid cysts are unilocular in structure and have a smooth surface. They usually are lined by squamous epithelium with hair follicles leading to the formation of sebaceous material and hair. Other structures like teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid tissue, and mucous membranes can also be found. 

Most patients are asymptomatic. Some patients may have symptoms because of the mass size of the teratoma. In other patients, ovarian teratomas can result in torsion of the ovary. Other rare complications include rupture of the cyst and spillage of contents into the abdominal cavity. 

Treatment of mature teratomas involves excision in order to prevent complications. Otherwise, mature teratomas are generally innocent. 

Other options: 

Option A - Immature teratomas such as solid teratomas of the ovary are solid and trabeculated. They also contain cartilage, bone, hair, and sebaceous material. There is no structural order. They are generally malignant. Grossly, they have a smooth external surface and are solid on sectioning. There may be areas of necrosis or hemorrhage. 

The following image shows both mature (left) and immature teratomas (right). 

Option C - Struma ovarii is a type of highly specialized teratoma that contains only thyroid tissue. If it is functioning, it may lead to hyperthyroidism. 

Option D - Granulosa cell tumors arise from the sex cords of the gonads. They are solid and generally produce estrogen. They can cause precocious puberty in children, hyperestrogenism in adults, and post-menopausal bleeding. They vary in appearance and range from microscopic to large, solid and cystic, encapsulated masses. If hormonally active, they may be yellow due to intracellular lipids.

The absence of the SRY gene results in the development of the ovaries and the Mullerian system.

In this situation, the gonads will develop into ovaries and the Mullerian duct will differentiate into the uterus, fallopian tubes, and the upper part of the vagina. The master gene responsible for this is the WNT4 gene.

Correct answer: A. Estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle

The image shows a characteristic ferning pattern of cervical mucus seen during the estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle. 

The characteristics of cervical mucous changes under the influence of estrogen and progesterone. During the estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle, the cervical mucus is thin and stretchy due to the presence of sodium chloride in the mucus which shows the characteristic pattern seen above. This pattern disappears once ovulation has taken place due to the activity of progesterone. If previously present, its disappearance is presumptive evidence of corpus luteum activity.  

At the time of ovulation, the mucus becomes thin, watery, and clear that can be stretched up to 10cm. This is called spinnbarkeit or thread test and is presumptive of ovulation. During the progesterone phase, the mucus becomes thick and tenacious, impermeable to the sperms.

Other signs of ovulation are

  • An increase in basal body temperature(BBT) after ovulation due to the thermogenic action of the hormone progesterone. 
  • Urinary LH peak (increase in LH) is usually seen 1 day prior to ovulation.
  • The growth of ovarian follicles is 20 mm or more in size on USG at the time of ovulation.

The menstrual cycle consists of three phases: the menstrual phase, the proliferative phase, and the secretory, or progestational, phase

The menstrual phase is characterized by the discharge of blood and endometrial debris from the vagina due to the withdrawal of progesterone and the degeneration of the corpus luteum (CL).

The proliferative phase is estrogen-dominant and lasts from the end of menstruation to ovulation. It results in the proliferation of endometrial glands and thickened endometrium.

The secretory or progestational phase is progesterone dominant which converts the thickened, estrogen-primed endometrium to a richly vascularized, glycogen-filled tissue for early nourishment of a developing embryo. If fertilization and implantation do not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates and a new follicular phase and menstrual phase begin again.

The non-contraceptive uses of oral contraceptives include all except protection against sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), including HIV.

Oral hormonal contraceptives can be combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) or progesterone-only minipills.

COCPs are a combination of ethinylestradiol at a dose of 20–30 mcg and an orally active progestogen. It is taken starting on the first day of the cycle for 21 days. They are taken at a fixed time of the day, preferably after a meal. Mala-N and Mala-D both contain levonorgestrel (0.15 mg) + ethinylestradiol (30 mcg). Mala-N is supplied free of cost in Family Planning Clinics in India. Each strip contains 21 hormonal tablets and 7 non-hormonal (iron) tablets. 

The mechanism of action is the prevention of ovulation by suppression of the pituitary hormones FSH and LH. Progesterone also acts on the cervical mucus, making it thick and impenetrable by sperm. The pregnancy rate with the COCP is 0.3 per 100 woman-years.

Benefits of the COCP:

  • It is effective in controlling fertility.
  • It causes regular cycles and reduces menstrual blood loss and are, therefore, useful in menorrhagia and polymenorrhea.
  • It lowers the incidence of benign breast neoplastic diseases, such as fibrocystic disease.
  • It reduces the incidence of functional ovarian cysts and ovarian (Option A) and endometrial malignancy (Option D). The incidence of ovarian cancer is reduced by 40% and that of uterine malignancy, by 50%, if taken for 1 year; this effect lasts as long as 10 years after stoppage.
  • It reduces the incidence of ectopic pregnancy (Option B) by suppressing ovulation and reducing the risk in pelvic inflammatory disease.
  • It is useful in endometriosis, acne, and polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD).

Side effects:

  • Higher incidence of breast cancer reported among users
  • Suppression of lactation
  • Occurrence of pituitary adenoma and adenoma of the liver
  • Reduced carbohydrate tolerance (therefore, contraindicated in diabetic women)
  • Migraine, depression, weight gain, and lethargy (due to progesterone)
  • Increased risk of pulmonary embolism and cerebral thrombosis

Ninety-nine percent of women will regain normal menstrual cycles within 6 months of stopping the pills, while the return of fertility is slightly delayed.

Barrier methods like condoms prevent the transmission of STDs.

An ovarian tumor in a young woman which consists of primordial germ cells and is histologically similar to seminoma suggests a diagnosis of an ovarian dysgerminoma. It does not secrete sex hormones.

Dysgerminoma usually arises in young women or in children, with an average incidence at the age of 20. It is the most common malignant germ cell tumour diagnosed during pregnancy. They are primitive neoplasms that do not have the potential for further differentiation. They are the only germ cell malignancy with a significant rate of bilateral ovarian involvement (15-20%).

The tumor is neutral and does not secrete either male or female sex hormones. It secretes placental alkaline phosphatase (ALP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and β-hCG. Serum LDH and the isoenzymes LDH-1 and LDH-2 may be used in monitoring individuals or disease recurrence.

Microscopically, there is a monotonous proliferation of large, rounded, polyhedral clear cells that are rich in cytoplasmic glycogen and contain uniform central nuclei with one or a few prominent nucleoli. The tumor cells are histologically identical to the seminoma of the testis. The counterpart of seminoma in females is dysgerminoma. 

Treatment involves fertility-sparing surgery with unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. It is highly radiosensitive and has a good prognosis.

Correct answer: D. Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal estradiol

Asherman's syndrome has Normal FSH, Normal LH, and Normal estradiol.

Asherman's syndrome is the presence of uterine synechiae, due to the destruction of large areas of the endometrium, most commonly as a result of trauma to the endometrium following pregnancy-related curettages. Oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea, dysmenorrhoea, abortion, and infertility are seen with uterine synechiae. The laboratory investigations and hormonal assays are generally normal in isolated cases of uterine synechiae. Diagnosis is generally established using hysteroscopy. Moth-eaten appearance on hysterosalpingography suggests a diagnosis of Asherman syndrome. Treatment is by hysteroscopic adhesiolysis. 

Condition Lab markers 
1. Sheehan's syndrome C. Low LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol
2. Premature Ovarian failure D. High LH, High FSH, Low estradiol
3. PCOS B. High LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol
4. Asherman's syndrome A. Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal estradiol

Premature Ovarian failure or premature menopause is the development of menopause before the age of 40 years. It is diagnosed when at least 2 serum FSH levels are elevated (>40 mIU/l) when measured at least 1 month apart in a woman <40 years. The other findings consistent with POF include low estradiol and an elevated FSH/LH ratio.

PCOS is a multisystem, metabolic, endocrine dysfunction that commonly occurs among women in the reproductive age group. LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls. Estrone(E1) levels are elevated but estradiol level in PCOS is low in comparison to Estrone (E1). 

Sheehan's syndrome/ pituitary apoplexy is hemorrhagic infarction of large pituitary adenomas or pituitary infarction due to traumatic major blood loss. If this blood loss occurs during delivery, it's called Sheehan's syndrome. Affected women may present with panhypopituitarism and may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to the deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to the deficiency of gonadotropins).

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laparoscopy

In the given clinical scenario, the investigation that will be most helpful in the diagnosis is laparoscopy.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterus. The patient usually presents with symptoms of abdominal pain, dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and infertility. The presence of puckered spots in the posterior fornix is pathognomonic of endometriosis. It is an estrogen-dependent disease of the childbearing age group. The most common site of occurrence is the ovary, followed by the pouch of Douglas.

The gold standard for the diagnosis of endometriosis is visual inspection by laparoscopy, preferably with histological confirmation. Typically, there are small black dots, the so-called powder burns/tattooing seen on the uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas. 

Role of laparoscopy in endometriosis:

  • To detect and diagnose pelvic endometriosis.
  • Locate the site of endometriosis and staging.
  • To take biopsy
  • To surgically treat endometriosis by ablation, removal.

Other investigations:

  • CA-125 levels are raised in endometriosis.
  • Monocyte chemotactic protein (MCP-1) levels are raised in the peritoneal fluid of women with endometriosis.
  • Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an echo-free cyst, low level echoes or clumps of high-density level echoes representing clots.

The image below shows powder burns/tattooing appearance of endometriosis on diagnostic laparoscopy.

Other options:

Option A: Hysteroscopy and Endometrial Biopsy: These evaluate conditions within the uterine cavity, such as polyps or hyperplasia, but endometriosis involves ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus, making this investigation unhelpful for its diagnosis.  

Option B: Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS): While TVUS can detect ovarian endometriomas, it cannot reliably identify peritoneal or deep infiltrating endometriosis, limiting its utility in providing a comprehensive diagnosis.  

Option C: Hysterosalpingography (HSG): This test is primarily used to assess tubal patency and uterine contour in infertility workups but does not provide direct visualization of endometrial implants, making it unsuitable for diagnosing endometriosis.

The verrucous growths may appear discrete or coalesce to form large cauliflower-like growths (as shown in the image below). Human papillomaviruses are implicated in causing this condition.

Genital warts:

Genital warts/ venereal warts/ condyloma acuminata are verrucous growths that affect the skin of the labia majora, perineum, perianal region, and vulva. They are most commonly caused by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11. The growths may be discrete or coalesce to form cauliflower-like growth. The disease is sexually transmitted. The growth of the warts is favored by vaginal discharge, the use of oral contraceptives, and pregnancy.

HPV causes structural changes in the epithelial cells of the skin. These abnormal epithelial cells are called koilocytes, and their presence is characteristic of HPV infection. The koilocytes have large hyperchromatic nuclei and a perinuclear halo.

Diagnosis is made by colposcopic studies. The lesions on the vulva are stained by toluidine blue. The skin with abnormal nuclei retains the blue dye. These abnormal areas are then biopsied for histopathological examination.

  • Local application of podophyllin 25% in alcohol or podophyllin 20% in tincture benzoin or podophyllin cream
  • 25% trichloroacetic acid plus 5% fluorouracil
  • Diathermy loop, laser ablation, cryotherapy for larger lesions
  • Surgical excision
  • Interferon ointment or local injection

A pregnant woman with a history of >4 births is referred to as a grand multipara.

Terminologies used in pregnancy:

Gravida indicates the number of times a female has been pregnant. It includes present as well as past pregnancy, irrespective of the period of gestation.

Para indicates the number of previous pregnancies that had progressed beyond the period of viability (28 weeks of gestation or more).

  1. A nullipara is one who has never completed a pregnancy to the stage of viability. She may or may not have aborted previously.
  2. A nulligravida is one who is not now and never has been pregnant.
  3. A primipara is one who has delivered one viable child. Parity is not increased even if the fetuses are many (twins, triplets).
  4. A primigravida is one who is pregnant for the first time.
  5. A multigravida is one who has previously been pregnant. She may have aborted or have delivered a viable baby.
  6. A multipara is one who has completed two or more pregnancies to the stage of viability or more. A pregnant woman with a previous history of more than four births is called a grand multipara.

It occurs mostly due to obstetric injuries such as prolonged labor, and instrumental or manipulative deliveries. Patients present with true incontinence characterized by constant dribbling of urine.

Small fistulas due to difficult childbirth can heal spontaneously. In the case of an established fistula, it is better to wait for about 3 months for all tissue inflammation to subside, before surgery is undertaken. Most vesicovaginal fistulas are repaired per vaginally. The various surgeries done for the repair of VVF are as follows:

  • Latzko procedure: It is done by denudation of vaginal epithelium around fistulous edges and approximation of raw surface with absorbable sutures. This technique is suited for post-hysterectomy fistula that is caused by cancer cervix (Option A). It can lead to narrowing of the vagina or vaginal atresia. Fistula located at the vaginal vault, post hysterectomy is the most difficult to treat, this technique is suited for such cases.
  • Chassar-Moir technique: Here, the vagina and bladder are separated and sutured into two layers taking care to avoid tension and overlapping suture lines. 
  • Ureteric implantation into the sigmoid colon in case previous surgeries fail.

Post-operatively, continuous bladder drainage for 14 days (Option C) along with antibiotics is recommended. Vaginal or speculum examination and intercourse are not advised for 3 months after surgery (Option D). Avoiding pregnancy for a year is also recommended. A cesarean section is usually done for future pregnancies.

Myomectomy refers to the removal of fibroids and preserving the uterus. It is indicated in fibroids which present with the following

Fibroids are benign estrogen dependant tumors of the uterine smooth muscles and connective tissue. 

Management of uterine fibroids in asymptomatic patients includes observation with regular follow-up regardless of the size of the fibroid. Surgery is indicated in cornual fibroids if it causes infertility or pedunculated fibroids (due to the risk of torsion). 

In symptomatic patients, medical therapy is done to shrink the fibroid. It acts as a preoperative adjunct. Surgical methods such as myomectomy, laparoscopic myolysis, hysterectomy, and endometrial ablation are tried for patients with persistent symptoms despite conservative management. Hysterectomy is done in postmenopausal women and in multiparous women who have completed their families or are not desirous of childbirth.

Sling operations are recommended in cases of nulliparous prolapse for those who wish to retain menstrual and child-bearing function. Mackenrodt’s and uterosacral ligaments of the uterus are strengthened, by using nylon or Dacron tapes as slings. A ring pessary is used for patients who cannot be surgically managed, such as pregnant patients, patients in puerperium, and very elderly women unfit for surgery. It is used in adjunct with pelvic floor physiotherapy. Pessaries provide mechanical support to the pelvic organs. The first step after fitting the pessary to check if the pessary is adequately retained is to ask the patient to perform Valsalva's manoeuvre or cough and see if the pessary is in place. After being placed, they need to be changed every 3 months. 

Fothergill's repair also known as Manchester's operation is suitable for women under 40 years who are desirous of retaining their menstrual and reproductive functions. It involves anterior colporrhaphy with amputation of the cervix. The mackenrodt ligaments are sutured in the front of the cervix and colpoperineorrhaphy is done. questions.text: A 24-year-old Rh-negative ‌G2P1 mother was delivered​ by cesarean section at 3​7 weeks gestation. The ba‌by is found to be Rh-posi​tive. To access fetomater‌nal transfusion a Kleihae‌ur Betke test was done wh​ich detected 20 ml of fet​al RBCs. What is the dose‍ of anti-D that should be​ administered to the moth‌er? (Assume fetal hematoc​rit to be 50 percent)
questions.raw_text: A 24-year-old Rh-negative G2P1 mother was delivered by cesarean section at 37 weeks gestation. The baby is found to be Rh-positive. To access fetomaternal transfusion a Kleihaeur Betke test was done which detected 20 ml of fetal RBCs. What is the dose of anti-D that should be administered to the mother? (Assume fetal hematocrit to be 50 percent)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 400 µg

10 µg of anti-D is required for every 1 mL of fetal whole blood or 0.5 mL of fetal RBCs.Hence for 20 mL of fetal RBCs, 400 µg of anti-D should be administered.

Kleihauer–Betke test is the most commonly used quantitative test for measuring the fetal red cells in the maternal circulation. The reagent used for the Kleihauer–Betke test is citric acid. It is also known as the acid elution test.

Principle: Fetal erythrocytes contain hemoglobin F, which is more resistant to acid elution than hemoglobin A in the maternal erythrocytes.

After exposure to acid, only fetal hemoglobin remains, such that after staining, the fetal erythrocytes appear red and adult cells appear as ghosts. These fetal cells are counted per 50 low-power fields. If there are 80 fetal erythrocytes in 50 low-power fields in maternal peripheral blood films, it represents a transplacental hemorrhage to the extent of 4 mL of fetal blood. 10 µg of anti-D is required for every 1 mL of fetal whole blood or 0.5 mL of fetal RBCs.

Fetomaternal hemorrhage can also be quantified using flow cytometry to measure red cell size. It is unaffected by maternal levels of fetal hemoglobin F or by fetal levels of hemoglobin A. Flow cytometry has been reported to be more sensitive and accurate than the Kleihaeur Betke test.

questions.text: A 56-year-old multiparous ‌woman presented with grad​e II/III uterine prolapse​ with cystocele. She comp‌lains of passing urine on​ coughing and sneezing. W‌hat is the type of urinar‌y incontinence seen in th​is patient?
questions.raw_text: A 56-year-old multiparous woman presented with grade II/III uterine prolapse with cystocele. She complains of passing urine on coughing and sneezing. What is the type of urinary incontinence seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stress incontinence

The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

Stress incontinence refers to the involuntary leakage of urine when there is increased intraabdominal pressure (eg, coughing, sneezing, laughing, Valsalva maneuver). There is an absence of detrusor muscle contraction, seen in urodynamic studies.

Causes:

  • Age and menopause - due to estrogen deficiency
  • Multiparity - due to loss of pelvic muscle tone
  • Obesity
  • Smoking
  • Constipation, chronic cough
  • Pelvic organ prolapse
  • Pregnancy - due to the effect of progesterone and pressure of the gravid uterus on the bladder neck.
  • Puerperium - due to descent of the bladder neck, loss of urethro-vesical angle, and reduced pelvic muscle tone 
  • Surgical repair of vesicovaginal fistula

Grading of genuine stress incontinence (GSI) :

  • Grade I: Incontinence with only severe stress, such as coughing, sneezing, and jogging.
  • Grade II: Incontinence with moderate stress, such as fast walking, and going up and down the stairs.
  • Grade III: Incontinence with mild stress such as standing.

Investigations are only done prior to surgery to confirm the diagnosis. They include the stress test, cotton swab or Q tip test, Marshall and Bonney’s test, urethroscopy, and urodynamic studies. These are not required prior to conservative management.

Conservative management includes Kegel's pelvic exercises, electric nerve stimulation, devices like pessaries, vaginal cones, and artificial sphincters. Medical treatment with estrogen creams, anti-adrenergic, venlafaxine, and imipramine may be useful.

Other options:

Option A: Overflow incontinence is an old term that refers to the inability to empty the bladder, with involuntary, continuous urinary dribbling. Currently, it refers to another presentation of urge incontinence. 

Option B: Urge incontinence is the involuntary escape of urine when there is an imminent need to urinate. It occurs due to detrusor muscle overactivity or detrusor instability. It is seen more commonly in old women with decreased bladder capacity, decreased sensation, and central nervous system (CNS) inhibition. 

Option D: Neurogenic bladder occurs in patients with neurogenic dysfunction leading to detrusor hyperreflexia. Conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and spinal injury give rise to this. They present with urgency or urge incontinence.

1,2,3,4 and 5 are suitable case for expectant management of placenta previa.

Risk factors for placenta previa

  • Multigravida
  • Age > 35 years
  • Smoking
  • Previous cesarean section or myomectomy
  • Abnormal placental size and lobes
  • Prior curettage

Clinical features of placenta previa:

  • Sudden-onset recurrent painless vaginal bleeding: First bleeding usually appears after the end of the second trimester or later and is usually mild and not fatal. This is called ‘Sentinel bleed’. 
  • The size of the uterus corresponds to gestational age. 
  • The uterus is relaxed, soft, no tenderness 
  • Floating head 
  • Fetal heart sound is present unless there is major separation and the patient is exsanguinated.
  • Slowing of fetal heart rate on pressing the head down into the pelvis which recovers promptly as pressure is relieved is suggestive of a low-lying placenta especially of posterior type: Stallworthy sign.

Degree of placenta previa:

There are four types of placenta previa depending upon the degree of extension of the placenta to the lower segment

  • Type—I (Low-lying): The major part of the placenta is attached to the upper segment and only the lower margin encroaches onto the lower segment but not up to the internal os.
  • Type—II (Marginal): The placenta reaches the margin of the internal os but does not cover it.
  • Type—III (Incomplete or partial central): The placenta covers the internal os partially (covers the
    internal os when closed but does not entirely do so when fully dilated).
  • Type—IV (Central or total): The placenta completely covers the internal os even after it is fully dilated.

Per-Vaginal Examination should not be done in suspected Placenta Previa, whereas it can be only done in the operation theatre with all the arrangements for C-section.

The image below shows the types of placenta previa.

Expectant management for placenta previa was advocated by Macafee and Johnson. The aim is to continue the pregnancy for fetal maturity without compromising maternal health. 

Prerequisites 

  • Availability of blood for transfusion whenever required 
  • Facilities for cesarean section should be available 24 h. 

Suitable cases for expectant management for placenta previa: 

  • Mother in good health (Hb ≥10 g%; hematocrit ≥30%) 
  • Duration of pregnancy <37 wk
  • No active vaginal bleeding 
  • Fetal well-being is assured (USG) 

Conduct of expectant treatment

  • Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if <34 wk

    • Dexamethasone 6mg IM 12 hours apart for 4 doses

  • Hb, Blood grouping and urine for protein 
  • Inspection of vulval pads, fetal surveillance with USG
  • Supplementary hematinics 
  • Rh Immunoglobin should be given to all Rh-negative (unsensitized) women
  • Use of tocolytics if there are uterine contractions.

The pregnancy is carried till 37 weeks as part of expectant management. During this time, if there is fetal distress or a bleeding episode, then terminate immediately.

The woman has had two pregnancies in total - the previous twin pregnancy and the current pregnancy, with the first pregnancy resulting in delivery at term. Hence, her obstetric score would be G2P1 (Gravida - 2, Para - 1). 

The obstetric score is used to summarise the past obstetric history as follows:

  • G - Gravidity, denoting the total number of pregnancies, including the present one
  • P - Parity, denoting the total number of pregnancies crossing the period of viability 
    • This includes both live births and stillbirths
    • The current pregnancy is not included
  • A - Abortus or the number of pregnancies that were lost for any reason, including induced abortions or miscarriages
  • L - Living children.

Multifetal pregnancies count as one for both gravida and para. A pregnant woman who delivers twins for the first time is expressed as primipara.

The GTPAL system includes the following:

  • Gravida
  • Term (>37 weeks)
  • Preterm (20w - 36w 6d)
  • Abortions (<20 weeks)
  • Number of living children

Note: The period of viability is when the fetus is capable of independent existence. The WHO defines it to be 24 weeks while the Indian definition is 28 weeks.

  • Gestrinone is an anti-estrogenic, anti-progestational, and mildly anabolic drug that reduces sex-hormone-binding globulin to release free testosterone. It also decreases the LH surge.   • Oral progestogens exert an anti-estrogenic effect and cause decidualization and endometrial atrophy. This causes disease regression. It doesn't prevent ovulation, thus is suitable for women who are trying to conceive. 
  • Mirena IUCDs reduce dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia. It is a single-sitting treatment with minimal side effects. 
  • Aromatase inhibitors like letrozole are anti-estrogens given for disease regression. 
  • Anti-inflammatory drugs like mefenamic acid and naproxen relieve dysmenorrhea.

Therapeutic procedures:

  • Aspiration of Peritoneal fluid from the cul-de-sac removes PGE2, relieves dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, and improves fertility 
  • Destruction of endometriotic lesions <3cm with diathermy, Nd-YAG laser or CO2 vaporization can be attempted. 
  • Larger lesions and chocolate cysts can be excised. 
  • Cystectomy can be done for pelvic pain but can reduce fertility potential. 
  • Laparoscopic breaking of adhesions relieves dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. It also restores tubal patency and improves ovulation. Pre-sacral neurectomy can be done simultaneously..

Correct answer: B. Repeated mid-trimester painless cervical dilatation

Cervical incompetence or insufficiency is characterized by repeated mid-trimester painless cervical dilatation. Escape of amniotic fluid followed by painless expulsion of products of conception can also be seen.

Risk factors for cervical incompetence:

  • Congenital uterine anomalies
  • Acquired -
    • Dilatation and currettage 
    • Dilatation and evacuation
    • Vaginal operative delivery through an undilated cervix
    • Amputation of cervix 
  • Multiple gestations
  • Prior preterm birth

Cervical incompetence or insufficiency is a functional or anatomical impairment in the retentive power of the cervix (or internal os). It is characterized by repeated, mid-trimester painless cervical dilatation. It leads to the escape of amniotic fluid followed by painless expulsion of the products of conception.

Cerclage is the procedure done to strengthen the cervix in patients with cervical incompetence. Contraindications of cervical cerclage include:

  • Ruptured membranes
  • Intrauterine infection
  • Uterine contractions
  • Vaginal bleeding
  • Cervical dilatation >4 cm
  • Fetal death or defect

Cervical incompetence is associated with various risk factors such as prior preterm birth, congenital uterine anomalies, iatrogenic (dilatation and curettage, induced abortion by dilatation and evacuation, vaginal operative delivery through an undilated cervix, amputation of the cervix, etc), and multiple gestations.

In the interconceptional period, diagnosis is made with the passage of number 6-8 Hegar's dilator beyond the internal os without resistance or pain. Investigations for cervical incompetence during pregnancy include:

  • Per speculum examination - shows cervical dilatation with herniation of membranes
  • Transvaginal ultrasound - funneling of internal os >1 cm and cervical length <25 mm
Prophylactic cervical cerclage is done between 12-14 weeks of gestation. Rescue or emergency cerclage is done when there is bulging or prolapse of membranes through a dilated cervix.
 
Shirodkar and McDonald's methods of cervical cerclage are the commonly performed cerclage procedures during pregnancy. In McDonald's method, a non-absorbable (mersilene) suture material is placed as a purse-string suture at the level of the internal os, whereas in the Shirodkar method, non-absorbable (mersilene) tape is used. Removal of stitch should be done at the 37th week of gestation. It can be removed earlier in case of preterm labor or if signs of abortion are seen. Laparoscopic abdominal cerclage is used for non-pregnant patients.

Episiotomy is a surgically planned incision on the perineum and the posterior vaginal wall during the second stage of labour. It is done to

To allow fetal lung maturity, the dose of betamethasone to be given is 12mg IM 24 hourly 2 doses.

Antenatal corticosteroids are recommended in a pregnancy less than 34 weeks to allow fetal lung maturation and to reduce the incidence of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), and necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). 

  • Betamethasone is the steroid of choice and it becomes useful if the delivery is delayed beyond 48 hours of the first dose with the effect lasting for about 18 days. 
  • Dexamethasone is another steroid that can be given in a dose of 6 mg 12 hourly 4 doses IM.  

Preterm labor is the onset of labor before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy (less than 259 days of gestation). It can occur in patients with a history of prior preterm birth, multiple pregnancies, and genital tract infection. Evaluation of cervical anatomy is the most important step in women with a history of preterm labor to look for cervical incompetence. 

It is diagnosed by:

  • Uterus - regular contractions at least one in every 10 minutes, or 4 contractions in 20 minutes or 8 contractions in 60 min with/without pain. 
  • Cervix - dilatation >2 cm and effacement >80% 
  • TVS - length of cervix <2.5 cm and funneling of the internal os >1 cm
  • Pelvic pressure, backache, vaginal discharge, or bleeding PV

The best predictors of preterm labor in a woman with a previous history of preterm birth are fetal fibronectin >50ng/ml and cervical length <2.5cm on transvaginal ultrasound.

Management includes short-term therapy with tocolytics, given in conjunction with steroids for 1-3 days to delay labor for at least 48 hours or to transfer the patient to a tertiary center (centers with NICU). The tocolytics include terbutaline, indomethacin, nifedipine, and atosiban. Contraindications to tocolysis include chorioamnionitis, preeclampsia/eclampsia, fetal distress, pregnancy >34 weeks, active labor, and placental abruption.

The phases of a clinical trial and their objectives are as given below.

Phase 1 (first in humans) is carried out in 10-100 participants. It aims to test the safety and tolerability of the drug. Usually, healthy volunteers are chosen. Sometimes patients with an advanced or rare disease are also considered. It generally lasts for 1-2 years.

Phase 2 (first in patients) checks the efficacy and dose-ranging of the drug. 50-500 patient subjects receive the experimental drug. It lasts for 2-3 years.

Phase 3 (multisite trial) is carried out for confirmation of the efficacy tested in phase 2. The indications are finalized and guidelines for therapeutic use are formulated. A few hundred to a few thousand patient subjects receive the drug. It lasts for around 3-5 years.

Phase 4 (postmarketing surveillance) tests for adverse effects, or those that occur only after long-term use and drug interactions. It is done in patients already on treatment with the approved drug. There is no fixed duration for this stage.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 11, 9, 7

The image given shows a positively/ right-skewed distribution where mean> median> mode. Hence, the mean, median, and mode must be 11, 9, and 7 respectively. None of the other options have such a sequence.

The observed value that occurs with the greatest frequency is known as the mode. If there are two values that occur with the same greatest frequency, the distribution is bimodal. If there are more than two such values, the distribution becomes multimodal. 

When all the values are listed in order, the value that divides the distribution in half is known as the median. When there are an even number of values, the median is obtained by calculating the mean of the two middle scores.

The mean (average) is obtained by summing up all the values and dividing the obtained sum by the total number of values in the distribution.

Skewed distributions are the ones that have asymmetric frequency distributions. They can be identified as positive (right) or negative (left) according to the location of the tail of the curve.

In the image, the tail is located on the positive side of the graph (right side) and so it is a positively or right-skewed distribution. A positively skewed data set contains a large number of low scores but a small number of very high scores. It is vice versa in negatively skewed distributions.

The mean in a positively skewed distribution is pulled up because of the relatively small number of very high scores. The mode is the most frequent and the highest point on the curve, while the median lies between the mean and mode. 

Other options:

Option A: Mean= median= mode is seen in a normal (unimodal) distribution.

Option C: Mean< median< mode is seen in a negatively skewed distribution.

Correct answer: A. Annual parasite incidence

The annual parasite incidence (API) is used to categorize states/union territories under the national framework for malaria elimination in India.

The national framework for malaria elimination in India was launched in February 2016 with the following goals:

  • Eliminate malaria throughout the entire country by 2030
  • Maintain malaria-free status in areas where transmission has been interrupted and prevent re-introduction

It uses the annual parasite index to classify states/union territories into four categories.

  • Category 0 (Prevention of re-establishment phase): States/union territories with zero cases
  • Category 1 (Elimination phase): States/union territories with all their districts having API <1
  • Category 2 (pre-elimination phase): States/union territories with API <1, but some of their districts having API≥1
  • Category 3 (Intensified control phase): States/union territories with API≥1

API is calculated by the formula: confirmed cases during one year X 1000 / population under surveillance.

Regions with API≥ 2 are considered high-risk areas and are eligible for vector control.

Correct answer: B. Less than 10/100 mL

According to WHO guidelines, the quality of drinking water is considered to be satisfactory if the presumptive coliform count is 0/100 mL.

Drinking water should not contain any pathogenic organisms or bacteria indicative of faecal contamination. The primary bacterial indicator used to assess this is the coliform group of organisms. This is because they are present abundantly in the human intestine and can be easily detected by culture methods. 

The presumptive coliform test can be done by the multiple tube method or membrane filtration techniques. In the multiple-tube method, the water to be tested is inoculated into tubes containing a suitable liquid medium. These tubes are then incubated for 48 hours and examined. The test is called presumptive because the reaction observed in the tube may occasionally be due to other organisms. The presumption that the reaction is due to coliform organisms has to be confirmed. McConkey's lactose bile salt broth with bromocresol purple 25 as an indicator is used as the media. Escherichia coli or thermotolerant coliform bacteria should not be detected in any 100 ml sample. 

In samples of chlorinated water, confirmation of the presumptive test is necessary. This is done by subculturing the positive tubes in two tubes of brilliant green bile broth. It is based on the fact that E.Coli is the only coliform that can produce gas from lactose at 44°C.

Supplementary indicator organisms include fecal streptococci and sulfite-reducing clostridia.

The influenza pandemic is an example of a cyclical trend.

A cyclical trend is a type of periodic fluctuation. It occurs in cycles that are spread over short periods of time. This can be days, weeks, months, or even years. Influenza pandemics are known to occur at intervals of 7- 10 years, due to antigenic variations. Some non-infectious conditions can also display cyclical trends. An example of this is road traffic accidents occurring more frequently on the weekends. Knowledge of the cyclical pattern of diseases can be used to protect communities against the same.

Other options:

Option A: Seasonal trend is a type of period fluctuation which refers to seasonal variation of diseases. Examples of diseases that follow this trend include measles, malaria, and upper respiratory tract infections. It can be related to environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity. Some non-infectious conditions which follow this trend are sunstroke, hay fever, and snakebite.

Option B: Secular or long-term trend signifies the changes seen in the occurrence of a disease over a long period of time. It implies a consistent change in a particular direction such as a progressive increase or decrease. Examples of conditions that follow this pattern are coronary heart disease and lung cancer which have shown a consistent upward trend. A decline in the occurrence of diseases such as tuberculosis and diphtheria has been noted in developed countries. 

Option C: Point-source epidemic is a type of common-source epidemic. In this type of epidemic, there are no secondary waves and the epidemic curve rises and falls rapidly. There is a clustering of cases within a narrow interval of time. All the cases develop within one incubation period of the specific disease.

questions.text: At PHCs, vaccines are stor‌ed in:
questions.raw_text: At PHCs, vaccines are stored in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ice lined refrigerators

Ice-lined refrigerators (ILRs) are the main method of vaccine storage in primary health centres (PHCs).

ILRs are an important part of the cold chain and they maintain a temperature of 2 to 8 degree Celsius for storage of vaccines. They have different temperature zones for different vaccines and they are stored accordingly in the baskets that are provided in most ILRs. Dial or digital thermometers are used to record temperatures inside an ILR.

Inside the ILR there is a lining of water containers (ice packs or tubes) fitted all around the walls. When the refrigerator is functioning the water in the containers freezes and cools the cabinet. When the electricity supply fails, then the ice lining maintains the inside temperature of the refrigerator at a safe level for vaccines. Therefore, the temperature is maintained in ILR for a much longer duration than in the deep freezers and domestic refrigerators. Thus ILR is an ideal option for safe storage of vaccines.

questions.text: The non-communicable disea‌se (NCD) clinic at the di​strict hospital screens p​eople above the age of 50‌ years with positive fami‍ly history for diabetes. ‍What type of screening is‌ this?
questions.raw_text: The non-communicable disease (NCD)  clinic at the district hospital screens people above the age of 50 years with positive family history for diabetes.  What type of screening is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High-risk screening

The non-communicable disease/ NCD clinic at the district hospital screening people above the age of 50 years for diabetes is a type of high-risk screening. 

Screening is searching or testing for diseases or defects that are not evident in apparently healthy individuals. High-risk or selective screening is screening applied selectively to high-risk groups defined on the basis of epidemiological research. For example, screening the other members in families of patients with diabetes or hypertension that tend to aggregate in families. It is an effective and economical method of screening.  

Other options:

Option A: Mass screening is the screening of a population or a sub-group of the population for a disease irrespective of the particular risk an individual may run of contracting the disease in question. It is not a useful preventive measure unless there is a  suitable treatment that alters the duration or outcome of a disease.

Option B: Multiphasic screening is the application of two or more screening tests (instead of carrying out separate screening tests for a single disease) to a large number of people in the form of health questionnaires, clinical examinations, and investigations. It has not shown any benefit to the population in terms of mortality and morbidity reduction and has instead increased the cost of health services.

Option C: Prospective screening is screening people for the benefit of others. For example, screening immigrants for infectious diseases such as tuberculosis to protect the home population from the disease.

Note: Prescriptive screening is defined as the presumptive screening of patients for unrecognized diseases for their own benefit. It usually does not arise from a patient's request. Examples include screening for bacteriuria in pregnancy and screening for hemolytic disease in a neonate.

questions.text: You conduct a study to det‌ermine the association be​tween computer use and vi​sual impairment and get a‌ correlation coefficient ‍of +0.4. Which of the fol‍lowing scattergrams best ‌represents your findings?‌
questions.raw_text: You conduct a study to determine the association between computer use and visual impairment and get a correlation coefficient of +0.4. Which of the following scattergrams best represents your findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2

In the given clinical scenario having a correlation coefficient of +0.4 shows a positive weak correlation and the scattergram that best represents this finding is graph number 2.

Correlation is used to assess the strength and direction of the association between two variables (such as smoking and lung cancer). The correlation coefficient (denoted by r) is represented by a plus or minus sign, followed by a number (Example: -0.88). The correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to +1.

The numerical indicates the strength of correlation:

  • Correlation coefficients greater than ± 0.5 are considered strong and are likely to establish (if positive correlation) or disprove (if negative correlation) the association between two factors.
  • Correlation coefficients between 0 and ± 0.5 are regarded as weak.

The sign indicates the direction of the correlation.

  • Plus sign (+) suggests that both the variables being studied are positively correlated. This means that the high value of one variable is associated with a high value in another. An example is an association between salt intake and blood pressure readings.
  • Minus sign (-) suggests that both the variables being studied are negatively correlated. A high value of one variable such as cigarette consumption is associated with a low value of another variable such as life expectancy.

The relationship between two correlated variables can be represented graphically in the form of a scattergram. Each point represents one observation including both the variables and so would be equal to the sample size.

questions.text: A 45-year-old man living i‌n Nellore, Andhra Pradesh​ presents with the follow​ing lesions on his teeth.‌ What is the most likely ‍diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 45-year-old man living in Nellore, Andhra Pradesh presents with the following lesions on his teeth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fluorosis

The above image along with the endemic area of Andhra Pradesh is diagnostic of Dental fluorosis.

Dental fluorosis (also termed mottled enamel) is an extremely common disorder, characterized by hypomineralization of tooth enamel caused by ingestion of excessive fluoride during enamel formation.

Fluorosis occurs when drinking water contains excess amounts of fluorine, in the range of 3-5mg/L. It is endemic in parts of India- Andhra Pradesh (Nellore, Nalgonda, Prakasam), Punjab, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu. 

Mechanism:

  • In the extra-cellular environment of maturing enamel, an excess of fluoride ions alters the rate at which enamel matrix proteins (amelogenin) are enzymatically broken down and the rate at which the subsequent breakdown products are removed.
  • Fluoride may also indirectly alter the action of protease via a decrease in the availability of free calcium ions in the mineralization environment.
  • This results in the formation of enamel with less mineralization.
  • This hypomineralized enamel has altered optical properties and appears opaque and lustreless relative to normal enamel.

Classification:

The two main classification systems which are used in the grading of severity of dental fluorosis are Dean’s system and TF system.

Symptoms correspond to levels of fluoride intake:

  • Dental fluorosis: (1.5mg/L) Occurs if excess fluoride is ingested during the period of tooth calcification, i.e. in the first 7 years of life. Best seen on the upper incisors and almost exclusively affects only permanent teeth. It causes mottling on dental enamel, the appearance of chalky-white patches on the teeth, and loss of shine in the early stages. The white spots progressively turn yellow and can even become brown-black. The loss of enamel gives a corroded appearance. 
  • Skeletal fluorosis: (3-6mg/L) Occurs due to the heavy deposition of fluoride in the skeleton. Fluorosis stimulates osteoblastic activity, fluorapatite crystals are laid down in bone and these are usually resistant to secondary osteoclastic resorption. This leads to calcium retention, osteosclerosis, and osteophytosis. Ossification of ligaments and fascial attachments is characteristic.
  • Crippling fluorosis: (>10mg/L) Can lead to permanent disability. 

Genu valgum and osteoporosis of the lower limb are seen in a newer form of fluorosis in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. It is seen in people consuming jawar (sorghum), as it promotes greater retention of ingested fluoride.

Interventions for Fluorosis 

  • Change the drinking water source with a lower fluoride content (0.5 to 0.8 mg/L). Running surface water contains lower quantities of fluorides than groundwater sources.
  • Chemical treatment in a water treatment plant can be moderately expensive. The National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur developed a technique for removing fluoride by a chemical treatment called the Nalgonda technique. 
  • Fluoride supplements should not be prescribed for children who drink fluoridated water.
  • The use of fluoride toothpaste in areas of endemic fluorosis is not recommended for children up to 6 years of age

The SPEAK protocol is used to assess health literacy in the geriatric population in a clinical setting.

Health literacy is defined as the degree to which individuals have the capacity to obtain, process, and understand basic health information needed to make appropriate health decisions. The SPEAK protocol provides a simple framework that healthcare providers can use to assess literacy. SPEAK stands for:

  • S - Speech
  • P - Perception
  • E - Education
  • A - Access
  • K - Knowledge

Option A: The GATHER approach is mainly used for counseling (usually, family planning and reproductive counseling) to help people make decisions about health. It stands for:

  • G – Greet
  • A – Ask
  • T – Tell 
  • H – Help 
  • E – Explain 
  • R – Return 

Option C: The SPIKES protocol is used to convey distressing information and break bad news in an organized manner to patients and families. It stands for:

  • S - Setting
  • P - Perception
  • I - Invitation or information
  • K - Knowledge
  • E - Empathy
  • S - Summarizing or strategizing.

The demographic cycle has 5 stages:

  • Stage 1: High stationary population 
  • Stage 2: Early expanding population 
  • Stage 3: Late expanding population 
  • Stage 4: Low stationary population 
  • Stage 5: Declining population

In a high stationary population, there is a high birth rate and a high death rate that cancel each other and the population remains stationary.

The early expanding population is marked by a decline in the death rate but the birth rate stays constant. Many countries in South Asia and Africa are in this phase. 

In the late expanding population there is a further fall in the death rate, with the birth rate beginning to fall. The population is still increasing due to a net increase in births. India has entered this phase. 

A low stationary population is characterized by low birth and low death rate, and this can result in a stationary population. It has occurred in most industrialized countries as a demographic transition shifting from high birth and high death rates to low birth and low death rates.

A declining population is one where the birth rate is lower than the death rate, causing population decline. Examples include East European countries like Germany and Hungary.

questions.text: A medical officer is condu‌cting a case-control stud‌y and employs matching to​ select controls similar ‌to the cases. Which of th‌e following types of bias‍ is likely to be reduced ​as a result?
questions.raw_text: A medical officer is conducting a case-control study and employs matching to select controls similar to the cases. Which of the following types of bias is likely to be reduced as a result?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Confounding bias

Matching controls to be similar to the cases is likely to reduce confounding bias or bias due to confounding factors.

A confounding factor is one that is related to both exposure and disease and is distributed unequally in study and control groups. Irrespective of being associated with the exposure under study, the confounding factor might itself serve as a risk factor for the disease. Hence, the elimination of these confounding factors is essential before carrying out a case-control study. 

Matching, which is usually done in analytical studies (such as a case-control study), is the process where the participants in two groups (cases and controls in this case) are matched based on factors that are known to influence the outcome of disease (such as age, gender, race, etc.) to stop the potential confounders from distorting the results.

Other strategies to eliminate confounding factors include randomization, stratified randomization, and restriction.

Other options:
Option A - Recall bias in case-control studies occurs because history recollection is better in the case group as they have a stronger exposure than the control group. This bias can be reduced by decreasing the recall period as much as possible.

Option C - Selection bias is a type of sampling bias that occurs because of the nonrandom allocation of subjects such that the study population is not representative of the target population. The best way to reduce this is by randomization to create groups with similar distributions of known and unknown variables. 

Option D - Interviewer bias is a type of bias that occurs because the interviewer is aware of the case group and the hypothesis being tested, which can influence interviews and analysis. This can be reduced by blinding to reduce their influence on interviews and interpretation of outcomes.

The vector for bubonic plague is Xenopsylla cheopis. It is also called a rat flea. It also transmits murine typhus, chiggerosis, and hymenolepsis diminuta. It can be identified by the presence of a conical-shaped head, the presence of thorax, abdomen, and three pairs of legs. 

Plague is a zoonotic disease caused by Yersinia pestis. It is a gram-negative, non-motile, coccobacillus that exhibits bipolar staining with special stains like Wayson's stain. The reservoir of infections is wild rodents like field mice, gerbils, skunks, etc. In India, Tatera indica is the main reservoir. The important vector of plague is rat flea, also called Xenopsylla cheopis.

Humans acquire the disease by the bite of an infected flea, by direct contact with the tissues of the infected animal, or by droplet infection from cases of pneumonic plague. 

Human plague mainly presents as:

Bubonic plague- This is the most common type of disease. The patient develops a sudden fever, chills, headache, and painful lymphadenitis. Within a few days, the lymph nodes in the groin, axilla, or neck enlarge and are called buboes. This is followed by the suppuration of the buboes. Bubonic plague cannot spread from person to person as the bacilli are locked up in the buboes and do not find a way or easy exit.

Pneumonic plague- It develops as a complication of bubonic-septicemic plague. 

Septicemic plague- It occurs when the infection spreads to blood.

questions.text: Arrange the following in o‌rder of the demographic c‌ycle. 1. Early expanding ​population 2. Declining p‌opulation 3. Low stationa‌ry population 4. Late exp‍anding population 5. High​ stationary population
questions.raw_text:
Arrange the following in order of the demographic cycle.

1. Early expanding population

2. Declining population

3. Low stationary population 

4. Late expanding population

5. High stationary population
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5, 1, 4, 3, 2

The correct order according to the demographic cycle is high stationary population (5) --> early expanding population  (1) --> late expanding population (4) --> low stationary population (3) -->  declining population  (2).

The demographic cycle has 5 stages:

  • Stage 1: High stationary population 
  • Stage 2: Early expanding population 
  • Stage 3: Late expanding population 
  • Stage 4: Low stationary population 
  • Stage 5: Declining population

In a high stationary population, there is a high birth rate and a high death rate that cancel each other and the population remains stationary.

The early expanding population is marked by a decline in the death rate but the birth rate stays constant. Many countries in South Asia and Africa are in this phase. 

In the late expanding population there is a further fall in the death rate, with the birth rate beginning to fall. The population is still increasing due to a net increase in births. India has entered this phase. 

A low stationary population is characterized by low birth and low death rate, and this can result in a stationary population. It has occurred in most industrialized countries as a demographic transition shifting from high birth and high death rates to low birth and low death rates.

A declining population is one where the birth rate is lower than the death rate, causing population decline. Examples include East European countries like Germany and Hungary.

questions.raw_text:
Which among the following disorders does not follow the classic mendelian inheritance?

  1. Angelman syndrome
  2. Marfan syndrome
  3. Kearns-Sayre syndrome
  4. Prader -Willi syndrome
  5. Duchenne muscular dystrophy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3, and 4

Out of the given options, Angelman syndrome (1), Kearns-Sayre syndrome (3), and Prader-Willi syndrome (4) do not follow a classic Mendelian inheritance pattern.

The non-mendelian inheritance pattern is used to describe mitochondrial inheritance, trinucleotide repeat disorders, and genetic imprinting.

Angelman syndrome and Prader-Willi syndrome arise due to genetic imprinting. Here, the gene expression depends on the parental origin of the chromosome. It results due to an imbalance in the active copies of a specific gene. In Angelman syndrome, the maternal copy is affected while the paternal one is affected in Prader-Willi syndrome. Both the syndromes present with developmental delays and mental retardation. 

Kearns-Sayre syndrome is a mitochondrial disorder that results in lactic acidosis, pigmentary retinitis, and progressive external ophthalmoplegia. 

The classic forms of genetic inheritances such as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked inheritance are referred to as Mendelian inheritance forms.

Autosomal dominant inheritance is marked by the presence of one abnormal gene on one of the autosomes/ chromosomes 1-22. Autosomal recessive inheritance requires both copies of the same to be abnormal. If genes located on the X chromosome are affected, an X-linked pattern of inheritance with males being affected more commonly is seen. 

Other Options:

Option 2: Marfan's syndrome follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Features include tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens subluxation, and aortic root dilatation. 

Option 5: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder that is characterized by the involvement of the proximal muscles of the lower limbs. Calf hypertrophy is a characteristic feature.

During your neonatal rotation, a final year student asks you to explain the score which evaluates the baby at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth. Which among the following is an incorrect statement regarding it?

  2. 0 points are assigned if the baby is floppy
