  5. 2 points if the baby coughs in response to the insertion of a nasal catheter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3 and 4

The score which evaluates the baby at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth is the APGAR score, and statements 3 and 4 are incorrect.

The Apgar score is a method of systematically evaluating newborn infants immediately after birth. It measures appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, and respiration. It is performed at 1 minute and again at 5 minutes after birth.

Statements 3 and 4 are incorrect because 0 points are assigned if the pulse is absent, and respiratory rate is not used in calculating the APGAR score, but the respiratory effort is considered.

The maximum score is 10 which indicates the fetus is in the best possible condition. Scores of 0-3 require immediate resuscitation, although resuscitation should ideally be started before the  1-minute APGAR score is calculated. 

APGAR score can be used to assess the response to resuscitative efforts and should be calculated every 5 minutes for up to 20 minutes if the 5-minute Apgar score is less than 7.

Causes of Low APGAR scores include:

  • Fetal distress
  • Prematurity
  • Analgesics, narcotics, sedatives
  • Airway obstruction (Eg: choanal atresia)
  • Pneumonia and sepsis
  • Previous episodes of fetal asphyxia (recovered)

False-negative APGAR score is when the score is normal, but there is acidosis or high fetal catecholamine levels.

A 3-year-old boy last vaccinated at 12 weeks of life presents to you with a high-grade fever, cough, and a rash. The parents say that the rash shown below started from the forehead and behind the ears, and then it spread to the neck and body. Which of the following is true regarding this child's condition?

  1. Causative agent is an RNA paramyxovirus
  2. The secondary attack rate in susceptible contacts is ≥90%
  3. Forchheimer spots are characteristic
  4. Jeryl Lynn strain of vaccine is used for prevention
  5. Most complications are due to secondary bacterial infections.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, and 5

The clinical scenario with the symptoms, incomplete vaccination history, and regional distribution of the red maculopapular rash is suggestive of measles. Options 1,2 and 5 are correct regarding this condition.

Measles is caused by a single-stranded, lipid-enveloped RNA paramyxovirus. Contact with large droplets or small-droplet aerosols is the route of transmission. Infection results in respiratory tract epithelial necrosis and lymphocytic infiltration. Clinical features include high fever, cough, coryza, and a rash.

Koplik spots appear 1-4 days before the onset of the rash. They appear as discrete red lesions with bluish-white spots at the level of the premolars. It can also involve the lips and gingiva. This is followed by the appearance of the rash that starts on the forehead, neck, and behind the ears. It then spreads to involve the torso and extremities. The image below shows Koplik's spots.

Confirmation of the diagnosis can be made by IgM assay. Affected children need to be isolated for 4 days after the beginning of the rash to prevent its spread. Management is mainly supportive by the maintenance of hydration and oxygenation. 

Most complications are secondary to bacterial infections. Pneumonia is the most common cause of death and acute otitis media is the most common complication. Croup, bronchiolitis, encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis are the other complications.

Secondary attack rates in susceptible contacts are usually ≥90%. Vaccination against measles is the most effective way to prevent the condition. It is contraindicated in individuals with severe immunosuppression.

Rubella, also known as German measles is a viral disease that presents with low-grade fever, sore throat, rash, and lymphadenopathy. Forchheimer spots are tiny rose-colored lesions or petechial hemorrhages seen on the soft palate. It is usually seen with the onset of the rash. The rash starts on the face and neck and then involves the torso and extremities. It is shown in the image below. 

The Jeryl Lynn strain of virus is used for vaccination against mumps. It is a systemic viral illness caused by a paramyxovirus characterized by parotitis.

questions.raw_text: A teacher complains that a 7-year-old girl with falling grades is inattentive in class and has unresponsive episodes with staring. On hyperventilation, her symptoms increase and her EEG findings show a 3Hz spike and wave discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Typical Absence seizure

The clinical vignette of a child who is inattentive in class and has unresponsive episodes with staring with EEG showing a 3Hz spike and wave discharge is suggestive of typical absence seizures.

Absence seizures are a form of generalized seizures marked by unresponsiveness, staring, and eye flutter which usually last for a few seconds. GABAB receptors, T-type Ca2+ channels, and K+ channels situated within the thalamus are involved in the pathophysiology of absence seizures.

It is of two types:

  • Typical absence seizures  
  • Atypical absence seizures  

Typical absence seizures are associated with 3-Hz spikes and slow wave discharges on EEG. It usually starts by the age of 5-8 years and can occur up to a hundred times per day. Hyperventilation can precipitate seizures and EEG changes. They last only for a few seconds and do not have an aura. It can be accompanied by eyelid flutter or upward rolling of the eyes. Simple automatisms such as lip smacking or picking at clothing can also be seen. There is no postictal period and the child usually resumes whatever activity he/she was engaged in prior to the episode. 

Atypical absence seizures are associated with 1-2-Hz spike-and-slow-wave discharges. Head atonia and myoclonus can also be seen during the seizures. It is precipitated by drowsiness and is generally more difficult to treat. 

Juvenile absence seizures occur at a later stage and are similar to typical absences. It is marked by 4-to-6 Hz spike-and-slow-wave and polyspike-and-slow-wave discharges. It is associated with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

EEG is the diagnostic test for absence seizures. An MRI would appear normal and so is not useful. Ethosuximide is the drug of choice for typical absence seizures. Its mechanism of action is the inhibition of T-type calcium channels. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and oxcarbazepine have all been associated with aggravation of absence seizures and even absence status epilepticus in children with absence epilepsy.

The following epilepsy syndromes are associated with the absence seizures:

  • Childhood absence epilepsy
  • Juvenile absence epilepsy
  • Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
  • Myoclonic absence epilepsy
  • Lennox-gestaut syndrome

Other options:

Option A: Myoclonic seizures can be focal, multifocal, or generalized. It is marked by the rapidity of jerks (<50 mseconds). EEG changes depend on the type of myoclonic seizure.

Option B: Myoclonus is very brief, abrupt, and involuntary jerky contractions of a single muscle or muscle group. Some causes of myoclonus in children include hiccups (physiologic), meningitis, and electrolyte disturbances.  

Option D: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy also known as Janz syndrome is a type of generalized epilepsy seen in young adults. It presents as myoclonic jerks in the morning and generalized tonic-clonic or clonic-tonic-clonic seizures upon awakening. Sleep deprivation and photic stimulation can precipitate the episodes. 4-5 Hz polyspike-and-slow-wave discharges can be seen on EEG.

Correct answer: B. Nasogastric tube feeding

In the given clinical scenario of a baby born at 29 weeks of gestation and 2 kg birth weight, nasogastric tube feeding can be advised as a routine primary feeding method.

The feeding of neonates depends on their gestational age and it depends on the level of maturity of the neonate. In this scenario, as the baby is 2 kg (low birth weight) and was born at 29 weeks of gestation, nasogastric tube feeding is preferred. Babies born before 32 weeks will not have the coordination between swallowing and breathing. So, paladai feeding can only be used occasionally. Babies born after 34 weeks will have a completely mature sucking pattern and breastfeeding is more preferred.

Based on birth weight, babies can be classified into

  • Low birth weight (LBW) - Birth weight < 2.5kg
  • Very low birth weight (VLBW)- Birth weight <1.5kg
  • Extremely low birth weight (ELBW)- Birth weight <1kg

All LBW infants, irrespective of their initial feeding method should receive only breast milk. This can be given as expressed breast milk (mothers' own milk) to those infants fed by paladai or gastric tube. An alternative is human donor milk. When there is a contraindication to breastfeeding or if the mother is sick, formula feeds can be given. Term formula feed in babies with birth weight >1500 g and preterm formula feed in VLBW babies can be given. All hemodynamically stable LBW babies should receive Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC).

LBW can result from preterm birth (born before 37 completed weeks) IUGR (intrauterine growth restriction) or both. Prematurity and low birth weight are the leading causes of neonatal mortality.

questions.raw_text: A 3-month-old infant who was born at term was presented with complaints of lethargy and poor feeding. On examination, the infant had a puffy face, enlarged fontanelles, and protruding tongue, as shown below. The lower limb x-ray revealed an absence of distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphysis. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital hypothyroidism

The given clinical scenario and the image are suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism.

The clinical features of congenital hypothyroidism include a puffy face, enlarged fontanelles, protruding tongue, prolonged jaundice, lethargy, and a history of poor feeding. The absence of distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyses denotes the onset of congenital hypothyroidism. These epiphyses are normally present at birth.

Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability. Thyroid dysgenesis is the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism in India accounting for about 75% of all cases.

Congenital hypothyroidism is mostly asymptomatic at birth and is detected mainly by the neonatal screening of TSH levels in the first few weeks of life. Clinical features present after maternal thyroxine wanes.

Screening is usually done on day 2-day 4 postnatally, and usually, dried blood samples are used for this. The most commonly used strategy is screening for TSH first, as they have higher sensitivity compared to the T4-based screening.

In untreated hypothyroidism, as the child grows older, there is a discrepancy between chronological age and osseous development. Epiphyseal dysgenesis wherein there are multiple foci of ossification in the epiphyses, is common. X-rays of the skull reveal large fontanelles, wide sutures, and intersutural (wormian) bones. Radiotracer uptake study with radioactive iodine or technetium should be done as soon as primary congenital hypothyroidism is diagnosed.

Treatment with levothyroxine should be started within 2 weeks in order to maintain normal cognitive and physical development. Thyroxine of dose 10-15 μg/kg/day should be started and adjusted to achieve the normal free T4 range. TSH may be elevated up to 2 years of age with a reset of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. 

Other options:

Option A- Down’s syndrome also presents with developmental delay and hypothyroidism. They have characteristic facial features such as a flat face, depressed nasal bridge, upslanting palpebral fissures, and a single palmar crease. The image shown below depicts an infant with Down's syndrome. Radiological features include atlantoaxial dislocation.

Option B-  Congenital rickets is a rare condition resulting from severe maternal vitamin D deficiency and can present with symptomatic hypocalcemia, intrauterine growth retardation, decreased bone ossification along with classic rachitic changes.

Option D- Hurler's syndrome is a mucopolysaccharidosis which may present after 6 months with hepatosplenomegaly, coarse facial features, corneal clouding, large tongue, prominent forehead, joint stiffness, short stature, and skeletal dysplasia.

Image 1  C. Tetralogy of Fallot
Image 2  D. Transposition of great arteries
Image 3 A. Ebstein's anomaly
Image 4 B. TAPVC

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)  is the most common cyanotic heart disease encountered beyond the age of 1 year. It is characterized by a tetrad of:

  1. Severe right ventricle outflow obstruction
  2. Large ventricular septal defect (VSD)
  3. Aorta overriding VSD
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy

In TOF, the hypertrophied right ventricle causes the rounded apical shadow to be uptilted so that it is situated higher above the diaphragm than normal. This on X-rays appears as a boot-shaped heart or Coeur en sabot.

Transposition of great arteries (TGA) is characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. Because of this, the pulmonary and systemic circulations remain separate. The cardiac silhouette usually has an egg-on-side appearance due to cardiomegaly and a narrow mediastinum. Normal to increased pulmonary blood flow is also seen. 

Ebstein anomaly is a rare cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by the downward displacement of an abnormal tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. In some cases, there can be massive cardiomegaly resulting in a box-shaped heart. 

Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVC) occurs due to the anomalous connection of pulmonary veins instead of joining to the left atrium resulting in pulmonary venous blood reaching the right atrium. In supracardiac TAPVC the configuration of the heart and the superior mediastinal borders resemble a snowman. It is also referred to as the figure of 8 sign.

The above clinical vignette of a child with poor appetite, sparse easily pluckable hair, and the image showing flaky paint dermatosis are suggestive of Kwashiorkar.

Kwashiorkor results due to severe protein and essential amino acid deprivation along with adequate calorie intake. It is particularly seen in children at the time of weaning, to a diet consisting majorly of corn, rice, or beans. 

The clinical features include a classic cutaneous finding of diffuse reddish-brown scaling dermatosis that has been likened to cracked skin, peeling paint, enamel paint, flaky paint, or crazy paving. This is due to the typical scaling and irregular fissuring. Nails are thin and soft. Hairs are thin and sparse and display a flag sign consisting of alternative light and dark bands of hair. The consistent feature is peripheral edema due to the associated hypoproteinaemia. Edema of the face results in moon facies. Abdominal distention (pot belly) is a feature and is due to hepatomegaly from increased fatty deposition due to a lack of available apolipoproteins.

Marasmus patients do not demonstrate hypoproteinaemia or edema. There is distension of the abdomen due to hypotonia of the abdominal musculature. These patients typically have wrinkled, loose, and dry skin. The hair and nails often grow slowly and may show brittleness. The hair falls out easily and often shows features of alopecia.

Option B: Pellagra results from a deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3). It is characterized by the classic presentation of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Casal's necklace is a lesion seen around the neck, which is a characteristic feature seen in pellagra.

Below is the image showing Casal's necklace.

Option C: Vitamin A deficiency can result in phrynoderma that is characterized by keratotic follicular papules along the anterolateral thighs and posterolateral arms. It is seen in the deficiency of vitamin B complex, C, E, and essential fatty acids as well.

questions.text: A 10-day-old female neonat‌e with hypoxic-ischemic e‍ncephalopathy (HIE) is hy‌per-alert with normal EEG​. Examination shows hyper​active tendon reflexes, m‌ydriatic pupil, and clonu‌s. What stage of HIE is s‍he in?

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stage 1

According to Sarnat staging of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), a hyperalert neonate with mydriatic pupil, hyperactive tendon reflex, clonus, and normal EEG belongs to stage 1. 

HIE is a brain injury that prevents adequate blood supply to the infant's brain. 

Sarnat staging of HIE:

Signs Stage 1 Stage 2  Stage 3
Level of consciousness Hyperalert Lethargic Stuporous, comatose
Muscle tone Normal Hypotonic Flaccid
Posture Normal Flexion Decerebrate
Tendon reflex/clonus Hyperactive Hyperactive Absent
Myoclonus Present Present Absent
Moro reflex Strong Weak Absent
Pupils Mydriasis Miosis Unequal, poor light reflex
Seizures None Common Decerebration
EEG findings Normal Low voltage changing to seizure activity

Burst suppression to isoelectric
Duration <24 hours if progress it; otherwise, can remain normal 24 hours to 14 days Days to weeks
Outcome Good Variable Death, severe deficits

Maternal causes for HIE are hypoventilation during anesthesia, cyanotic heart disease, respiratory failure, or carbon monoxide poisoning. Failure of oxygenation due to severe anemia, massive blood loss, and intracranial or adrenal hemorrhages are fetal causes of HIE. 

Hypoxia and ischemia cause anaerobic metabolism that generates a large amount of lactate and inorganic phosphates accumulation of toxic byproducts and overactivation of receptors. This leads to increased cellular permeability to sodium and calcium ions, resulting in cytotoxic edema and neuronal death. The most sensitive imaging modality for detecting hypoxic brain injury in neonates is an MRI.

Therapeutic hypothermia within the first 6 hours of life reduces mortality and major neurodevelopmental impairment. High-dose erythropoietin is used as an adjuvant to therapeutic hypothermia. Antiepileptic medications like phenobarbital and levetiracetam can be used to treat seizures. 

 Poor prognostic factors in HIE are:

  • Initial blood ph less than 6.7
  • Low (0-3) 10  in Apgar score
  • Delayed onset of spontaneous breathing
  • Seizure onset in less than 12 hours
  • Burst suppression pattern in EEG
  • Basal ganglia or thalamic lesion
  • Oliguria or anurias for more than 24 hours
  • Decerebrate posture

Development in a child is the maturation of functions and skills for optimal functioning of an individual. Developmental milestones are easily identifiable events that occur during the developmental process. It is assessed under the following domains.

  • Gross motor
  • Fine motor
  • Personal and social development
  • Language

A baby will reach out for objects with both hands, also known as bidextrous reach by the age of 4 months. It is a key fine motor milestone. 

A child is able to sit with his arms forward for support, known as the tripod position at around 6-7 months. The ability to sit without any support develops by 8 months. It is part of gross motor development. 

By around 9 months, the baby can wave bye-bye. He/she also repeats any activity that can get an appreciative response from the observers. It is a social and adaptive milestone.

By the age of 18 months, the baby has a vocabulary of 8-10 words. By the age of 2, increases to 100 words which can be joined to form simple sentences.

questions.text: A 9-month-old boy presents‌ with progressive pallor ‍and abdominal distension.‌ Red cell distribution wi​dth is normal. The periph​eral smear is shown below‌. What is the diagnosis?
questions.raw_text: A 9-month-old boy presents with progressive pallor and abdominal distension. Red cell distribution width is normal.  The peripheral smear is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thalassemia

The clinical history and peripheral blood smear showing target cells and aniso-poikilocytosis, along with the normal red cell distribution width(RDW), are suggestive of thalassemia.

Thalassemia is a hemoglobinopathy that arises due to deficient synthesis of the globin chains. Depending on the chain affected, it is classified into α-thalassemia and β-thalassemia.

β-Thalassemia arises due to the deficient synthesis of β-chains. Normal adult RBCs have HbA, along with HbA2 and fetal haemoglobin (HbF) in small amounts. There is a deficit in the synthesis of HbA with an elevation of HbA2 and HbF levels in β-thalassemia. 

α-Thalassemia is caused by deficient synthesis of α-chains. It can also present as an α-thalassemia trait, with trivial hematologic abnormalities. Excess of β- and γ-globin chains form Bart hemoglobin (γ4) in fetal life and HbH (β4) after birth. Severe deficiency leads to hydrops fetalis.

Ineffective erythropoiesis leads to bone marrow hyperplasia and extramedullary hematopoiesis, which can involve the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes. In β-thalassemia major, anemia manifests 6 to 9 months after birth. HbF levels are markedly elevated. The presence of bony anomalies such as frontal bossing, prominent facial bones, and dental malocclusion is typical.

The image below shows thalassemic facies (frontal bossing and maxillary hyperplasia) in a child with thalassemia major. 

Laboratory findings: Infants with severe β-thalassemia diseases experience increasing anemia following the newborn stage. The RBCs exhibit microcytosis, hypochromia, and target cells. Usually observed are nucleated RBCs, a distinct anisopoikilocytosis, and relative reticulocytopenia. Without transfusions, the Hb level frequently drops to 6 g/dL in a gradual manner.

The RDW shows the size difference in the red blood cells. Low RDW means all the red blood cells are small and uniform in size, while a large RDW means that the cells vary in size. It is normal in case of thalassemia as all cells are uniformly small in size. It increases in iron deficiency anaemia because of presence of small and normal sized RBCs.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) confirms the diagnosis of thalassemia. It shows the absence of HbA and high levels of HbF.

Other options:

Option A: Glossitis, stomatitis, darkening of the skin on the knuckles and terminal phalanges, and enlargement of the liver and spleen are characteristics of megaloblastic anemia. Peripheral smear in megaloblastic anemia is characterized by macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (shown below).

Option B: Iron deficiency anemia has high RDW. Peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic anemia along with target cells.

Option D: Megaloblastic anemia has a particular subtype called pernicious anemia. It is caused by insufficient vitamin B12 absorption through the gastrointestinal pathway, leading to vitamin B12 insufficiency. Macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils are frequent observations in the peripheral smear associated with megaloblastic anemia. Neutrophil hypersegmentation is an early symptom of the disease and typically occurs beyond 3 to 5 lobes.

Meningitis has fever accompanied by lethargy, irritability, signs of meningeal irritation like the Kernig sign-flexion of the hip 90 degrees with subsequent pain with extension of the leg, and Brudzinski sign-involuntary flexion of the knees and hips after passive flexion of the neck while supine. Increased ICP is suggested by headache, emesis, bulging fontanel or widening of the sutures, oculomotor (anisocoria, ptosis) or abducens nerve paralysis, hypertension with bradycardia, apnea or hyperventilation, stupor, coma, or signs of herniation. A lumbar puncture is essential to obtain CSF for Gram stain and culture, which is the most important step in the diagnosis of meningitis.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Indomethacin

NSAID's like ibuprofen and indomethacin are used in the medical management to induce closure of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

Patent ductus arteriosus is the failure of the closure of ductus arteriosus. It usually connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta distal to left subclavian artery branching. It gives rise to a continuous murmur, which is heard throughout the cardiac cycle. It results in decreased oxygenated blood supply to the lower half of the body. It closes by itself in 2-4 weeks, unless it is large.

Medical management involves ruling out other causes of continuous murmur and any other duct dependent lesion. In the absence of either, prostaglandin inhibitor like Indomethacin or Ibuprofen may be given. But these are contraindicated in Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC). 

A recent edition of AIIMS neonatology protocol book says that paracetamol is equally effective as Ibuprofen and can be given in case NSAIDs are contraindicated.

Note:

  • Prostaglandin E1 is a ductal smooth muscle relaxant and is used to maintain an open ductus arteriosus in the newborn with ductal-dependent congenital heart disease.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Should be performed only by the mother

Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) can be carried out by the mother or any other caregiver.

KMC was introduced for the prevention of neonatal hypothermia in low birth weight/ premature newborns. It has 4 components—

  • Skin-to-skin positioning of the newborn on the mother’s chest.
  • Adequate nutrition through breastfeeding.
  • Early discharge and ambulatory care.
  • Support for mother and family for child care.

Evidence shows that-

  • It is at least equivalent to incubators, in terms of safety and thermal protection (measured by mortality)
  • Reduces severe morbidity by way of facilitating breastfeeding
  • Humanization of neonatal care
  • Promoted bonding between mother and child

Eligibiilty criteria for KMC:

It is indicated for all hemodynamically stable low birthweight babies. Short sessions of KMC can be initiated in babies on medical treatment like IV fluids or oxygen therapy. Initiation of KMC can vary with the birth weight of the baby.

  • Birthweight <1200 g - It may take days to weeks for initiation of KMC
  • Birthweight 1200-1800 g - Only a few days may be taken before KMC initiation
  • Birthweight >1800 g - KMC can be initiated immediately after birth

All mothers without any serious illness can provide KMC

Positioning for KMC: The baby is placed between the mother's breast in an upright position. The hips are abducted and flexed in the frog position and the arms are also flexed. The abdomen of the baby should be at the level of the mother's epigastrium. In this position, the mother's breathing would stimulate the baby and prevent the development of apnea.

The duration of KMC should be gradually increased from short sessions of more than one hour to 24 hours a day.

Correct answer: A. Wilson's disease

The given clinical scenario of a child with neurological symptoms (intentional tremors and poor scholastic performance) and liver disease (icterus and hepatomegaly) is suggestive of Wilson's disease. 

Wilson's disease is an autosomal-recessive condition caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, which encodes for the ATPase that removes copper, preventing its accumulation in the liver and brain.

Clinical features:

  • Liver disease is the most common manifestation in children which can present as hepatomegaly (cirrhosis in advanced stages) with or without splenomegaly, subacute or chronic hepatitis, and acute liver failure.
  • Neurologic features consist of dysarthria, dystonia, rigidity, tremors, and choreiform movements due to copper deposition in the basal ganglia. Psychiatric symptoms encompass personality changes, such as irritability and anger, as well as depression and anxiety. Kayser–Fleischer (KF) rings (deposition of copper in Descement's membrane) are present in 95% of patients with neurological symptoms and absent in half of the young patients with liver-related Wilson disease. After treatment KF ring resolves. Coomb's negative hemolytic anemia may also be seen.
  • Hemolytic anemia can result from the release of copper into the circulation from the liver. Additional manifestations of Wilson's disease comprise renal tubular acidosis, delayed puberty, and osteoarthritis.

Diagnosis is made by the presence of a KF ring and decreased levels of serum copper and ceruloplasmin. Increased 24-hour urine copper excretion is seen. Hepatic copper content greater than 250 μg/g dry weight measured by liver biopsy is the gold standard. 

Copper intake should be restricted to <1 mg/day. Initial treatment involves copper-chelating agents D-penicillamine and trientine with concurrent use of pyridoxine. Penicillamine may worsen neurologic symptoms, so trientine is an alternative. Ammonium tetrathiomolybdate is another chelating agent being investigated for patients with neurologic disease. 

Zinc is used in presymptomatic patients due to its ability to impair the absorption of copper. Liver transplantation is considered in advanced stages. 

Other options:

Option B: Huntington's chorea is a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat disorder with an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. It is characterized by involuntary movements known as chorea.

Option C: Glutaric aciduria is an autosomal recessive disease that manifests in the 1st year of life. It is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase. Clinical features are hypotonia and jitteriness at birth, progressive hyperkinetic movements (dystonia, choreoathetosis), and may have seizures. 

Option D: Hepatitis A is a viral infection transmitted by the fecal-oral route, which is the commonest, parenteral route, and also by sexual transmission. The onset of jaundice is preceded by symptoms like nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and mild fever. Hepatitis A resolves completely but a relapse may occur in a few cases.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

The region marked 1 which shows the anterior horn of the spinal cord is affected in spinal muscular atrophy.

Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is an autosomal recessive pattern disease characterized by progressive degeneration of the motor neurons. It results from a continuation of apoptosis that normally occurs in the embryonal period. This results in extensive neuronal degeneration and gliosis of the anterior horns of the spinal cord and brainstem motor nuclei.

Clinically SMA is classified into four types:

  • SMA type I/ Werdnig-Hoffmann disease
  • SMA type II
  • SMA type III/ Kugelberg-Welander disease
  • SMA type IV

SMA type I is seen before the age of six months. Children present with hypotonia, proximal muscle weakness, frog-leg posture, and tongue fasciculations. Involvement of the intercostal respiratory muscles causes a paradoxical abdominal breathing pattern and weak cough. Deep tendon reflexes are usually absent. It should be kept as one of the differential diagnoses for floppy infant syndrome.

SMA type II is seen between the age of 6-18 months. Children present with developmental delay, scoliosis, speech, and deglutition problems.

The proximal muscles involving the shoulder girdle are affected in SMA type III. Muscle hypertrophy might be present rather than atrophy.

SMA type IV (adult phenotype) presents with mild muscle weakness in the second or third decade of life. 

The gold standard for diagnosis is testing for SMN1 (survival motor neuron) gene deletion/ mutation. Supportive therapy enabling the patient to be maximally functionally independent is the mainstay in management.

Correct answer: A. Hypomagnesemia

The given clinical scenario of a child with diarrhea, muscular weakness, and hypokalemia not responding to treatment is most likely due to hypomagnesemia.

The major cause of hypomagnesemia in this scenario is severe diarrhoea/gastrointestinal loss which in turn worsens the hypokalemia. In such cases, hypokalemia can not be corrected unless the underlying hypomagnesemia is addressed. 

Treatment failure in hypokalemia due to hypomagnesemia is mediated by two mechanisms:

  • ↓ Magnesium → inhibits Na+/ K+ - ATPase activity → ↓ influx of potassium into the cell → secondary kaliuresis.
  • ↓ Magnesium → decreased block of ROMK (renal outer medullary K+ channel) potassium efflux channels → increased potassium secretion by distal nephron

Therefore in the presence of hypomagnesemia, hypokalemic patients are clinically refractory to potassium supplementation therapy.

Hypokalemia is defined as a plasma concentration of K+ <3.5 meq/L. The following are various causes of hypokalemia:

  • Inadequate intake
    • Diet, potassium-free intravenous fluids, potassium deficient TPN
  • Excessive potassium excretion
    • Hyperaldosteronism
    • Medications 
  • Potassium losses
    • Direct loss of potassium from GI fluid (diarrhea)
    • Renal loss of potassium (to conserve sodium in response to gastric losses) 
  • Metabolic
    • Intracellular potassium shifts from metabolic alkalosis or insulin therapy

Clinical features 

  • Weakness and paralysis
  • Intestinal ileus
  • Risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias
  • Broad flat T waves, ST depression, and QT prolongation are most marked when serum K+ <2.7 mmol/L
  • Sodium chloride and bicarbonate retention lead to metabolic alkalosis

Management includes potassium supplementation with concurrent cardiac monitoring. Treat hypomagnesemia by supplementation. High dose propranolol if due to excess sympathetic activity

questions.raw_text: An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital after an eye injury sustained while cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel. A foreign body was suspected to be impacted in his eye. Which of the following is the best investigation for foreign body localization?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT

CT scan is the best method for intraocular foreign body (IOFB) localization.

The foreign bodies most likely to penetrate and be retained in the eye are minute chips of iron or steel. While chipping stone with an iron chisel, the chip of the iron chisel is more likely to enter the eye than the stone. A foreign body entering the eye may cause damage by:

  • mechanical effects
  • introduction of infection
  • reacting with the intraocular tissues

Anteroposterior and lateral view X-rays are recommended for locating an IOFB as most foreign bodies are radio-opaque. Ultrasonographic localization can tell the position of even non-radiopaque foreign bodies. CT scan is the best method of IOFB localization.

MRI is contraindicated for metallic IOFB.MRI can be detrimental for a patient with a history of an intraocular foreign body (IOFB) after cutting stone with a hammer and chisel. It can cause further damage by producing movements of the foreign body if it is magnetic. The use of MRI is contraindicated for metallic (iron) foreign bodies and is not recommended as a screening procedure.

Management: A foreign body should always be removed unless:

  • it is inert and probably sterile
  • little damage has been done to vision 
  • the process of removal will destroy sight

 

Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and cause atrophy.

Clinical features:

  • Iris: first stained greenish and later turns reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis.
  • Pupil: iron deposition in sphincter leads to mydriasis.
  • Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract.
  • Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium.
  • Secondary open-angle Glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.

questions.raw_text: A 61-year-old university professor presents with a loss of vision in his left eye. He describes the sensation as a curtain being drawn over his affected eye. questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retinal detachment

The given clinical scenario and the B-scan suggest a diagnosis of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. It is due to the accumulation of fluid between neurosensory retina(NSR) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) due to a retinal tear.

Definition of retinal detachment: The separation of the neurosensory retina from the RPE.

Types of Retinal detachment:

A. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment- fluid accumulates after a break (tear) occurs in the retina.

  • Causes:
    • High myopes
    • Retinoschisis-splitting of neurosensory retina plus vitreous degeneration
      • Typical retinoschisis-split at the level of the outer plexiform layer
      • Atypical retinoschisis-split at the level of the nerve fiber layer
    • Trauma
    • Pseudophakia
    • Aphakia
  • The most dangerous type of retinal break is horseshoe tear.
  • The most dangerous location of retinal break is the supero-temporal retina. 
  • Clinical features
    • Photopsia-flashes of light due to vitreoretinal traction at the site of the break
    • Floaters
    • Visual field defect- a black curtain/veil in front of the eye
  • Signs
    • Hypotony- as the liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE.
    • Shafers sign-pigments in the anterior vitreous (tobacco dusting) are a feature of fresh retinal detachment.
    • The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is corrugated with undulations.
  • Treatment
    • Prophylactic laser barrage
    • Scleral buckling
    • Pneumatic retinopexy
    • Pars plana vitrectomy 

B. Tractional retinal detachment: Fibro-vascular membranes in the vitreous due to long-standing retinal neovascularization exert traction on the retina. 

  • Causes
    • Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
    • Central retinal venous occlusion
    • Eales disease
    • Retinopathy of Prematurity(ROP)
  • Signs
    • The detached retina is concave in configuration. No breaks are seen
  • Treatment
    • Pars plana vitrectomy with endo photocoagulation. 

C. Exudative retinal detachment: Exudative fluid from the choroid, collects in the subretinal space leading to retinal detachment.

  • Causes
    • Inflammatory conditions like choroiditis, posterior scleritis
    • Choroidal tumours like melanoma
    • Toxaemia of pregnancy
    • Malignant hypertension
    • Coats disease
  • Clinical features
    • Floaters due to vitritis but no photopsia
    • Visual field defect
  • Signs
    • The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is smooth. No break is seen.
    • Shifting fluid is seen.
  • Treatment
    • Systemic steroids
    • Treatment of the cause

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoblastoma

This child with a whitish pupillary reflex and Flexner-Winterstein rosettes on histopathological examination has retinoblastoma. Flexner Winterstein rosettes refer to an arrangement of columnar cells around a central lumen, which is highly characteristic of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of immature retinal neural cells and is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14. It belongs to small round blue cell tumours because the immature retinal neural cells are seen as small round cells with large nuclei.

White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision. Image below showing leukocoria of left eye

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumour include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

The histopathological image of retinoblastoma is shown below.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of Vincristine, Carboplatin, and Etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.
Enucleation is done when
  • The tumor involves more than half of the retina
  • The optic nerve is involved
  • Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

Other options:

Option B - Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Patients usually present with headaches, ataxia, and signs of brainstem involvement.

Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin.

Option C - Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. The child usually presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. There are 4 subtypes - embryonal, alveolar, botyroid, and pleomorphic. Cells show light microscopic features of striated muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin.

Option D - Astrocytoma of the retina and optic nerve head is rare. It is usually asymptomatic and is most frequently seen in tuberous sclerosis. Fundus examination reveals a yellowish or white plaque, nodule, or mulberry-like lesion. These lesions are semitransparent peripherally and calcified centrally.

The correct match is as follows:

Vossius ring is a circular ring of faint or stippled opacity, seen on the anterior surface of the lens due to brown amorphous granules of pigment lying on the capsule of the lens. It is usually seen after blunt trauma to the eye and orbit.

It usually has about the same diameter as the contracted pupil. The force of the blow drives the cornea and iris backward and thus producing an impression of the iris on the lens as shown below. The resorption of the pigment results in discrete subcapsular opacities.

Arcus senilis (AS) or arcus lipoides/Gerontoxon.is usually an age-related lipid degeneration of the peripheral corneal that forms a light grey or bluish ring. AS is caused by leakage of lipoproteins (phospholipids and cholesterol) from limbal capillaries into the corneal stroma. Characteristically it is separated from the margin by a narrow zone of comparatively clear cornea.

It is the most common peripheral corneal opacity and is usually found in the elderly where it is considered a benign condition. When AS is found in patients less than 40 years old it is termed arcus juvenilis. It represents an increased risk for cardiovascular disease and warrants screening for an underlying lipid disorder.

  • corneal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles)

  • corneal opacity is seen in later stages.

Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydrodissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. The given history mentions decreased visual acuity 3 months post-cataract surgery and the presence of posterior capsular opacification is suggestive of after-cataract. A posterior capsulotomy (creating a hole in the posterior capsule) using an Nd: YAG laser is the mainstay of treatment.

Posterior capsular opacification, otherwise known as after cataract/secondary cataract, is the most common late complication of uncomplicated cataract surgery. It occurs due to the proliferation of lens epithelial cells that have been left out inside the capsular bag after cataract surgery. The rate of posterior capsule opacification following extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) and phacoemulsification varies with the age of the patient, the surgeon, the surgical technique, the type of intraocular lens used, and the duration after surgery.

  • Slowly worsening blurring
  • Glare and occasionally monocular diplopia

  • Soemmering's ring: present as a white annular proliferation that is formed at the periphery of the capsular bag.
  • Fibrosis type: present as fibroblastic metaplasia of the epithelial cells

  • Surgical treatment: Posterior capsular opacification is managed by creating an opening on the posterior capsule along the visual axis, a procedure called a posterior capsulotomy.

Correct answer: A. Exudative RD

The given clinical scenario with the presence of shifting fluid is suggestive of exudative retinal detachment. 

Exudative RD is characterized by the accumulation of fluid beneath the retina in the absence of a retinal break or traction. Fluid leaks outside the vessels and accumulates under the retina. RD does not occur as long as the retinal pigment epithelium is pumping the leaking fluid into the choroidal circulation. Causes:

  • Inflammatory conditions like choroiditis, posterior scleritis.
  • Choroidal tumours like melanoma.
  • Toxaemia of pregnancy
  • Central serous retinopathy
  • Coats disease

Patients may present with painless progressive visual field defects without photopsia. Floaters may be present if there is an associated vitritis. Clinical signs include:

  • Convex configuration of the retinal detachment, with a smooth surface
  • A detached retina is very mobile
  • Shifting fluid sign- Subretinal fluid detaches the area of the retina under which it accumulates. In the upright position, it collects under the inferior retina. But in the supine position, the inferior retina flattens, the fluid shifts posteriorly which detach the superior retina.
  • The cause of the RD may be apparent. 
  • Leopard spots- Scattered areas of clumped subretinal pigment may be seen after the detachment has flattened

Retinal detachment (RD) is the result of the accumulation of fluid between the retina and the retinal pigment epithelium. It is classified into the following:

  • Rhegmatogenous RD- due to a tear or break in the retina
  • Secondary RD - due to some other preceding event
    • Exudative RD
    • Tractional RD

The recommended treatment for ROP stage 2 in zone I (categorized as type I/low-risk ROP) is careful observation and follow-up.

Retinopathy of prematurity occurs in premature infants with low birth weight, with a typical history of exposure to oxygen in high concentrations leading to bilateral proliferative retinopathy. 

Stages of Retinopathy of Prematurity:

  • Stage 1- demarcation line formation at the edge of vessels, dividing the vascular from the avascular retina.
  • Stage 2- intraretinal ridge formation
  • Stage 3- ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation into the vitreous.
  • Stage 4- subtotal retinal detachment
  • Stage 5- total retinal detachment
  • 'Plus' disease is characterized by dilatation and tortuosity of blood vessels in at least two quadrants of the posterior fundus. It signifies the progression of the disease.

Location:

Zone I: Circular area with a radius twice the distance from disc to the fovea, with the disc as the center. (as shown in the image)
Zone II: It covers the area beyond zone I circumferentially till nasal ora serrata.
Zone III: It consists of residual temporal crescent anterior to zone II.

These zones are shown in the image below:

 

Treatment is based on guidelines set by the early treatment of retinopathy of prematurity trial (ETROP).

Type 1: Treatment within 72 hours (High risk)

  • Any ROP + plus disease
  • Stage 3 ROP in zone I
  • Stage 2/3 in zone II + plus disease.

Type 2: Observation (Low risk)

  • Stage 1/2 in zone I only and no plus disease
  • Stage 3 ROP within zone II and no plus disease.

This can be summarized in the table below:

    Stage 1   Stage 2   Stage 3
Zone I Observation Observation Treatment
Zone II - without plus disease   Observation  Observation
Zone II- with plus disease   Treatment Treatment

 

ROP of any stage in any zone, if associated with 'plus' disease, should receive treatment urgently.

Treatment includes laser ablation of the avascular peripheral retina, anti-VEGF medication (bevacizumab), and pars plana vitrectomy for advanced disease. The high-risk patients requiring treatment should receive it within 72 hours.

The given inferences of various tests are suggestive of conductive deafness and Schwabach’s test is lengthened in conductive deafness.

TUNING FORK TESTS:
I) Rinne’s test:

A vibrating tuning fork is placed on the patient’s mastoid and when he stops hearing, it is brought beside the meatus. If he still hears, air conduction is better than bone conduction.

  • Positive - when the air conduction (AC) is longer or louder than bone conduction (BC). Seen in normal persons and persons with sensory-neural deafness.
  • Negative - when the bone conduction is better than air conduction. Seen in patients with conductive deafness.

II) Weber test:

A vibrating tuning fork is placed in the middle of the forehead or the vertex and the patient is asked in which ear the sound is heard.

  • Normal - heard equally in both ears
  • Conductive deafness - lateralized to the worse ear
  • Sensorineural deafness - lateralized to the better ear.

III) Absolute Bone Conduction test:

Here, the patient’s bone conduction is compared with that of the examiner. The external auditory meatus of both the patient and the examiner should be occluded ( by pressing the tragus inwards) to prevent the ambient noise from entering through the AC route.

  • Normal - same as the examiner.
  • Conductive deafness - same as the examiner.
  • Sensorineural deafness - reduced than that of the examiner.

IV) Schwabach test:

Here, again the bone conduction of the patient is compared with that of the normal hearing person(examiner) but the meatus is not occluded. 

  • Normal - same as the examiner
  • Conductive deafness - lengthened as compared to the examiner
  • Sensorineural deafness - shortened as compared to the examiner

questions.text: Which of the following are​ the objective tests for ‍the hearing? Brainstem-ev‌oked response audiometry ‌Otoacoustic emissions Pur‌e tone audiometry Tympano​metry
questions.raw_text:
Which of the following are the objective tests for the hearing?

  1. Brainstem-evoked response audiometry
  2. Otoacoustic emissions
  3. Pure tone audiometry 
  4. Tympanometry
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 4

Brainstem-evoked response audiometry (BERA), otoacoustic emissions (OAE), and tympanometry are objective tests for hearing. 

The objective tests of hearing are:

  • Evoked response audiometry
    • Electrocochleography
    • Auditory brainstem response
  • Otoacoustic emissions
  • Impedance audiometry
    • Tympanometry
    • Acoustic reflex measurements

Objective tests in ENT are diagnostic procedures that provide measurable, examiner-independent results. 

Brainstem-evoked response audiometry (BERA) or Auditory brainstem response (ABR) is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway. It elicits brainstem responses to auditory stimulation. Click stimuli or tone bursts lead to the generation of electrical potentials which are picked up from surface electrodes on the vertex.

Otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) refer to an objective test that records the low-intensity sounds produced by the outer hair cells of a normal cochlea. It can be elicited by a microphone in the external auditory canal and is then analyzed by a computer. They test the function of the cochlea. They are used to test hearing in neonates, and sedated/unconscious patients, and to differentiate cochlear from retro-cochlear hearing loss. 

Tympanometry is a component of impedance audiometry. It is an objective test of the middle ear and eustachian tube functions (conductive compartment of hearing). Here, the compliance of the tympanic membrane, i.e., how much it moves to the pressure differentials applied from the external ear is measured. This is plotted on a graph, to obtain a tympanogram. 

Note- Pure tone audiometry is a subjective test for hearing as it relies on the patient's responses to pure tone stimuli. Other examples of subjective tests include:

  • Tuning fork tests
  • Speech audiometry

The given clinical picture of an elderly diabetic patient with excruciating ear pain, facial palsy, and granulations on the floor of the external auditory canal points toward the diagnosis of malignant otitis externa. The correct statements are 2, 4 and 5.

Malignant otitis externa is an infective condition (not malignant). Technetium 99 scan is not used to monitor the disease. 

It is an inflammatory condition caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in elderly diabetics and immunocompromised patients. It is characterised by excruciating ear pain, profuse discharge and granulations on the floor of the external ear canal.

Necrosis of bone aids in the spread of infection. Infection may spread to the skull base and jugular foramen causing multiple cranial nerve palsies. Facial paralysis is the most common nerve palsy seen.

Gallium-67 scan is useful in the diagnosis and follow-up of the patient. It can be repeated every 3 weeks to monitor the disease and response to treatment. Technetium 99 bone scan reveals bone infection, but the test remains positive for a year or so and cannot be used to monitor the disease.

Treatment includes:

  • Control of diabetes.
  • Toilet of the ear canal. Remove discharge, debris and granulations or at dead tissue or bone.
  • Antibiotic treatment against P. aeruginosa for 6-8 weeks or more. If the patient is not responsive, treatment should be based on culture and sensitivity of ear discharge.

Antibiotics which are usually effective against pseudomonas aeroginosa are:

  • Gentamicin combined with ticarcillin (IV)
  • Third-generation cephalosporins (IV) e.g. ceftriaxone, ceftazidime along with an aminoglycoside
  • Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin and levofloxacin) combined with rifampin (Oral)

Tympanometry: It is used in evaluating the status of the middle ear and the functioning of the eustachian tube.

Principle: When a sound wave strikes the tympanic membrane, some of the sound energy is absorbed while the rest is reflected. A stiffer tympanic membrane would reflect more sound energy than a compliant one.

By changing the pressures in a sealed external auditory canal and then measuring the reflected sound energy, it is possible to find the compliance or stiffness of the tympano-ossicular system and thus find the healthy or diseased status of the middle ear.

Tympanometry is also used in evaluating the patency of the grommet inserted in the tympanic membrane for treating serous otitis media.

  • To absorb reflected sound
  • To change the pressure in the external auditory canal

  • Along the posterior belly of the digastric presenting as a swelling in the tip of the mastoid or the angle of the jaw
  • The upper part of the posterior triangle
  • Parapharyngeal space
  • Along with the carotid vessels.

  2. Drainage of the abscess in the neck with insertion of a drain through a separate incision
  3. IV antibiotics

It is situated at the posterior root of the zygoma.  Patients present with swelling in front and above the pinna with associated edema over the upper eyelid. Here the pus collects either superficial or deep to the temporalis muscle.

Option C: Luc abscess is defined as a subperiosteal temporal abscess. It develops following the spread of infection from the middle ear along the external auditory meatus, directly, to the temporal region. Swelling is present in the deep part of the bony meatus.

questions.explanation:

The procedure shown in the image is syringing, usually done for the removal of impacted wax. Reflex cough due to stimulation of the auricular branch of vagus can occur during this procedure.

Wax is made up of sebaceous and ceruminous gland secretions, hair, desquamated epithelial debris, keratin, and dirt. Factors contributing to the accumulation and impaction of excess wax may be a narrow, tortuous external canal, stiff ear, or obstructive lesions in the canal.

Patients with impacted wax may present with impaired hearing, tinnitus or giddiness. Long-standing impacted wax may ulcerate meatal skin and result in the formation of a wax granuloma.

Wax removal is achieved through syringing or other instrumental manipulation. Hard impacted mass may require prior softening with wax solvents in some cases.

The patient is seated, with the ear to be syringed facing the examiner. The patient wears a kidney tray over his or her shoulder and to collect the return fluid, the patient's head is tilted over the tray. A stream of water from the syringe is directed along the posterosuperior wall of the meatus as the pinna is pulled upwards and backward. The ear canal and tympanic membrane must be inspected and dried with a pledget of cotton at the end of the procedure.

Complications of syringing:

  • Vertigo– caloric stimulation of lateral semicircular canal if water is too hot or too cold
  • Rupture of the tympanic membrane
  • Reactivation of quiescent otitis media, if there is pre-existing perforation

Contraindications for syringing:

  • Presence of ear infection, tympanic membrane perforation
  • Presence of grommet or history of ear surgery.

Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. It arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium, comes out of it, and grows in the choana and nasal cavity. It is usually single and unilateral which are more commonly seen in children and young adults. 

It has 3 parts namely

  • Round and globular choanal part, and
  • Flat nasal part.

Diagnosis is made by radiograph of the paranasal sinuses reveals opacity of the involved antrum. Non-contrast CT scan reveals the extent of the polyp. Endoscopic examination reveals the antrochoanal polyp hidden posteriorly in the nasal cavity.

Endoscopic sinus surgery is the treatment of choice. Recurrence is uncommon after the complete removal of the polyp.

Correct answer: A. Rhinoscleroma

The given clinical scenario and the biopsy findings showing Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies are characteristic of rhinoscleroma.

Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (Frisch bacillus).

Mikulicz cells are large foam cells with a central nucleus and vacuolated cytoplasm containing causative bacilli. Russell bodies are homogenous eosinophilic inclusion bodies found in the plasma cells due to the accumulation of immunoglobulins secreted by plasma cells. Histology also shows infiltration of submucosa with plasma cells, lymphocytes and eosinophils.

Rhinoscleroma starts in the nose and extends to the nasopharynx, oropharynx, subglottic larynx, trachea and bronchi. It has 3 stages:

  1. Atrophic stage– Crusting and foul-smelling nasal discharge similar to atrophic rhinitis.
  2. Granulomatous stage– Painless, non-ulcerative granulomatous nodules with subdermal infiltration giving the feel of a woody nose.
  3. Cicatricial stage – Fibrosis leading to stenosis of vestibule, pharynx and larynx. 

Treatment is done by the use of antibiotics streptomycin and tetracycline for 4 to 6 weeks. Steroids to reduce fibrosis. Surgical intervention may be required to restore the airway and correct the nasal deformity. Treatment is stopped only when two consecutive cultures from the biopsy are negative.

Option C: Lupus vulgaris is a low-grade tuberculosis infection characterised by chronic vestibulitis and perforation of the nasal septum. Biopsy shows tuberculous granuloma and caseous necrosis.

Option D: Granulomatosis with polyangitis is a chronic granulomatous disorder presenting with crusting, granulation and saddle deformity of the nose. Biopsy shows necrosis and ulceration of mucosa, epithelioid granuloma and necrotizing vasculitis of the vessels.

CSF rhinorrhea refers to the leakage of clear or blood-tinged CSF into the nose. Fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid is the most common cause of this. Other causes include accidental or surgical trauma, infection and inflammation of the sinuses, neoplasms, and congenital lesions associated with skull base defects or may occur spontaneously.

Early cases of post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhea are managed conservatively by placing the patient in a semi-sitting position. Blowing of the nose, sneezing, and straining should be avoided. Prophylactic antibiotics can be administered to prevent meningitis. Persistent cases may be treated surgically by the intracranial or nasal endoscopic approach. The nasal endoscopic approach is useful for leaks from the frontal sinus, cribriform plate, and ethmoid or sphenoid sinuses.

Since it is absent in nasal secretions it helps to differentiate CSF from nasal secretions. It is also present in aqueous humor and perilymph. However, it cannot be used to localize the site of the leak.

Option D: CT cisternogram is done in cases where beta-2 transferrin detection is not available. It involves an intrathecal injection of iohexol followed by a CT scan. It is not preferred nowadays.

Note: Beta trace protein is another protein that is secreted by meninges and choroid plexus and is specific for CSF, but testing facilities are not widely available. An intrathecal fluorescein study may be performed preoperatively or intraoperatively to confirm the site of the defect.

Cottle test is positive in patients with a deviated nasal septum. It is used to assess the patency of the nasal valve and when positive, it indicates the abnormality in the vestibular component of the nasal valve.

In this test, the cheek is drawn laterally while the patient breathes quietly. If the nasal airway improves and the obstruction is relieved on the test side, the test is positive and indicates the surgery will be useful and the patient can be taken up for surgery.

The nasal valve area is the narrowest portion of the nasal passage. It is bounded medially by the nasal septum, superiorly and laterally by the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage, inferiorly by the floor of the piriform aperture and the nasal valve is the specific slit-like segment between the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage and the septum.

Conditions with a positive Cottle test:

  • Deviated nasal septum
  • Collapsed nasal valve - causes snoring and sleep apnoea
  • Valve stenosis

The below image depicts Cottle's test

The deviated nasal septum (DNS) may be caused by two main factors, trauma or developmental errors in addition to being dependent on racial and hereditary factors. Patients present with nasal obstruction, headache, sinusitis, and epistaxis and may manifest an external deformity as well.

Anatomically, DNS can be of various types

  • Anterior dislocation or the septal cartilage into one of the chambers
  • C-shaped deformity: the chamber on the concave side of the nasal septum will be wider and show compensatory hypertrophy of turbinates
  • S-shaped deformity: may cause bilateral nasal obstruction
  • Spur: a shelf-like projection often found at the junction of bone and cartilage
  • Thickening: thickening of a septum due to an organised hematoma may also cause obstruction

Treatment of DNS depends on the severity of symptoms. If asymptomatic, no treatment is required. When DNS causes a mechanical obstruction, submucosal resection or septoplasty (more conservative) may be done.

A parotid abscess refers to an infection and pus formation in the parotid space. It is caused most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. Post-surgical cases and debilitated patients with stasis of salivary flow are at risk of developing parotid abscesses.

Dehydration and fever are also present. Diagnosis is by ultrasonography or a CT scan. Multiple small loculi of pus are seen in the parenchyma. Aspiration of abscess can be done to determine the culture and sensitivity of the infective agent.

Surgical drainage under local or general anesthesia is carried out by a preauricular incision as employed for parotidectomy. A skin flap is raised to expose the surface of the gland, and the abscess or abscesses are bluntly opened working parallel to the branches of the VIIth nerve. questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rose position

Rose position is used in tonsillectomy surgery. 

In Rose's position, the patient is supine, with their head extended. A rubber ring is placed under the head to stabilize it and a pillow is placed under the shoulders to extend the head. Rose's position is also used in adenoidectomy and tracheostomy.

 

Indications of tonsillectomy are:

  • Recurrent episodes of acute tonsillitis – most common indication
  • Febrile seizures due to fever in tonsillitis
  • Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) - recurrent episodes in adults and a single episode in children
  • Hypertrophy of tonsils causing airway obstruction, difficulty in deglutition, interference with speech
  • Unilateral enlargement of tonsil with suspicion of malignancy
  • Chronic tonsillitis with bad taste or halitosis which is unresponsive to medical treatment (relative indication)
  • As a part of the surgical management of sleep apnea syndrome, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, and Eagle's syndrome.

Contraindications for tonsillectomy:

  • Haemoglobin level less than 10 g%.
  • Presence of acute infection in upper respiratory tract, even acute tonsillitis. Bleeding is more in the presence of acute infection.
  • Children under 3 years of age. They are poor surgical risks.
  • Overt or submucous cleft palate.
  • Bleeding disorders, e.g. leukaemia, purpura, aplastic anaemia or haemophilia.
  • At the time of the epidemic of polio.
  • Uncontrolled systemic disease, e.g. diabetes, cardiac disease, hypertension or asthma.
  • Tonsillectomy is avoided during the period of menses.

Other options:

Option A: The sniffing position involves flexion of the neck on the body and extension of the head on the neck which is done during tracheal intubation.

Option B: Semi fowler position is lying supine incline at an angle of 30 - 45 degrees. This position is used for patients who have cardiac or respiratory conditions, and for patients with a nasogastric tube. 

Option C: Reverse Trendelenburg position is lying flat with head 15 - 30 degrees higher than the feet. This position is used in ocular and ENT surgeries like minimally invasive cataract surgery and rhinoplasty.

questions.text: A 10-year-old boy with nas​al obstruction, nasal dis‍charge, sinusitis, and ch‌ronic suppurative otitis ‌media is scheduled for ad‌enoidectomy. Which of the​ following is a contraind‌ication for this procedur​e?
questions.raw_text: A 10-year-old boy with nasal obstruction, nasal discharge,  sinusitis, and chronic suppurative otitis media is scheduled for adenoidectomy. Which of the following is a contraindication for this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cleft palate

The presence of a cleft palate is a contraindication for adenoidectomy. 

Performing an adenoidectomy in a patient with a cleft palate can lead to velopharyngeal insufficiency, a disorder of the velopharyngeal valve. The function of this valve is to separate the oral and nasal cavities during actions like speaking, swallowing, vomiting, blowing, and sucking.

Velopharyngeal insufficiency leads to reduced speech intelligence as well as social and functional impairment. Patients have hypernasal speech, compensatory facial grimacing, and misarticulation.  

Indications for adenoidectomy include: 

  1. Symptomatic adenoid hypertrophy
  2. Recurrent sinusitis (Option A)
  3. Chronic otitis media (Option B) 
  4. Chronic suppurative otitis media and recurrent ear discharge
  5. Dental malocclusion (Option D) occurring due to a low-positioned tongue, and separated lips. 

Contraindications of adenoidectomy include: 

  1. Cleft palate or submucous palate
  2. Hemorrhagic diathesis
  3. Acute infection of the upper respiratory tract 

Adenoidectomy is performed under general anesthesia in Rose's position. Here the patient is supine with the head extended by using a pillow under the shoulders. The head is stabilized with a rubber ring and hyperextension of the neck should be avoided. 

A Boyle - Davis mouth gag is inserted after examining the nasopharynx. An adenoid curette with a guard is introduced into the nasopharynx to engage the adenoids. The adenoid tissue is shaved off with gentle sweeping movements with smaller curettes used to remove lateral masses while avoiding the eustachian tubes. Hemostasis is achieved by packing the area and electrocoagulation. Persistent bleeding can be treated with a postnasal pack. 

Complications of adenoidectomy include: 

  • Hemorrhage
  • Injury to the eustachian tube opening
  • Injury to pharyngeal musculature and vertebrae due to hyperextension of the neck and pressure of the curette
  • Griesel syndrome: neck pain and torticollis due to spasm of paraspinal muscles or atlantoaxial dislocation
  • Velopharyngeal insufficiency
  • Nasopharyngeal stenosis
  • Recurrence.

This clinical vignette is suggestive of laryngeal papilloma or recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.

It is the most common benign neoplasm of the larynx in children. It is caused by human papilloma DNA virus (HPV) types 6 and 11. Squamous papillomas can be seen in children, juvenile papillomatosis (as in this case), and in adults, adult-onset papilloma. 

It is thought that the patients acquire this condition from their mothers who had vaginal human papillomavirus infection during birth. It is usually seen in the supraglottic and glottic regions. Less commonly, the subglottis, trachea, and bronchi may be involved.

Clinically, the patient is typically a young child 3-5 years of age. They may present with hoarseness of voice, stridor, and breathing difficulty. The disease recurs requiring repeated surgical and medical management throughout childhood. Rarely, they may undergo malignant change. 

It is diagnosed using flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy and may later be confirmed by direct laryngoscopy or rigid bronchoscopy and biopsy.

  • Medical management using interferon-alpha has been tried as an adjuvant, but it is associated with significant side effects

Treatment of septal hematomas involves aspiration with a wide bore needle if small, and incision and drainage if large. The incision can be made parallel to the nasal floor. Removing a small piece of nasal mucosa will aid in drainage. After drainage, the nose has to be packed bilaterally to avoid reaccumulation.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is extremely radiosensitive, hence treatment of local and regional disease is invariably radiotherapy. 

  • Stage I and II are treated by radiotherapy alone while
  • Stage III and IV require concomitant radiation and chemotherapy or radiation followed by chemotherapy.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking.

  1. Keratinizing carcinoma

  3. Nonkeratinizing undifferentiated carcinoma.

questions.raw_text: A middle-aged man presents with unilateral nasal obstruction. To check for patency of the nasal valve, a Cottle test is performed. In which of the following cases is the test positive?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Deviated nasal septum

Cottle test is positive in patients with a deviated nasal septum. It is used to assess the patency of the nasal valve and when positive, it indicates the abnormality in the vestibular component of the nasal valve.

In this test, the cheek is drawn laterally while the patient breathes quietly. If the nasal airway improves and the obstruction is relieved on the test side, the test is positive and indicates the surgery will be useful and the patient can be taken up for surgery.

The nasal valve area is the narrowest portion of the nasal passage. It is bounded medially by the nasal septum, superiorly and laterally by the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage, inferiorly by the floor of the piriform aperture and the nasal valve is the specific slit-like segment between the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage and the septum.

Conditions with a positive Cottle test:

  • Deviated nasal septum
  • Collapsed nasal valve - causes snoring and sleep apnoea
  • Valve stenosis

The below image depicts Cottle's test

The deviated nasal septum (DNS) may be caused by two main factors, trauma or developmental errors in addition to being dependent on racial and hereditary factors. Patients present with nasal obstruction, headache, sinusitis, and epistaxis and may manifest an external deformity as well.

Anatomically, DNS can be of various types

  • Anterior dislocation or the septal cartilage into one of the chambers
  • C-shaped deformity: the chamber on the concave side of the nasal septum will be wider and show compensatory hypertrophy of turbinates
  • S-shaped deformity: may cause bilateral nasal obstruction
  • Spur: a shelf-like projection often found at the junction of bone and cartilage
  • Thickening: thickening of a septum due to an organised hematoma may also cause obstruction

Treatment of DNS depends on the severity of symptoms. If asymptomatic, no treatment is required. When DNS causes a mechanical obstruction, submucosal resection or septoplasty (more conservative) may be done.

Other options:

Epistaxis refers to bleeding into the nasal cavity and most commonly occurs in the little's area in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum. Cottle test to relieve nasal obstruction has no role here. Trotter's method is used as a first aid to arrest bleeding from the little's area.

Atrophic rhinitis refers to chronic inflammation of the nose with atrophy of nasal mucosa. The patients may present with nasal obstruction due to the crusting filling the roomy nasal cavity. Removal of the crust may relieve the obstruction but has the risk of bleeding.

The nasal polyp occurs due to edematous nasal mucosa. It can be an antrochoanal polyp arising from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum or an ethmoidal polyp arising from the middle meatus in the lateral wall of the nose. These polyps appear as globular mass and can be differentiated from turbinate hypertrophy by a probe test. Nasal obstruction resulting from polyps get resolved by conservative or surgical management.

Correct answer: A. Atrophic rhinitis

The clinical vignette of merciful anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and roomy nasal cavities, with dry greenish crusts, points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis.

Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. The exact etiology of this condition is not known. It is more common in females and starts around puberty. 

Clinically patients present with nasal obstruction, foul odor, and merciful anosmia. Merciful anosmia is when the patient has marked anosmia and is unable to smell the foul odor coming from their nose.

On examination of the nose, greenish or greyish crusting of the nasal passage, pale nasal mucosa, atrophied nasal turbinates, and epistaxis following the removal of the crusts. The roomy nasal cavity is seen due to the resorption of bones of the turbinates.

Treatment:

  • Nasal irrigation - using warm saline or an alkaline solution composed of sodium bicarbonate 1 part, sodium biborate 1 part, and sodium chloride 2 parts in 280 mL of water
  • Local antibiotics - Kemicetine antiozaena solution containing chloromycetin, oestradiol, and vitamin D2. 
  • 25% glucose in glycerine, estradiol spray, systemic use of streptomycin, potassium iodide, and placental extract.
  • Surgical management:
    • Young's operation.
    • Modified young operation.
    • Narrowing of the nasal cavity can be done by submucosal injection of Teflon paste, or by insertion of fat, cartilage, or Teflon strips under the mucoperiosteum.

Other options:

Option B: Nasal polyps are non-neoplastic masses of the edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. Nasal polyps can be antrochoanal polyps or ethmoidal polyps. They present with a polypoid mass in the nose.

Option C: Allergic rhinitis is associated with inferior turbinate hypertrophy and can cause chronic nasal obstruction. It is characterized by watery nasal discharge, sneezing, and itching in the nose.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inverted papilloma

On the basis of the given images, inverted papilloma could be the most likely underlying cause.

Inverted papilloma (Ringertz tumor or transitional cell papilloma or Schneiderian papilloma) is a benign neoplasm of the non-olfactory mucosa of the nose (also called the Schneiderian membrane) and paranasal sinuses.

The lateral wall of the nose in the middle meatus is the most common site of origin. The hyperplastic papillomatous tissue grows into the stroma.
It is common in the 4th to 7th decades of life with a male preponderance. It is almost always unilateral and presents with unilateral nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis. It can invade sinuses or the orbit, the latter of which causes proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation.
 
On examination of nose or endoscopy, it presents as a polypoidal mass resembling simple nasal polyps, as depicted by arrows in the endoscopic image above. A computed tomography(CT) scan and/or magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) show the location and extent of the lesion. MRI provides additional help to differentiate associated secretions in the sinus from the actual tumor mass. A biopsy is essential for diagnosis.
 
Medial maxillectomy is the treatment of choice, done preferably via endoscopy. Recurrence is common and malignancy has been observed in up to 15% of the cases.
 
Other options:
 
Option B: Carcinoma maxilla arises from the lining of the maxillary sinus and its early features include additional symptoms like facial paraesthesias, pain, or epiphora and depending on the direction of spread of the growth, would cause additional symptoms.
 
Option C: Esthesioneuroblastoma (olfactory neuroblastoma) arises from the olfactory epithelium in the upper third of the nose. It has bimodal peaks of incidence at 10–20 years and 50–60 years. Unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis are the most common symptoms. The tumour also invades the orbit and the surrounding structures, which results in other symptoms like proptosis, headache, epiphora, diplopia, and blurred vision.
 
Option D: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is seen almost exclusively in males in the age group of 10–20 years and is very rarely seen in older people and females. Profuse, recurrent, and spontaneous epistaxis is the most common presentation.
