questions.text: Where is the electrode pla‌ced in cochlear implant p​rocedures?
questions.raw_text: Where is the electrode placed in cochlear implant procedures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Scala tympani

The electrode of a cochlear implant is placed in the scala tympani.

A cochlear implant is a medical device that uses electricity to stimulate the spiral ganglion cells of the auditory nerve to restore sensorineural hearing loss. It converts sound to an electrical signal (transduction) and delivers this to the hearing nerve, which bypasses the damaged hearing apparatus. It cannot be used in patients with cochlear aplasia or without the VIIIth cranial nerve.

Cochlear implant:

  • An electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from a hearing aid.
  • Principle- surgery to place the electrode array within the scala tympani of the cochlea.
  • Indication- bilateral severe to profound deafness
  • Prerequisites- intact 8th nerve and higher auditory pathway
  • Surgical approach- facial recess (posterior tympanotomy) approach
  • The electrode of a cochlear implant is placed in the scala tympani. (Note: In the auditory brainstem implant, the site of the implant is the lateral recess of the 4th ventricle.)

The receiver-stimulator implanted during surgery (under the skin) and the electrode array (implanted in the scala tympani of the cochlea) are part of the internal component of the cochlear implant. Microphone, speech processor, and transmitter are part of the external component of the cochlear implant, which remains outside the body.

Cochlear implants replace the non-functional transducer system of hair cells of the cochlea and convert the sound signal to electrical impulses, which directly stimulate the fibers of cranial nerve VIII.

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). The diagnostic maneuver used in BPPV is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, the gold standard for diagnosing BPPV. The therapeutic maneuver is Epley's maneuver.

BPPV is one of the common causes of recurrent vertigo, and the episodes are brief (<1min) and are always provoked by changes in head position. The attacks are caused by free-floating calcium carbonate crystals usually dislodged from the posterior canal.

A patient presenting with vertigo should be evaluated for ruling out the central lesions (like a tumor in the fourth ventricle, multiple sclerosis, etc) before confirming the diagnosis of BPPV. Dix-Hallpike maneuver helps rule out central lesions and also diagnose BPPV.

  1. The maneuver starts with the patient in a sitting position.
  2. Their head is turned 45 degrees towards the ear to be tested.
  3. The examiner quickly brings the patient to a supine position with their head 30 degrees below the horizontal.
  4. The 45-degree head rotation is maintained during the procedure.
  5. Now the examiner observes the patient for nystagmus.

Correct answer: A. Meniere's disease

The possible clinical diagnosis for a 35-year-old male presenting with episodic vertigo, ear pressure and fullness, decreased hearing, and low-tone roaring tinnitus is Meniere's disease. It is also called endolymphatic hydrops.

The primary pathology in Ménière’s disease is the distension of the endolymphatic system due to an increased endolymph volume. This can result either from increased production of endolymph or its faulty absorption or both. Normally, endolymph secreted by stria vascularis, fills the membranous labyrinth, and is absorbed through the endolymphatic sac.

Meniere's disease is a chronic condition of the inner ear that affects balance and hearing. It is characterized by recurrent episodes of vertigo, which are brief and intense episodes of spinning dizziness. Patients may also experience a sense of pressure or fullness in the affected ear, along with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus (ringing or buzzing in the ear). The tinnitus associated with Meniere's disease is typically low-tone roaring in nature.

Other options:

  • Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is another common cause of vertigo, but it is characterized by brief episodes of vertigo triggered by specific head movements, such as rolling over in bed or looking up. BPPV does not typically cause ear pressure, hearing loss, or low-tone roaring tinnitus.
  • Labyrinthitis is an inflammation of the inner ear, usually caused by a viral or bacterial infection. It can cause vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus, but it is usually accompanied by other symptoms such as ear pain, fever, and a general feeling of illness.
  • Syncope refers to a temporary loss of consciousness and muscle tone, often caused by a decrease in blood flow to the brain. It is not associated with the symptoms described in the scenario, such as vertigo, ear pressure, hearing loss, or tinnitus.

Correct answer: A. Rhinoscleroma

The given clinical scenario and the biopsy findings showing Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies are characteristic of rhinoscleroma.

Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (Frisch bacillus).

Mikulicz cells are large foam cells with a central nucleus and vacuolated cytoplasm containing causative bacilli. Russell bodies are homogenous eosinophilic inclusion bodies found in the plasma cells due to the accumulation of immunoglobulins secreted by plasma cells. Histology also shows infiltration of submucosa with plasma cells, lymphocytes and eosinophils. 

The following image shows rhinoscleroma with Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies(marked in black arrows)

Rhinoscleroma starts in the nose and extends to the nasopharynx, oropharynx, subglottic larynx, trachea and bronchi. It has 3 stages:

  1. Atrophic stage– Crusting and foul-smelling nasal discharge similar to atrophic rhinitis.
  2. Granulomatous stage– Painless, non-ulcerative granulomatous nodules with subdermal infiltration giving the feel of a woody nose.
  3. Cicatricial stage – Fibrosis leading to stenosis of vestibule, pharynx and larynx. 

Treatment is done by the use of antibiotics streptomycin and tetracycline for 4 to 6 weeks. Steroids to reduce fibrosis. Surgical intervention may be required to restore the airway and correct the nasal deformity. Treatment is stopped only when two consecutive cultures from the biopsy are negative.

Option D: Granulomatosis with polyangitis is a chronic granulomatous disorder presenting with crusting, granulation and saddle deformity of the nose. Biopsy shows necrosis and ulceration of mucosa, epithelioid granuloma and necrotizing vasculitis of the vessels.

questions.text: During syringing, water je‌t is directed along _____​_
questions.raw_text: During syringing, water jet is directed along ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterosuperior wall

Syringing: Pinna is pulled upwards and backwards and a stream of water from the ear syringe is directed along the posterosuperior wall of the meatus.

This is derived from 2 anatomic facts:

  • The posteroinferior wall of EAC is supplied by the vagus nerve. Direct stimulation of this can lead to sudden cardiac arrest.
  • On manoeuvring the pinna to bring the EAC into a straight configuration, the posterior wall is straighter and easily accessible than the anterior wall.

Therefore, the direction of choice for the jet of water is along the posterosuperior wall. 

Complications

  • Vertigo – caloric stimulation of lateral semicircular canal if water is too hot or too cold.
  • Rupture of TM.
  • Reactivation of quiescent otitis media (if there is pre-existing perforation).

Contraindications for syringing

  • Presence of ear infection, TM perforation
  • Presence of grommet or H/O ear surgery

The above clinical scenario along is most likely suggestive of the diagnosis of Bezold's abscess.

Bezold abscess is defined as a complication of acute coalescent mastoiditis and is formed when pus breaks inferiorly, through the thin medial aspect of the tip of the mastoid and collects in the upper part of the neck, most commonly into the sheath of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.   • Along the posterior belly of the digastric presenting as a swelling in the tip of the mastoid or the angle of the jaw
  • The upper part of the posterior triangle
  • Parapharyngeal space
  • Along with the carotid vessels.

Treatment:

  1. Cortical mastoidectomy for coalescent mastoiditis
  2. Drainage of the abscess in the neck with insertion of a drain through a separate incision
  3. IV antibiotics

Other options:

Option A: Zygomatic abscess forms due to infection of the zygomatic air cells. It is situated at the posterior root of the zygoma.  Patients present with swelling in front and above the pinna with associated edema over the upper eyelid. Here the pus collects either superficial or deep to the temporalis muscle.

Option C: Luc abscess is defined as a subperiosteal temporal abscess. It develops following the spread of infection from the middle ear along the external auditory meatus, directly, to the temporal region. Swelling is present in the deep part of the bony meatus. 

Option D: Citelli’s abscess is formed posterior to the mastoid, occupying a position more towards the occipital bone. It is also considered an abscess of the digastric triangle. In any case, a diagnosis of Bezold abscess is more appropriate for this patient owing to the location of the abscess.

The above image shows a stapedotomy procedure performed in the middle ear.

It can be identified as a stapedotomy procedure by the following features in the image given:

  • The footplate of the stapes is not removed
  • The prosthesis is placed by creating a hole in the footplate of the stapes

Stapedotomy is the excision of the superstructure of stapes and drilling a hole in the footplate & placing a piston in the hole. It is done to bypass the immobile stapes using a piston which will take over the function of conducting sound.

Contraindications for Stapedotomy:

  • Positive Schwartze sign
  • Otitis externa
  • Meniere’s disease: can damage the inner ear while drilling a hole in the footplate
  • Young children
  • Professional athletes, pilots, construction workers, divers: Sudden change in pressure can displace the piston and cause vertigo.
  • Those who work in noisy surroundings: Surgery makes them more vulnerable to noise-induced hearing loss.

Otosclerosis is a primary disease of the bony labyrinth where foci of irregularly placed spongy bone replace part of the normally dense enchondral layer of the bony otic capsule. It is more commonly seen in females between 20-30 years of age and the hearing loss is aggravated during pregnancy and menopause.

Clinically, patients present with painless progressive bilateral conductive hearing loss and paracusis willisii (patient hears better in noisy surroundings as other people raise their voice to be heard). 

Tuning fork tests and audiometry will reveal the presence of conductive hearing loss. The bone conduction curve may show a dip, which is maximum at 2000Hz, known as Carhart’s notch.

The image shown below shows Carhart's notch.

Other options:

Options B and C: Stapes mobilization and Lempert’s fenestration operation are older procedures seldom performed these days.

Option D: Stapedectomy involves complete removal of the anterior and posterior portions of the footplate, leaving the membrane below the footplate intact. Now the oval window with its overlying membrane is covered with a piece of fascia and the prosthesis is placed over this.

Correct answer: B. Osteosarcoma

The given X-ray image showing the sunburst appearance is suggestive of osteosarcoma. 

Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant tumour of the bone, with bimodal age of distribution peaking in adolescence and during the 7th decade.

The most common site involved is the distal femoral metaphysis, which mainly presents with pain and swelling. Other sites commonly involved are the proximal tibia, proximal femur, and humerus.

  • Sunburst appearance → due to new bone formation along the blood vessels within the tumor
  • Periosteal reaction → due to the lifting of the periosteum of the bone. Periosteal reaction in osteosarcoma is irregular, unlike in osteomyelitis where it is smooth.

It usually occurs at a younger age and commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus. Most tumors have a balanced translocation (11;22) involving EWSRI gene and FL1 gene.

Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is seen in radiology (as shown below) and Homer-Wright rosettes, which are round groupings of cells with a central fibrillary core may be seen histologically.

On X-rays, they appear as a well-circumscribed, round, or oval lytic lesion in the centre of the epiphysis of long bones with areas of calcification within the tumour. On histology presence of "chicken wire calcification" is pathognomic.

The image below shows an X-ray with a well-circumscribed, round lytic lesion in the centre of the epiphysis of the tibia suggestive of chondroblastoma.

Correct answer: A. Fasciotomy

The given clinical scenario suggests acute compartment syndrome, and it is treated immediately with fasciotomy.

The classic features of ischemia in acute compartment syndrome include the 5 Ps:

  • Pain: Pain is the first symptom of acute compartment syndrome. Ischemic muscle is highly sensitive to touch. On the passive stretching of the muscles, severe pain can be elicited. 
  • Paresthesia: Paresthesia and hypoesthesia may be noted due to compression of nerves traversing the affected compartment. They are the first signs of nerve ischemia.
  • Pallor: Pallor of the skin may not always be seen. The skin outside the compartment may be normally perfused, as only the intra-compartmental perfusion may be affected.
  • Paralysis: Paralysis of muscle groups affected in that compartment is a late sign.
  • Pulselessness: Usually, the peripheral pulses and capillary return are intact in the early stages, unless there is a major arterial injury. If pulses are absent, arteriography is indicated. 

The diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring the intra-compartmental pressure using a split catheter introduced into the compartment. The difference between diastolic pressure and compartment pressure is known as the differential pressure (ΔP). A differential pressure (ΔP) of less than 30 mm Hg (4.00 kilopascals) is an indication for immediate compartment decompression.

Treatment: The threatened compartment must be promptly decompressed, merely splitting the plaster is utterly useless and the limb must be nursed flat, elevating the limb causes further decrease in end capillary pressure and aggravates the muscle ischemia. In the case of compartment syndrome in the leg, Fasciotomy means opening all four compartments. Wounds to be left open and inspected 2 days later, if tissues are healthy, the wounds can be sutured. If there is muscle necrosis, debridement to be carried out.

questions.raw_text:
Identify the correct statements about the deterministic effects of radiation.

  1. It is associated with damage to the DNA of cells.
  2. The severity of these effects is independent of the dose received.
  3. Examples include oligospermia, skin erythema, and epilation.
  4. Below the threshold dose, harmful effects do not occur.
  5. The fetus is more vulnerable to these effects between the 2nd to 20th week of gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4 and 5 are correct

Statements 3, 4, and 5 are correct about the deterministic effects of radiation.

The harmful effects of radiation may be classified into two general categories: Stochastic effects and nonstochastic/deterministic effects.

Non-stochastic/Deterministic effects: 

These effects do not occur below a threshold dose. The severity of the effect increases as the dose increases. These effects are associated with radiation-induced killing or malfunction of cells. Skin erythema, epilation, cataracts, and transient oligospermia are a few examples of nonstochastic/deterministic effects.

The fetus is most vulnerable to deterministic effects of radiation between the 2nd and 20th week of gestation. Usually, no deterministic effects occur at a dose below 100 mGy which is the threshold for most imaging modalities.

Stochastic effects: 

Stochastic effects of ionizing radiation are chance events associated with damage to the DNA of cells. They may result in cancer or heritable effects. The incidence of these effects is directly proportionate to the dose of radiation in organs or tissues, but the severity of the effect is independent of the dose received. (All or none phenomenon)

questions.text: A 25-year-old male was in ‌a major RTA 6 weeks back.​ Since then he has been e​xperiencing frequent intr‌usive flashbacks and nigh‍tmares about the incident​. He avoids the place whe‍re the accident occurred.​ What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Post traumatic stress disorder

The given clinical scenario with re-experiences (flashbacks and nightmares), avoidance of the stimuli associated with the attacks, and hyperarousal (impaired sleep and anxiety) for more than one month are suggestive of post-traumatic stress disorder(PTSD).

PTSD is a psychiatric disorder characterized by increased stress and anxiety occurring after a stressful or traumatic event, (e.g., witnessing or being involved in violent accidents, crime, war, assault, kidnapping, natural disaster, life-threatening illness, physical or sexual abuse). 

The predisposing factors for this condition include:

  • Presence of childhood trauma
  • Borderline, paranoid, dependent, or antisocial personality disorder traits
  • Inadequate family or peer support system
  • Female gender
  • Genetic susceptibility to psychiatric illness
  • Recent stressful life changes
  • Recent excessive intake of alcohol

Symptoms of PTSD can be divided into four types:

  • Intrusion symptoms
    • Flashbacks- The individual may act and feel as if the traumatic event is reoccurring 
    • Nightmares of the event
  • Hyperarousal 
    • Increased startle response
    • Insomnia
    • Hypervigilance
    • Difficulty concentrating
    • Reckless and self-destructive behavior
    • Irritability and anxiety
  • Avoidance symptoms:  
    • avoiding memories, thoughts, and feelings of the event
    • avoiding external reminders of the traumatic event
  • Negative cognitions and mood associated with the traumatic event
    • Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event
    • Feelings of depersonalization and derealization
    • Anhedonia
    • Negative emotional state- fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

The duration of these symptoms should be > 1 month to label it as PTSD.

Psychotherapies found to be effective for PTSD include exposure therapy, trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy, eye movement desensitization, and abreaction. SSRIs may be prescribed as first-line treatment.

Other options:

Option A: Adjustment disorder is an emotional response to stressful situations like financial issues, medical illnesses, or relation­ship problems that develop within 3 months of the stressor. The stressor in adjustment disorder can be of any severity. In adjustment disorder, the individual does not experience intrusive symptoms like flashbacks and nightmares, hyperarousal symptoms, and avoidance symptoms.

Option B: Acute stress disorder presents with the same symptoms as PTSD, but the symptoms usually occur immediately after the trauma and persist for a period of 3 days to upto 1 month after the trauma.

Option C: Persistent complex bereavement disorder occurs after the death of a loved one. Since the death, for 12 months or more, the individual may experience persistent yearning/longing for the deceased, intense sorrow, emotional pain, preoccupation with the deceased, and the circumstances of the death.

questions.text: A 12-year-old boy with aca‌demic and behavioral prob​lems at school over the p​ast year was diagnosed wi‌th attention-deficit hype‍ractivity disorder. Which​ of the following neurotr‍ansmitters plays a key ro​le in the pathophysiology‍ of this condition?
questions.raw_text: A 12-year-old boy with academic and behavioral problems at school over the past year was diagnosed with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. Which of the following neurotransmitters plays a key role in the pathophysiology of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dopamine

Dopamine has been hypothesized as the key neurotransmitter involved in the pathophysiology of attention-deficit hyperactive disorder.

The prefrontal cortex of the brain has been implicated in Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) because of its high utilization of dopamine and its reciprocal connections with other brain regions involved in attention, inhibition, decision-making, response inhibition, working memory, and vigilance. Apart from dopamine, imbalances in the levels of norepinephrine also play a role in this disorder.

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neuropsychiatric condition affecting children, adolescents, and adults around the world, characterized by a pattern of diminished sustained attention, and increased impulsivity or hyperactivity. They often have significant impairment in academic functioning as well as in social and interpersonal situations.

The clinical features of ADHD are :

  • Inattention- difficulty focusing, distractibility, not listening or following instructions, failure to finish tasks, forgetfulness, losing/misplacing objects.
  • Hyperactivity- fidgety, unable to sit still, as though driven by a motor, hyper-talkative, interrupts, blurts out answers.
  • Impulsivity- action before thought, abrupt shifts in activity, lack of organization, jumping up in class.
  • Other symptoms may include memory and thinking deficits and specific learning disabilities. 

A variety of medications and behavioral interventions are used to treat ADHD. The most widely used medications are methylphenidate, d-amphetamine, and other amphetamines. These drugs are stimulants that affect the level of the neurotransmitter dopamine at the synapse. Interventions used to treat ADHD include several forms of psychotherapy, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy, social skills training, support groups, and parent and educator skills training. A combination of medication and psychotherapy is more effective than either treatment alone.

Correct answer: B. Etomidate

Etomidate is considered to be the most appropriate induction agent for cardiac patients. 

Etomidate has minimal effect on cardiovascular function due to its lack of effect on the sympathetic nervous system and on the function of the baroreceptors. They act on alpha 2 adrenoreceptors and increase blood pressure which helps to maintain cardiovascular stability after the induction. 

Etomidate is the induction agent of choice in patients with cardiovascular disease, reactive airway disease, and intracranial hypertension,

Due to its unique hemodynamic stability, it is used as a short-term sedative in hemodynamically unstable patients like patients requiring cardioversion or in patients with unstable angina for minor operative procedures.

Long-term use of etomidate in trauma or terminally ill patients will cause a reversible inhibition on 11 beta-hydroxylase which decreases cortisol production and increase 11 deoxycorticosterone. This results in adrenocortical suppression.

Other options:

Option A- Ketamine has a stimulatory effect on the sympathetic nervous system and results in increased blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output. This leads to an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption and so it is contraindicated in ischemic heart disease.

Option C- Propofol is a myocardial depressant agent. It reduces sympathetic activity, leading to vasodilatation that results in a reduction of blood pressure and a decrease in cardiac output.

Option D- Thiopentone is also a myocardial depressant agent. It causes peripheral vasodilatation, reduction in the ventricular filling, negative inotropic effect, and reduction in a sympathetic outflow from CNS. this results in a reduction in blood pressure and a decrease in cardiac output.

questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient‌ comes with chronic right​ shoulder pain. While exa​mining the patient, the f‌ollowing test elicits wea‍kness in the right should​er. Which of the followin‍g muscles/tendons is impl​icated here?

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supraspinatus

The test depicted in the image is the empty can test and the muscle/tendon implicated here is the supraspinatus.

In this test, the patient is asked to resist the downward force by the examiner, when the arms are in the position of 90° abduction, 30° flexion, and complete internal rotation(as if emptying a can, hence the name of the test). The result is positive if the affected side is weaker than the normal side and indicates a tear in the supraspinatus tendon.

Other options:

Option B: Infraspinatus – Resisted external rotation - The patient flexes elbows to 90 degrees and stands holding his/her arm close to the body. The patient then externally rotates both arms while the examiner applies resistance; lack of power on one side signifies weakness of infraspinatus. 

Option C: Teres minor cannot be assessed separately. But it can assessed along with infraspinatus as they both perform external rotation of the shoulder joint. ‘Lag sign’ and the ‘Drop sign’ are used for this purpose.

The lag sign is performed by asking the patient to lift his arms slightly away from the body and place them in maximum external rotation. A positive test is elicited when the patient cannot maintain that position on one side and allows the arm to drift into a more neutral position. This suggests a tear of the infraspinatus, teres minor, or supraspinatus. 

The drop sign is similar, here the arm is in 90 degrees of abduction, the elbow flexed to 90 degrees and the arm maximally externally rotated. When the examiner lets go, the patient would normally hold that position, but if the arm ‘drops’, it denotes a positive test

Option D: Subscapularis –Lift-off test - The patient places one arm behind his or her back with the dorsum of the hand resting against the mid-lumbar spine. The patient’s hand is lifted off the back and the patient is told to hold it there. The inability to do this signifies subscapularis weakness.

questions.raw_text: A patient stopped alcohol consumption for 3 days and presented with irritability, disorientation, paranoid delusions, agitation, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?

Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The given clinical scenario of a patient who has not consumed alcohol for the past 3 days presenting with disorientation, paranoid delusions, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium is suggestive of delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal.

The clinical features of delirium tremens are as follows:

  • Altered sensorium with disorientation
  • Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations
  • Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, hypertension, and sweating
  • Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy
  • Altered sleep-wake cycle

Other options:

Option B: Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits or malabsorption.

It is an acute neurological disorder characterized by

  • Global confusion
  • Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex
  • Ataxia - mainly affecting the gait
  • Vestibular dysfunction

It may resolve with thiamine therapy or progress to Korsakoff's syndrome.

Option C: Korsakoff’s psychosis can follow Wernicke’s encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency. It is a chronic amnestic syndrome that is characterized by the following clinical symptoms in an intact and responsive patient:

  • Impaired mental syndrome, especially recent memory
  • Anterograde amnesia
  • Confabulation

Option D: Alcohol-induced psychosis is characterized by the development of auditory hallucinations or paranoid delusions in the context of heavy drinking or alcohol withdrawal. These patients have a clear sensorium, unlike the patients having delirium tremens.

  • Betel quid which contains areca nut and tobacco leaf
  • Environmental factors like:

    • Radiotherapy
    • Anxiety, depression, stress

The most common presentation of lichen planus is a well-defined area of purple-colored, itchy, flat-topped papules. This description is known as the characteristic "6 Ps" of lichen planus: planar (flat-topped), purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, and plaques.

  • Saw-toothed appearance of the Rete ridges
  • Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate is present at the dermo-epidermal junction.

Osteoarthritis is the most common cause of chronic knee pain in individuals of age >45 years. In the early phases, there is episodic joint pain following overactive use of the diseased joint. As the disease progresses, there is continuous pain and may be associated with stiffness of the affected joint. Morning stiffness if present, is usually brief for around 30 minutes.

The joints involved in osteoarthritis are: 

  • Hip and knee joints
  • Distal and proximal interphalangeal joints (DIP, PIP)
  • First carpometacarpal joint (base of the thumb)
  • First metatarsophalangeal joint (MTP)
  • Cervical and lumbosacral spine

On examination, there is tenderness in the joint. A crepitus is felt on joint movement and the range of movements is painfully restricted. Bouchard's and Heberden's nodes may be palpated in PIP and DIP respectively.

Characteristic features of osteoarthritis seen on plain X-ray are:

  • Marginal osteophyte formation
  • Localized joint space narrowing
  • Sclerosis of the underlying bone

Other hallmark features include flexor tendon tenosynovitis, swan neck deformity, boutonniere deformity, Z-line deformity, and trigger finger.

  • Progressive:

    • Mural thickening and enhancement.
    • Poorly enhancing renal parenchyma.
  • End-stage:

    • Amorphous dystrophic calcification that involves the entire kidney - putty kidney

Treatment involves short-course therapy with antitubercular drugs like pyrazinamide, isoniazid, and rifampicin. Partial nephrectomy, nephrectomy, or reconstructive surgery is often done.

They are excessively fearful of perceived threats and deceit and often read hidden demeaning or threatening meanings into benign remarks. They tend to be extremely jealous, hostile, argumentative, and defensive. Their paranoia prevents them from establishing any overly-involved relationship. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the skin with systemic manifestations. Plaque psoriasis is the most common type.

  • The peak occurrence is between 16 to 22 years and between 57 to 62 years. They usually present with itching and a papulosquamous rash.
  • The lesions are red, and scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin.
  • They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone which is called the Woronoff ring.
  • They commonly appear in the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs.
  • Koebner or isomorphic phenomenon- describes the appearance of new lesions along the site of trauma (linear lesions)

Nail findings are commonly seen across all types of psoriasis. Patients present with pits, ridges, and grooves of the nail plate. In the case of nail bed involvement subungual oil drops, subungual hyperkeratosis, and distal onycholysis can be seen.

The characteristic histopathological finding in psoriasis consists of multiple neutrophilic foci in the parakeratotic stratum corneum i.e Munro’s microabscesses and spongiform neutrophils in the spinous layer of the epidermis i.e spongiform pustules of Kogoj.

The topical application of steroids, retinoids, vitamin D, and emollients is the mainstay of management. Phototherapy and oral methotrexate, acitretin, and cyclosporine can also be used.

questions.text: Which of the following rad‌ioisotopes is used in a P​ET-CT scan?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following radioisotopes is used in a PET-CT scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 18F-FDG

18F-FDG is the radioisotope used in a PET-CT scan.

Positron emission tomography - CT (PET-CT):

  • PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer.
  • It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron.
  • A glucose analogue called FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is used in PET imaging. FDG is taken up by metabolically active cells, where it undergoes phosphorylation to form FDG-6-phosphate. Unlike glucose, FDG-6-phosphate cannot undergo further metabolism and becomes trapped within the cell. (So, the patient must be fasted for 4-6 hrs prior to imaging).
  • The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner. 
  • Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose.
  • Imaging is started 60 minutes following FDG injection.

Indications of PET-CT:

  • PET-CT is used in oncology imaging to detect malignant cells as they demonstrate increased glucose metabolism relative to normal tissues.
  • It is indicated for the differentiation of a malignant from a benign lesion.
  • It is indicated in tumour staging and evaluation of tumour recurrence.

Areas of normal physiological uptake in PET CT:

  • Brain tissue
  • Skeletal muscle, especially after strenuous activity, and laryngeal muscles following speech
  • Myocardium
  • Gastrointestinal tract, e.g. intestinal wall
  • Genitourinary tract (FDG is excreted via the renal system and passes into the collecting systems)
  • Brown fat (FDG accumulates here as glucose and ATP are required for heat production)
  • Thymus
  • Bone marrow

Other options:

Option A: 16F-FDG (Fluorodeoxyglucose) is a radiolabeled glucose analogue used in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) to assess metabolic activity in tissues. It is particularly useful for detecting cancer, and infections, and monitoring neurological disorders due to its ability to highlight areas with high glucose consumption.

Option C: Carbon-11 (C-11) is used for certain types of PET imaging, particularly in neurology and oncology.

Option D: Gallium-68 (Ga-68) is used for imaging certain types of neuroendocrine tumours and somatostatin receptor imaging.
